title: Rent Payment
bodyText: Tenant shall pay Landlord monthly rent of {{monthly_rent}} (Monthly Rent) in advance on the due date specified in this Lease, without demand, deduction, or setoff, except as permitted by applicable law. If the due date falls on a weekend or legal holiday, rent is due on the next business day.

title: Late Fee
bodyText: If Tenant fails to pay Monthly Rent in full within {{late_fee_grace_days}} days after it is due, a late fee of {{late_fee_amount}} will be assessed. Acceptance of a late payment does not waive Landlord's right to require full payment of Rent on the date it is due or to pursue any other remedy available under this Lease.

title: Returned Checks / Dishonored Payments
bodyText: If any payment of Rent is returned for insufficient funds or otherwise fails, Landlord may require that the payment be replaced by a cashier's check, certified check, or money order, and may charge Tenant a fee associated with the failed payment, not to exceed the maximum amount permitted by applicable law. If more than two of Tenant's payments during the Term are returned for insufficient funds, Landlord may require all future payments of Rent be made by cashier's check, certified check, or money order.

No conflict with this clause's generic mechanics; the actual NSF cap lives in Title 6 general banking law (§6-08-16), not landlord-tenant law, and isn't restated here. | KS CHECKED 2026-08-30 (v59 canvass): K.S.A. 60-2610(g) caps the service charge on a dishonored check at $30. This clause's unqualified 'any fee associated with the failed payment' was flagged as a possible conflict, since unlike landlords-access and holdover it carries NO self-limiting 'to the extent permitted by applicable law' language. TAYLOR'S DECISION: leave as is, no KS override. Reasoning: 60-2610(g) caps the charge the drawee/vendor imposes, and under this clause the landlord recovers that charge as a pass-through loss rather than setting its own fee, so the effective ceiling is $30 either way. See edu-nsf-fee-cap-ks. | Also confirmed for KS: no payment-method fee ban (no analog to N.D.C.C. 47-16-20.1); Kansas does not restrict charging for particular payment methods. | MN re-audit 2026-09-03: MN's returned-check fee cap identified (Minn. Stat. §604.113, $30 service charge) — see edu-returned-check-fee-cap-mn. NO CLAUSE EDIT MADE and no MN override created: this clause does not hardcode a dollar figure, so it does not conflict with the cap, matching the disposition WY reached for the same situation. §5a.1 JUDGMENT: the finding is STATE-DRIVEN (each state's bad-check statute differs — WY $30, MN $30, KS/NE/ND/SD各 their own), but requires no shared-clause change because the clause is figure-agnostic. Flagged instead: the clause's phrase 'may charge Tenant any fee associated with the failed payment' is unbounded on its face and could read as authorizing more than the statutory cap in every tagged state. NOT edited here — it is tagged CO;WY;KS;NE;MN;ND and a rewording triggers §5a.1 across six states. Recommend a scoped shared-clause pass. | SHARED-CLAUSE PASS 2026-09-03 (§5a.1). TRIGGER: every one of the six tagged states has a cap and a row recording it (CO nsf-fee-limit-co; WY edu-returned-check-fee-cap-wy; KS edu-nsf-fee-cap-ks; NE edu-bad-check-restitution-vs-nsf-fee-ne; ND edu-returned-check-fee-cap-nd; MN edu-returned-check-fee-cap-mn, $30 under §604.113). The unbounded word 'any' was therefore wrong in all six simultaneously — a clause that promised landlords something no tagged state allows. | SD ADDED 2026-09-07 (SD re-audit, Tier A of the L.2 exhaustive generic-clause audit). SD displayed only 13 LEASE_CLAUSE rows against 60-75 for every other state; 46 generics had no SD tag and no SD override. Triaged per L.2, not bulk-extended. Tier A = boilerplate with no SD statutory interaction, or self-limiting text that defers to applicable law. S5a.1 JUDGMENT: adding a state tag changes `states` only - no bodyText, rule_type or content_type change - so no other tagged state's rendering is affected and NO propagation to other state logs is owed. State-driven, not uniform. Self-limiting - 'not to exceed the maximum amount permitted by applicable law' - so it survived the 57A-3-421 amendment from $40 to $60 without carrying a hardcoded figure. The clause that deferred held; the education row that hardcoded broke. | OH: no statutory cap. §1319.16's $30-or-10% ceiling binds a COLLECTION AGENCY (§1319.12(A)(2) excludes a landlord collecting its own account) and does not apply. title: Amounts Due Upfront
bodyText: Tenant will pay Landlord the following amounts, at the time specified for each: [specify what is due and when here, e.g. first month's Monthly Rent ({{monthly_rent}}) due at signing; Security Deposit ({{security_deposit}}) due at signing; Pet Deposit ({{pet_deposit}}) due at signing; last month's Monthly Rent due on the Start Date]. title: Application of Payments
bodyText: Each payment Tenant makes will be applied first to the Monthly Rent due for the current or oldest unpaid rental period, and only then to any other fees, charges, or amounts due under this Lease, unless Tenant directs otherwise in writing for a particular payment or applicable law requires otherwise. Nothing in this provision limits any statutory right Tenant may have to cure nonpayment of Rent.

title: Late Fee Limit
bodyText: Any late fee assessed under this Lease will not exceed the greater of $50.00 or 5% of the amount of Rent past due, and no late fee will be assessed until at least 7 days after Rent is due, as required by Colorado law. title: Late Fee Guidance
bodyText: Landlord and Tenant agree that if Tenant fails to pay rent when due, the actual damage to Landlord from that late payment would, from the nature of the case, be impracticable or extremely difficult to fix. Landlord and Tenant therefore agree that {{late_fee}} shall be presumed to be the amount of damage sustained by Landlord from a late payment of rent. This amount is a presumed measure of Landlord's actual damages and is not a penalty.
notes: CA: REWRITTEN 2026-09-19 against Civ. Code s1671 (primary text supplied by Taylor). CONFIRMED STANDARD INVERSION - the prior dormant row recited the s1671(b) test ('a reasonable estimate of Landlord's actual damages'), which is the wrong test for a residential lease. s1671(c)(2) routes a lease of real property for use as a dwelling to subdivision (d), NOT (b). Under s1671(d) a liquidated-damages provision is VOID, except that the parties may agree on an amount presumed to be the damage 'when, from the nature of the case, it would be impracticable or extremely difficult to fix the actual damage.' Two consequences the old text got backwards: (1) the default is voidness, not validity; (2) the burden flips - under (b) the party attacking the clause must prove it unreasonable, while under (d) the landlord must bring the clause within the exception. The new body text is drafted to track (d)'s exception language rather than the (b) standard. s1671(a) yields to any other statute expressly prescribing a liquidated-damages rule for the contract - none found for residential late fees in the sections read, but note s1950.5 expressly governs security, so deposit-forfeiture provisions route there and not through s1671. NOT CONFIRMED: the old row's assertion that 'California does not set a statutory cap on late fees' is consistent with everything read this pass but is NOT a full-chapter proof-of-absence - no dedicated late-fee cap search was run. Do not upgrade that limb to CITED without one. Also unread: Orozco v. Casimiro and Del Monte Properties v. Dolan are the cases usually cited for applying s1671(d) to residential late fees; both are pointers only, neither has been read. EXTEND SCREEN 2026-09-19: now supersedes the base row `late-fee`, which is blocked for CA. s1951.5 RESOLVED 2026-09-19 (primary text supplied): it reads in its entirety 'Section 1671, relating to liquidated damages, applies to a lease of real property.' CONFIRMATORY, NOT CORRECTIVE, as predicted - s1671(c)(2) already reached a lease of real property for use as a dwelling on its own terms, and s1951.5 removes any argument that s1671 is confined to contracts for goods and services. No change to this row's analysis; the earlier flag is cleared. MILITARY TENANTS, added 2026-09-19: Mil. & Vet. Code s403(b) - no fine or penalty accrues during a court stay of an action to enforce the lease, and a court may relieve a service member from a late fee incurred while in service if military service materially impaired their ability to pay. Applies during service and within 120 days after. See edu-military-default-judgment-ca. || OPEN ITEM CLOSED 2026-09-28, gap-discovery source 4 (outside-title search). This row's notes said the 'California does not set a statutory cap on late fees' limb was NOT a proof of absence and must not be upgraded without a dedicated late-fee cap search. That search has now been run on the official leginfo code full-text search: 'late fee' in the Civil Code returns 13 sections and 'late charge' 23. Reviewed by section and title, the hits are common interest development assessments (ss5650, 5655, 5658, 5665, 5685, 5720, 6808, 6812), mortgage and deed-of-trust late charges (ss2954.4, 2954.5), retail installment and consumer credit (ss1812.402, 1812.626, 1812.643, 1799.91), debt collection (s1788.102), s3273.23, and the WATER SUBMETER sections. NO general cap on residential rent late fees exists, so the s1671(d) analysis in this row is the whole of the law on the amount. ONE REAL EXCEPTION, and it is new to the library: Civ. Code s1954.213 caps late fees on SUBMETERED WATER bills at $7 on the first bill and $10 on each subsequent bill, with all late fees in any 12-month period limited to 10 percent of the unpaid amount, and bars any late fee until 25 days after the bill is sent. Water charges are not rent (s1954.213(d)), so that cap does not touch a rent late fee - but a landlord who submeters has two different late-fee regimes running at once. See edu-water-submeter-billing-ca. SCOPE of the search: statutes only, exact phrases and the two word forms run; regulations, local ordinances and case law were not searched, and Orozco v. Casimiro and Del Monte Properties v. Dolan remain unread.

title: NSF Fee Limit
bodyText: If Tenant pays rent or any other amount due under this Lease by check, draft or order for payment and it is not honored for lack of funds, because Tenant has no account with the drawee, or because Tenant stops payment, Tenant shall be liable to Landlord for the amount of the payment and a service charge of {{nsf_fee}}, not to exceed $25 for the first such instrument and $35 for each subsequent one. No service charge is owed if Tenant stopped payment to resolve a good faith dispute with Landlord, if Tenant provides written confirmation from Tenant's financial institution that the instrument was returned due to an error by that institution, or if Tenant provides written confirmation that the account had insufficient funds because of a delay in a regularly scheduled direct deposit of a social security or government benefit assistance payment.
notes: CA: REWRITTEN 2026-09-19 against Civ. Code s1719(a) (primary text supplied by Taylor). Figures CONFIRMED - $25 first, $35 each subsequent 'to that payee' - but the prior dormant row carried three defects. (1) FRAMING: it said the cap applies 'as required by California law'. s1719(a)(1) is a statutory ENTITLEMENT capped at those amounts, not a requirement to charge. Third CA row found reciting a landlord option as a legal mandate, after month-to-month-notice-ca and the CO entry-notice precedent. (2) INSTRUMENT SCOPE - the substantive defect. The old row capped the fee for any 'dishonored or returned payment'. s1719(a)(6) defines the trigger as making, uttering, drawing or delivering a CHECK, DRAFT OR ORDER for the payment of money upon a bank or depository that refuses to honor it. A returned ACH debit or a declined card is not obviously an instrument drawn by the tenant, so s1719 may not reach electronic payment methods at all. That cuts both ways: the old row asserted a statutory safe harbour over payment types the statute may not cover, and for those types a returned-payment fee in a residential lease is an ordinary liquidated-damages provision governed by s1671(d) - VOID unless actual damages were impracticable or extremely difficult to fix. See late-fee-safe-harbor-ca; the two rows are now linked by that analysis. Clause scoped to checks, drafts and orders accordingly. (3) OMITTED EXCEPTIONS: s1719(a)(3) good-faith-dispute stop payment, where the payee recovers only on CLEAR AND CONVINCING evidence that no good faith dispute existed; (a)(4) written confirmation of financial institution error; (a)(5) written confirmation that the shortfall came from a delayed direct deposit of SOCIAL SECURITY OR GOVERNMENT BENEFIT ASSISTANCE. A flat fee clause misstates the law against benefit recipients in particular. All three now in body text. Note s1719(a)(6)(C): a STOP PAYMENT counts as passing a check on insufficient funds, subject to the good-faith-dispute carve-out. CROSS-CHAPTER: s1719 sits in Part 3, Obligations Imposed by Law - outside the landlord-tenant title. Instruction 7 pattern, fourth confirmation in CA. EXTEND SCREEN 2026-09-19: now supersedes the base row `returned-payments`, which is blocked for CA. s1719 NOW READ IN FULL 2026-09-19 - three additions. (1) TREBLE DAMAGES, s1719(a)(2): after a written demand by CERTIFIED MAIL stating the section's provisions, the check amount and the service charge, the drawer has 30 DAYS to pay; failing that, liability becomes the unpaid check amount PLUS TREBLE that amount, not less than $100 nor more than $1,500, in place of the service charge. (2) EXCEPTIONS to the service charge: a STOP PAYMENT in a good-faith dispute (payee must prove no good-faith dispute by clear and convincing evidence, s1719(a)(3), (b)); written confirmation of BANK ERROR (a)(4); and a delayed SOCIAL SECURITY or government benefit deposit (a)(5). For a stop payment, the demand must be in the prescribed s1719(c) form, sent certified with a receipt in evidence (d), and the payee must show a reasonable effort to reconcile before suing (e). s1719(j)(2): liability arises only ONCE per check. (3) NO POSTDATED-CHECK EXCLUSION anywhere in s1719 - candidate 427.4's North Dakota trap does not exist here. The ACH/card scope caveat stands: every limb is framed around a 'check, draft, or order'.

title: Returned Payments
bodyText: If any payment Tenant makes under this Lease by check, draft, order of payment, debit card order, or electronic funds transfer is refused by the drawee because of lack of funds, lack of credit, or lack of an account, or if Tenant stops payment on it with intent to defraud, Tenant will pay Landlord the bank fees Landlord actually incurred in tendering the payment, plus a service charge of $25 if the face value does not exceed $50, $30 if the face value exceeds $50 but does not exceed $300, or $40 if the face value exceeds $300, or 5 percent of the face value, whichever is greater. Landlord may require that the payment be replaced by a cashier's check, certified check, or money order. If more than two of Tenant's payments during the Term are returned, Landlord may require all future payments of Rent to be made by cashier's check, certified check, or money order. This Section does not limit any other remedy Florida law gives Landlord for a dishonored payment.
notes: FL: DORMANT ROW REWRITTEN AND ACTIVATED 2026-09-26 (instruction 21). Primary text pasted by Taylor 2026-09-26 from flsenate.gov/Laws/Statutes/2026 (official 2026 Florida Statutes), read section-open with history lines. Supersedes returned-payments (base not tagged FL: the rewritten row states the measure the base's 'maximum amount permitted by applicable law' points to, and both cannot display). Controlling text: Fla. Stat. §68.065(2) (s. 1, ch. 2013-113 latest): 'In lieu of a service charge authorized under subsection (3), s. 832.062(4)(a), or s. 832.07, the payee ... may lawfully collect bank fees actually incurred ... plus a service charge of $25 ... $30 ... $40 ...; or 5 percent of the face value ..., whichever is greater.' What the pre-rigor row got right: the $25/$30/$40 tiers and the $50/$300 break points. What it got wrong: (1) the 5% alternative applies at EVERY tier, not only above $300; (2) actual bank fees are recoverable IN ADDITION; (3) the statute covers drafts, orders of payment, debit card orders and electronic funds transfers, not only checks (§68.065(1)); (4) it reaches stop-payments only with intent to defraud. The tiers also appear in §832.08(5), the state attorney's diversion-fee schedule, which is not a landlord cap. Additional remedy: after a 30-day written demand in the §68.065(4) form, treble damages (minimum $50) plus costs and fees in a civil action (§68.065(3)); hardship waiver (7) (edu-dishonored-payment-remedies-fl). The charge is not designated rent (library default), so it cannot be demanded in a §83.56(3) 3-day notice as rent. Replacement-method sentences carried from the base; no Florida payment-method statute in Part II (acceptable-payment-methods tagged FL).

title: Use of Security Deposit
bodyText: Tenant shall pay Landlord a security deposit of {{security_deposit}} (Security Deposit) prior to occupancy. Landlord may apply the Security Deposit to remedy a Tenant default under this Lease, including past due Rent, and to repair damage to the property caused by Tenant or Tenant's guests beyond ordinary wear and tear. Landlord will not apply the Security Deposit to normal wear and tear or to any damage or defective condition that preexisted the tenancy. Landlord may apply the Security Deposit to cleaning costs only if the property is substantially less clean at the end of the Term than it was at the start of the Term. The Security Deposit will not relieve Tenant of any obligation to pay Rent due under this Lease prior to its termination.

Stat. §76-1416(2) permits applying the deposit 'to the payment of rent and the amount of damages which the landlord has suffered by reason of the tenant's noncompliance with the rental agreement or section 76-1421' — substantively the same rent-plus-damages-beyond-wear-and-tear framing this clause already uses. No last-month's-rent restriction like Kansas's, so no override needed. Not extended to WY in this pass — WY currently has no clause of this type at all (security-deposit-use-wy doesn't exist), a separate, pre-existing gap noticed while resolving this, not fixed here since it's outside this session's Nebraska-specific scope. | MN extended (Minnesota session, whole-library audit): matches Minn. No conflict. | ND extended (North Dakota session 1, statute walk): N.D.C.C. § 47-16-07.1(3) permits application to pet/negligence damage, unpaid rent, and cleaning/repair costs necessary to restore the property, reasonable wear and tear excepted — compatible with this clause's existing self-limiting language. No ND-specific override needed. | SD extended (South Dakota session 1, whole-library generic-clause audit): SDCL 43-32-6.1's deposit-application concept (deposit secures performance of the rental agreement) is compatible with the generic's existing self-limiting language (default/damage beyond wear-and-tear, not preexisting conditions); no SD-specific override needed for the use/application language itself. Return mechanics are SD-specific and handled separately by security-deposit-return-sd. | WY ADDED 2026-08-28 (deposit split, Taylor's decision): WY previously folded application language into security-deposit-return-wy. Split to the CO pattern. Compatible with Wyo. Stat. 1-21-1208(a). TWO DELIBERATE GIVEAWAYS accepted: (1) cleaning deductions only if 'substantially less clean', vs 1208(a)'s 'clean to the condition at start'; (2) 1208(a)'s catch-all 'any other costs this Lease provides for' not carried over. Both more tenant-favorable than WY requires. | NV: Read in full 2026-09-24 against NRS 118A (revisor text Rev. 4/15/2026, 2025 session incorporated). Stat. §83.49 does not bar applying the deposit during the tenancy (contrast NJ 46:8-21.1); §83.43(14) defines security deposits as money held 'as security for the performance of the rental agreement'. Return mechanics sit in security-deposit-return-fl (instruction 24 family). A pet deposit is 'deposit money' (§83.43(4)). s5a.1: states-only change, no propagation owed. | AZ: Applies as written. This clause is narrower (no wear and tear, cleaning only if substantially less clean), which is a landlord choice, not a conflict. §33-1310(15): a reasonable charge for redecorating or cleaning is not "security". title: Security Deposit: Holding, Notice and Interest
bodyText: Landlord will hold the Security Deposit in trust for Tenant and will not mingle it with Landlord's own property. Landlord will deposit or invest it in an interest-bearing account or fund of the kind New Jersey law requires, located in New Jersey. Within 30 days after receiving the Security Deposit, Landlord will notify Tenant in writing of the name and address of the institution or fund holding it, the type of account, the current interest rate, and the amount deposited. Landlord will give the same notice within 30 days after moving the deposit to another institution, fund or account, within 30 days after any transfer of ownership or control of the property, and with each annual interest payment. The interest earned belongs to Tenant and will be paid to Tenant in cash each year, or credited toward Rent due on the renewal or anniversary of this Lease or, if Landlord has given Tenant written notice, on January 31 of each year. If Landlord fails to hold the deposit, give a required notice, or pay interest as described here, Tenant may give Landlord written notice to apply the Security Deposit, plus interest at 7 percent per year, toward Rent due, after which Landlord may not demand a further security deposit; for a missed annual payment or annual notice alone, Tenant must first give written notice and allow Landlord 30 days to comply.

Pre-rigor row had the topic and 'annual interest' right; it missed: (1) the 30-day written notice with institution, account type, rate and amount, repeated on transfer, account change and each annual payment (46:8-19(c)); (2) the account-type split - 10+ units: insured NJ money-market fund or variable-rate NJ bank account (46:8-19(a)); fewer than 10 units: interest-bearing NJ bank account at the time/savings rate (46:8-19(b)); (3) cash payment or rent credit on anniversary/renewal or Jan 31 by election; (4) the tenant's 7%-interest rent-offset remedy and permanent loss of further deposits, with a 30-day cure only for annual-payment/notice failures; (5) scope: the Act excludes owner-occupied premises with not more than two rental units unless the tenant gives 30 days' written notice invoking it (46:8-26) - builder should suppress this row for that case only if no invocation notice; (6) seasonal (<=125 days) rentals exempt from the investment requirement (46:8-19(d)). title: Security Deposit Interest
bodyText: If the Security Deposit exceeds fifty dollars or one month's Rent, whichever is greater, the portion of the Security Deposit in excess of that amount will bear interest at the rate of five per cent per annum for any period during which Tenant remains in possession of the property for six months or more. Landlord will compute and pay that interest to Tenant annually. No interest is owed on the portion of the Security Deposit at or below fifty dollars or one month's Rent, whichever is greater.

title: Tenant Maintenance & Cleanliness
bodyText: Tenant will keep and maintain the property in a clean, safe, and sanitary condition, and will regularly dispose of garbage and waste in a clean and safe manner. Tenant will use all appliances, fixtures, and equipment in a safe and reasonable manner consistent with their intended purpose, will not obstruct access to doors and windows, and will maintain the property in the same condition as it was delivered to Tenant, except for ordinary wear and tear and any condition that applicable law requires Landlord to repair or remedy.

title: Repair Notices: Tenant's 7-Day Remedies
bodyText: Florida does not set a deadline for starting repairs. Instead, a tenant's remedies start with a written notice. If Landlord materially fails to comply with the building, housing and health codes (or, where there are none, the structural and plumbing duties in Fla. Stat. §83.51(1)) or with material lease provisions, the tenant may deliver written notice specifying the problem and stating that the tenant intends to terminate. If Landlord has not complied within 7 days after delivery, the tenant may terminate the lease. A tenant may instead give written notice specifying the problem and stating that the tenant intends to withhold rent; 7 days after delivery, the tenant may raise the material noncompliance as a complete defense to an eviction for nonpayment, and the court decides how much the rent is reduced for the lost value. This notice may go to Landlord, the person designated to receive notices, a resident manager, or whoever collects the rent. If the failure is due to causes beyond Landlord's control and Landlord keeps making every reasonable effort to fix it, the lease may be ended or altered: a tenant who vacates an untenantable unit owes no rent while it stays uninhabitable, and a tenant who stays in a unit that is not untenantable gets a proportional rent reduction. Failures of the additional duties for apartment buildings and similar units (pest extermination, locks and keys, common areas, garbage removal, heat, running water and hot water, Fla. Stat. §83.51(2)) cannot be raised as a defense to an eviction for possession.

Primary text read section-open 2026-09-26 from the official 2026 Florida Statutes (flsenate.gov / leg.state.fl.us), with per-section history lines. What the pre-rigor row got right: the 7-day written-notice period. What it got wrong: Florida imposes no duty to 'begin remedial action within 7 days'; the 7 days is the cure window after which TENANT remedies open, and it covers only §83.51(1) (codes or, absent codes, structural components and plumbing) and material lease provisions, not a health-or-safety test. Controlling text: Fla. Stat. §83.56(1)(a)-(b) (termination; beyond-control rules; last amended s. 2, ch. 2026-143, which amended (2)(a)); §83.60(1)(a)-(b) (withholding defense; notice recipients; s. 12, ch. 2013-136); §83.51(2)(c) (noncompliance with (2) is not a defense to possession); §83.60(2) (tenant raising any defense other than payment must deposit accrued rent into the court registry). title: Repair Notices: Tenant's Remedies and Deadlines
bodyText: Arizona law does not set a deadline for a landlord to begin repairs. The day counts come from the tenant's remedies. If the landlord materially fails to comply with the lease, the tenant may give written notice that the lease will end on a date at least 10 days after the landlord receives it unless the breach is remedied within 10 days. If the landlord's failure to maintain the property materially affects health and safety, the period is 5 days. If the landlord remedies the breach in time, the lease does not end, and the tenant cannot terminate over a condition the tenant, a family member or a guest caused. For a repair costing less than $300 or half the monthly rent, whichever is greater, the tenant may give written notice and, if the landlord does not comply within 10 days (or as promptly as an emergency requires), have a licensed contractor do the work and deduct the actual and reasonable cost from rent after giving the landlord an itemized statement and a lien waiver. If the landlord deliberately or negligently fails to supply running water, gas or electric service, hot water, heat, air-conditioning or cooling where installed, or other essential services, the tenant may give reasonable notice and then buy the service and deduct its cost from rent, recover damages for the reduced rental value, or move to substitute housing and stop paying rent for that period (with limited recovery of any extra cost). The tenant may also recover damages and obtain a court order for the landlord's noncompliance, and in an eviction for nonpayment may counterclaim, in which case the court may order rent paid into court.

WRONG: Arizona imposes no duty to BEGIN remedial action by any deadline; 5 and 10 days are the tenant's termination-notice cure windows (A.R.S. §33-1361(A)), and 10 days is also the repair-and-deduct window (§33-1363(A)). 'As required by Arizona law' was false. Pattern holds (one real fact, operative rule missed). title: Repairs — Tenant's Statutory Remedies
bodyText:
[This entire Section must be printed in bold or underlined type. Tex. Prop. Code §92.056(g).]
REPAIRS AND TENANT'S STATUTORY REMEDIES. If Landlord fails to repair or remedy a condition that materially affects the physical health or safety of an ordinary tenant, Tenant may have remedies under Sections 92.056 and 92.0561 of the Texas Property Code. In general, Tenant must give notice of the condition to the person to whom, or at the place where, Rent is normally paid, and must not be delinquent in Rent when any required notice is given. Unless Tenant sends the first notice by certified mail, return receipt requested, by registered mail, or by another form of mail that allows tracking of delivery by the United States Postal Service or a private delivery service, Tenant must give Landlord a subsequent written notice after Landlord has had a reasonable time to repair. Seven days is presumed to be a reasonable time to repair; that presumption may be rebutted based on the date Landlord received the notice, the severity and nature of the condition, and the reasonable availability of materials, labor, and utilities. If Landlord is liable under Section 92.056, Tenant may: (1) terminate this Lease; (2) have the condition repaired or remedied and deduct the cost from Rent as provided by Section 92.0561; and (3) obtain judicial remedies under Section 92.0563. Repair and deduct is available only under the conditions in Section 92.0561, which include limits on the amount that may be deducted (in any one month, not more than one month's Rent or $500, whichever is greater), a requirement that the repair be made by an independent contractor or repairman who is licensed where the city requires it and in compliance with building codes, and a requirement that Tenant give Landlord a copy of the repair bill and receipt with the balance of the Rent.

title: Repair Timeline
bodyText: For a condition affecting an essential service (such as heat, water, electricity, or plumbing), Landlord will remedy the condition within 7 days of receiving notice from Tenant, or Tenant may terminate this Lease. For any other condition Landlord is responsible to repair under this Lease, Landlord will remedy it within 30 days. If the loss of an essential service poses an imminent and serious threat to Tenant's health or safety, Tenant may terminate this Lease on 48 hours' written notice if Landlord does not remedy it, as required by Oregon law.

title: Possession Delay
bodyText: If Landlord is unable to deliver possession of the property to Tenant by the Start Date, through no fault of Landlord, this Lease will remain in full force, but Tenant will not be obligated to pay Monthly Rent for the period Tenant is unable to take possession. If Landlord has not delivered possession within 30 days after the Start Date, Tenant may terminate this Lease by written notice to Landlord, in which case all amounts paid to Landlord by Tenant will be returned and both parties will be released from further obligation under this Lease.
notes: CO added - verified this session (statute walk + full-library audit; content itself unchanged WY added 2026-08-21 (full-library cross-check pass): generic mechanics, no CO-specific statutory language or number, confirmed no conflict with WY findings from this project. | MN extended (Minnesota session, CO;WY-scoping resolution): no general MN statute found conflicting with this clause's 30-day/proportional-rent-relief mechanic for ordinary failure-to-deliver-possession situations. NOTE: Minnesota does have its own narrower statute, § 504B.153, but it applies specifically to NEW CONSTRUCTION delays with a different remedy structure — that's a distinct, more specific scenario not covered by this generic clause. FLAG FOR FUTURE SESSION: consider a dedicated `possession-delay-mn` (or a conditional new-construction rider) if Steinoak wants to capture § 504B.153's specific new-construction remedy; not urgent since the generic clause doesn't conflict with it, just doesn't duplicate it. | ND extended (North Dakota session 1, same scoping review): North Dakota has no statute addressing failure to deliver possession at all (confirmed absent this session) -- no conflict, cleaner than Minnesota's case which had a narrow new-construction-specific statute to work around. | SD extended (South Dakota session 1, Title 21-16 review): SDCL 43-32-19(1) gives tenant a termination right for landlord's failure to deliver possession/repair after reasonable written request, but doesn't dictate specific lease mechanics while the tenant awaits delivery; the generic's self-limiting language is compatible. | PASS 2 CLARIFICATION (South Dakota): SDCL 43-32-19(1) gives the tenant a termination right if Landlord fails to deliver possession within a 'reasonable time after written request' - an open standard, not a fixed number of days. title: Default by Tenant
bodyText: Tenant will be in default under this Lease if Tenant fails to pay Rent when due and does not cure the failure within the time period specified by applicable law after receiving written notice from Landlord. Tenant will also be in default if Tenant fails to comply with any other obligation under this Lease and does not cure the failure after receiving written notice, except where applicable law permits Landlord to proceed without giving Tenant an opportunity to cure. Except as required by applicable law, Tenant's failure to pay an assessed late fee, apart from the underlying Rent itself, will not by itself entitle Landlord to terminate this Lease or pursue eviction. If Tenant is in default, Landlord may exercise all rights and remedies available under applicable law, including terminating this Lease, regaining possession of the property, and recovering unpaid Rent, late fees, and reasonable costs and expenses, less amounts obtained from the Security Deposit. Landlord will use reasonable efforts to mitigate damages resulting from Tenant's default to the extent required by applicable law. To the extent permitted under applicable law, the prevailing party may recover from the other party court costs and reasonable attorneys' fees and expenses incurred in connection with any legal proceedings related to this Lease.
notes: CO added - verified this session (statute walk + full-library audit; content itself EDITED this session | CORRECTED 2026-08-20 (caught by Claude CLI review): added explicit carve-out that an unpaid late fee alone cannot trigger termination/eviction, consistent with CO law that a late fee is distinct from rent and cannot be grounds for eviction on its own. WY added 2026-08-21 (full-library cross-check pass): generic mechanics, no CO-specific statutory language or number, confirmed no conflict with WY findings from this project. | MN extended (Minnesota session, CO;WY-scoping resolution): cure-period language defers to 'applicable law' rather than hardcoding a number, so it doesn't shorten any MN statutory cure right (MN has no general statutory cure period for lease violations, confirmed absent this session). Fee-shifting sentence is already mutual ('prevailing party') — compatible with MN's automatic-mutuality rule (§504B.172), no conflict. | Cross-state plain-language cleanup (Minnesota session, follow-up to MN's plain-language audit): long compound sentence split into shorter ones, no substantive change. Not a legal requirement for this clause's other tagged states (only MN's Plain Language Contract Act, Minn. Stat. §325G.31, was confirmed to apply this project) — done as a general readability improvement since the pattern was found library-wide, not MN-specific. | ND extended (North Dakota session 1, CO;WY-maintenance-scoping review resolved by reading the full CO and MN decision logs directly): defers to 'applicable law' for cure timing, no ND-specific conflict. Fee-shifting language ('prevailing party') matches N.D.C.C. § 47-16-13.6 exactly, which awards attorney's fees 'to the prevailing party' -- mutual, not one-way. This resolves ND's piece of the standing fee-shifting-mutuality question (though the broader cross-state consolidation across CO/WY/KS/NE/MN remains a separate open item). | 5a.1 RETROACTIVE CLASSIFICATION 2026-08-28: the prevailing-party attorney-fee rewrite here was STATE-DRIVEN (forced by C.R.S. 38-12-801(3)(a)(II)), not uniform, and was inherited by WY/MN/ND/SD without classification - the exact failure mode 5a.1 exists to prevent. Checked for WY 2026-08-28: WY has NO reciprocity statute (see edu-no-fee-reciprocity-wy), so a landlord-only clause would be enforceable there and the mutual language is a voluntary giveaway. Taylor's decision 2026-08-28: KEEP mutual language for WY. MN, ND, and SD remain unclassified for this edit. | CROSS-STATE FEE-SHIFTING CONSOLIDATION COMPLETED 2026-09-06 (ND re-audit). The standing open item -- 'is this clause's fee language genuinely mutual, and does it work in every tagged state?' -- is resolved. Operative sentence: 'To the extent permitted under applicable law, the prevailing party may recover from the other party court costs and reasonable attorneys' fees and expenses incurred in connection with any legal proceedings related to this Lease.' FIVE DISTINCT STATE ARCHITECTURES, not one question: (1) CO -- a landlord-only fee clause is VOID and the lease must be drafted mutual; 'prevailing party' SATISFIES this. (2) MN -- fee clauses are made mutual BY OPERATION OF LAW regardless of lease text; consistent, no conflict. (3) KS (K.S.A. 58-2547) and NE (§ 76-1415(1)(c)) -- attorney-fee clauses are BANNED OUTRIGHT in either direction; this clause is correctly NOT tagged to either, and a library-wide check confirmed ZERO LEASE_CLAUSE rows tagged KS or NE contain attorney-fee language. (4) ND -- § 47-16-13.6 awards fees to 'the prevailing party' by statute; clause language matches exactly. (5) WY -- American Rule, no reciprocity statute, contract governs. OPEN FLAG FOR WYOMING, surfaced not resolved: per edu-no-fee-reciprocity-wy the Wyoming Supreme Court requires a contract to 'unequivocally provide' for fee recovery before fees may be awarded. This clause hedges twice -- 'TO THE EXTENT PERMITTED UNDER APPLICABLE LAW' makes the entitlement conditional on an external referent, and 'MAY recover' is permissive rather than mandatory. Under a strict unequivocal-provision standard that phrasing may not suffice, which would leave a WY landlord with NO fee recovery in a state whose default is that each side bears its own. No Wyoming case applying the standard to comparable hedged language was located, and no edit is made on that basis -- flagged for Taylor. Note the hedge exists for a reason: it is what makes the clause safe to share with CO and MN. Any WY fix should be a WY-specific override, NOT an edit to the shared text. | WYOMING FLAG RETRACTED 2026-09-06 after reading the actual case law rather than this library's characterisation of it. NO WY-SPECIFIC OVERRIDE IS NEEDED. The Wyoming standard is EXPRESS CONTRACTUAL AUTHORISATION, not a heightened magic-words test: Cowardin v. Finnerty (Wyo. 1999) -- 'absent statutory or contract language expressly authorizing recovery of attorney fees, parties are responsible for payment of their own attorney fees'; Emken, 2006 WY 112, ¶ 8 -- 'a prevailing party may be reimbursed for its attorney fees when express statutory or contractual authorization exists'; Thorkildsen v. Belden, 2012 WY 8; Circle Resources v. Hassler, 2023 WY 22, ¶ 8 -- 'A prevailing party may, however, be reimbursed for attorneys' fees when provided for by contract or statute.' The Wyoming failure cases are ones where the contract said NOTHING about fees. Cowardin is explicit: 'Given the absence of any reference to attorney fees in the purchase agreement, Sellers were not entitled to recover attorney fees.' THIS CLAUSE EXPRESSLY REFERS TO ATTORNEY FEES, NAMES THE PREVAILING PARTY, AND USES THE COURT'S OWN FORMULATION. The supposed defect -- 'may recover' being permissive -- is the verb the Wyoming Supreme Court itself uses in stating the rule. 'To the extent permitted under applicable law' is a savings clause; no Wyoming authority was located suggesting a savings clause defeats otherwise-express authorisation, and the circularity concern raised earlier in this session was speculative. PROCESS NOTE: the flag originated from this library's own edu-no-fee-reciprocity-wy row, which characterises the standard as requiring a contract to 'unequivocally provide' for fees. The cases say 'expressly authorizing' / 'express... authorization'. Raising a structural change to a four-state shared clause on a secondary characterisation, without reading the cases, was the Addendum L.5 failure committed in the same session that wrote L.5. CA: extended to California 2026-09-19 after re-screen against the full CA pass (the extend manifest had deferred tagging until the blocked set was resolved, and the step was then missed). No CA conflict found. | NV: Read in full 2026-09-24 against NRS 118A (revisor text Rev. 4/15/2026, 2025 session incorporated). Applies as written: promises a cure opportunity for every non-rent breach, more generous than 118A.430 (5 days for remediable breach; none for a breach that cannot be remedied) - lawful. Prevailing-party fee sentence is the form 118A.220(1)(c) permits. PROVISIONAL pending NRS Ch. 40 read. | NV (text batch 2, 2026-09-24): PROVISIONAL CLEARED. NRS 40.2516: 5-day perform-or-quit, lease saved by performing within 5 days, no notice if the breach cannot be cured; NRS 40.2514: 3-day notice to surrender with NO cure for unauthorized assignment/sublet, waste, unlawful business, nuisance, or controlled-substance violations (other than simple possession). The clause promises a cure for every non-rent breach - more than NV requires for 40.2514 grounds; lawful, but a product choice worth knowing. NRS 40.252: a landlord may not shorten statutory notice periods by contract - the clause defers to law, so no conflict. | TX: Read in full 2026-09-25 against Tex. Prop. Code chs. 24, 54, 91, 92 and 301 (official statutes.capitol.texas.gov text for chs. 24/54/91/301). Applies as written. Tex. Prop. Code s24.005(a) as amended by S.B. 38 (89th Leg., R.S., eff. Jan. 1, 2026): 3 days' written notice to vacate unless the lease sets a shorter or longer period; for a tenant NOT previously late before the month of the notice, a nonpayment notice must be a NOTICE TO PAY RENT OR VACATE - so 'the time period specified by applicable law' for a rent cure has a Texas referent. Cure for non-rent defaults is voluntary (Texas requires none). Prevailing-party fee sentence matches s24.006(b)-(c): a lease fee clause entitles the prevailing landlord AND makes fees reciprocal for a prevailing tenant. Mitigation sentence: s91.006. Base chosen over -ks-ne because it carries the fee sentence. | NJ: 2026-09-26 tag REMOVED same session (research pass): its attorney-fee sentence triggers N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.66/-61.67 (implied reciprocal tenant fee covenant; mandatory bold reciprocity sentence in any lease fee clause). NJ override default-by-tenant-nj pending primary text of 2A:18-61.66/-61.67. s5a.1: states-only change. | CURE CARVE-OUT ADDED 2026-09-26 (Taylor's decision, targeted fix at the FL sync; checklist instruction 33): the non-rent cure promise now ends 'except where applicable law permits Landlord to proceed without giving Tenant an opportunity to cure.' Before, promising a cure for every breach could contractually give up a state's no-cure termination grounds (the logs record such grounds for at least NV §40.2514, ND ch. 47-32, MN §504B.171, CA CCP §1161(4) and NE). UNIFORM: self-limiting, adds no landlord right where no such law exists. Propagation notes appended to every tagged state's log. | AZ: Applies as written, instruction 33 checked. Rent: A.R.S. §33-1368(B), 5 days after written notice. Non-rent: 10-day cure notice, or 5 days for a §33-1341 breach materially affecting health and safety (§33-1368(A)). No-cure grounds the carve-out ("except where applicable law permits Landlord to proceed without giving Tenant an opportunity to cure") must and does cover: (1) immediate termination for a material and irreparable breach on the premises (§33-1368(A), trial within 3 days under §33-1377(E)); (2) a second noncompliance of the same or similar nature, 10 days after a notice with no cure; (3) material falsification of criminal record, eviction record or current criminal activity on the application ("not curable"). Attorney fees: §33-1315(A)(2) allows only a prevailing-party clause in writing, which is what this row has; §33-1368(C) lets the landlord recover reasonable fees anyway. Mitigation: §§33-1305(A), 33-1370(C). Late-fee sentence: Arizona reinstatement before filing requires past-due rent plus a reasonable late fee set forth in a written lease (§33-1368(B)); the row's promise not to evict over a late fee alone is the library default (NJ decision), recorded as a judgment call in AZ log s6. s5a.1: states-only change, no propagation owed.

title: Surrender at End of Term
bodyText: Upon the expiration or earlier termination of this Lease, Tenant will surrender possession of the property and return all keys to Landlord immediately. The property will be left in the same condition as at the start of the Term, except for ordinary wear and tear, and free of all personal property of Tenant and any occupants. Personal property left at the property after Tenant vacates may, to the extent permitted by applicable law, be treated as abandoned and disposed of at Tenant's cost.
notes: CO added - verified this session (statute walk + full-library audit; content itself unchanged WY added 2026-08-21 (full-library cross-check pass): generic mechanics, no CO-specific statutory language or number, confirmed no conflict with WY findings from this project. | SD extended (South Dakota session 1, Title 21-16 review): no SD-specific surrender/move-out statute found beyond the security-deposit-return mechanics (handled separately by security-deposit-return-sd); generic mechanics compatible as-is. | OH: Ohio has NO abandoned-property disposal procedure for conventional tenancies (§§1923.12-.14 are manufactured-home-park only) and §5321.15(B) bars seizing a tenant's possessions for rent except by court order. Any disposal language must be reviewed before OH ships. CA: extended to California 2026-09-19 after re-screen against the full CA pass (the extend manifest had deferred tagging until the blocked set was resolved, and the step was then missed). The 'to the extent permitted by applicable law' hedge is doing real work in CA: disposal must follow Civ. Code ss1980-1991 to keep the s1989 liability shield, removing belongings outside that procedure is barred by s789.3(b)(3), no storage cost may be charged if reclaimed within two days (s1990(c)), and service members' property needs a court order (Mil. & Vet. s409.1(b)). See edu-abandoned-property-ca. | NV: Read in full 2026-09-24 against NRS 118A (revisor text Rev. 4/15/2026, 2025 session incorporated). Applies as written on its hedge; NV disposal mechanics (118A.460) in abandoned-property-nv. Base chosen over -mn-nd/-ks-ne, which cross-reference sections that do not exist in an NV lease. | TX: Read in full 2026-09-25 against Tex. Prop. Code chs. 24, 54, 91, 92 and 301 (official statutes.capitol.texas.gov text for chs. 24/54/91/301). Applies as written. Self-limit ('to the extent permitted by applicable law') is necessary in Texas: s54.044(d) lets a landlord remove the contents of abandoned premises and s92.0081(b)(2) permits exclusion for that purpose, but no Texas statute read prescribes a notice/storage/disposal procedure for abandoned (non-lien) property. Seizure/sale for unpaid rent is a separate, lease-authorized lien process (landlord-lien-tx). Post-writ property is handled by the officer under s24.0061. Variants not used - they cross-reference sections absent from a Texas lease. | FL: Applies as written (tag-first screen). Instruction 31: Florida has no good-cause renewal; expiration ends the tenancy (Fla. Stat. §§83.57, 83.575, 83.58). The self-limit 'to the extent permitted by applicable law' is load-bearing: Fla. Stat. §§715.10-715.111 is an OPTIONAL procedure (§715.101(2)) giving the landlord nonliability (§715.11) after notice (§§715.104-.106), storage with reasonable care (§715.107), and public sale or, under $500, retention or disposal (§715.109); reasonable storage costs are chargeable (§715.111) and sale costs come out of proceeds. §83.67(5) allows removing property only after surrender, abandonment, death of the last tenant or lawful eviction. 'At Tenant's cost' is within those limits. Opt-out legend: abandoned-property-release-fl. s5a.1: states-only change, no propagation owed. | AZ: Applies as written. A.R.S. §33-1370(I): if the tenant returns the keys and leaves property, the landlord may remove and dispose of it immediately without liability unless the parties agreed otherwise in writing; otherwise §33-1370(D)-(H) storage and sale procedure. "To the extent permitted by applicable law" carries the load. Instruction 31: Arizona has no just-cause or good-cause renewal rule in ch. 10. s5a.1: states-only change, no propagation owed.

title: Early Termination
bodyText: Tenant may terminate this Lease before the end of the Term by providing Landlord at least 30 days' written notice. Tenant will pay an early termination fee equal to one month's Rent ({{monthly_rent}}) or 30% of the remaining Rent due under the Term, whichever is greater, and remains responsible for Rent and other obligations up to the termination date. Landlord may terminate this Lease early by providing Tenant at least 30 days' written notice if Tenant breaches a material term of this Lease and fails to cure the breach within 10 days of receiving written notice, or if Tenant vacates or abandons the property without notifying Landlord. Nothing in this Section limits any right either party has under applicable law. This includes a Tenant's right to terminate without penalty due to active military service under the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act, due to the property becoming uninhabitable through no fault of Tenant, or — except as prohibited by law in the case of a Tenant's death — any other termination right or limitation provided by applicable law.
notes: CO added - verified this session (statute walk + full-library audit; content itself EDITED this session WY added 2026-08-21 (full-library cross-check pass): generic mechanics, no CO-specific statutory language or number, confirmed no conflict with WY findings from this project. | MN extended (Minnesota session, CO;WY-scoping resolution): the clause's '10 days to cure' for landlord-initiated termination is more generous than Minnesota law requires (MN has no general statutory cure period for material lease violations, confirmed absent this session) — unlike KS/NE, where a real statutory cure period (14 days) made this clause's shorter figure a rights-shortening conflict. No conflict for MN. | Cross-state plain-language cleanup (Minnesota session, follow-up to MN's plain-language audit): long compound sentence split into shorter ones, no substantive change. Not a legal requirement for this clause's other tagged states (only MN's Plain Language Contract Act, Minn. Stat. §325G.31, was confirmed to apply this project) — done as a general readability improvement since the pattern was found library-wide, not MN-specific. | ND extended (North Dakota session 1, same scoping review): no numeric conflict with N.D.C.C. §§ 47-16-16/17's landlord/tenant termination rights, neither of which specifies a notice period or cure timeline that would contradict this clause's 30-day/10-day figures. | SD extended (South Dakota session 1, Title 21-16 review): generic mechanics (30-day notice + 1 month's rent fee) are not statutorily mandated for SD but not prohibited either; no conflicting SD statute found (SDCL 43-32-19's tenant-termination causes are different grounds, not a fee framework). | OH: no Ohio conflict, but the greater-of-one-month-or-30% fee carries real §5321.14 unconscionability exposure, and Ohio's mitigation duty (Lemstone, commercial holding) is waivable — do NOT stack a waiver with this fee. CROSS-STATE FLAG RAISED AND NOT RESOLVED 2026-09-19 - it is wider than first recorded. The fee of 'one month's Rent or 30% OF THE REMAINING RENT, whichever is greater' appears IDENTICALLY in this row and its KS and NE variants, i.e. across EIGHT states (CO, WY, KS, NE, MN, ND, SD, OH). California is the only state where it was removed, because Civ. Code s1671(d) makes a liquidated-damages provision in a DWELLING lease void unless fixing actual damages would be impracticable, with s1951.5 confirming s1671 reaches leases of real property. Every state applies some liquidated-damages or penalty doctrine, and a percentage-of-remaining-rent charge is its classic target. The identical figure in all eight suggests it was INHERITED rather than verified state by state. UNLIKE the setoff flag, this CANNOT be fixed by a savings clause - where such a term is void it is the AMOUNT that offends, and 'as permitted by law' does not cure it. Needs a per-state read of liquidated-damages law before the next lease goes out. CA: early-termination-ca. FLAG DOWNGRADED AND CLOSED 2026-09-19 — MY ESCALATION WAS OVERSTATED. I recorded the 30%-of-remaining-rent fee as an unresolved eight-state risk needing a fresh per-state read. The library already answered it: each state's own session screened this clause (MN Plain Language Act check; ND - no conflict with N.D.C.C. ss47-16-16/17; SD - not mandated but not prohibited, no conflicting statute; OH - no conflict but real s5321.14 unconscionability exposure and do NOT stack with a mitigation waiver; KS and NE - the cure-period figure was corrected and the tenant's voluntary 30-day-plus-fee right expressly left intact). THE ACTUAL POSITION: CALIFORNIA IS THE OUTLIER, not the other eight. Civ. Code s1671(d) is a PER SE statutory bar on liquidated damages in a dwelling lease; no other state in the library has one. Everywhere else the ceiling is CASE-BY-CASE UNCONSCIONABILITY - statutory in KS, NE and OH (s5321.14), general doctrine in SD (53-9-3) and by common law in WY and MN, with CO's express liquidated-damages prohibition confined to the death-of-tenant context (edu-death-of-tenant-co). So the fee is NOT void per se outside CA; it is lawful-but-exposed, and the exposure rises with the size of the figure. PRODUCT GUIDANCE: keep the fee configurable, set it defensibly against actual re-letting loss, and in OH never combine it with a waiver of the mitigation duty. Savings sentence preserves 118A.340 and 118A.345 rights. | NV (text batch 2, 2026-09-24): NRS 118.175 (read): on abandonment the landlord must make reasonable efforts to re-rent at fair rental, and the former tenant owes actual damages. The contractual early-termination fee is an agreed option, not abandonment; OH's warning applies - never pair the fee with a waiver of that mitigation duty. | TX: Read in full 2026-09-25 against Tex. Prop. Code chs. 24, 54, 91, 92 and 301 (official statutes.capitol.texas.gov text for chs. 24/54/91/301). Applies as written. Contractual option. Tex. Prop. Code s91.006: landlord's duty to mitigate on abandonment is non-waivable, and the clause does not purport to waive it. title: Holdover Tenancy
bodyText: If Tenant does not vacate the property by the end of the Term, Landlord may pursue any remedy allowed by applicable law to recover possession. Landlord will also be entitled to recover from Tenant holdover damages in the maximum amount permitted by applicable law for each day Tenant remains in possession after the end of the Term. Alternatively, Landlord may accept Tenant's continued payment of Rent, in which case this Lease will be deemed to continue on a month-to-month basis on the same terms and conditions, terminable by either party upon written notice as required by applicable law.
notes: CO added - verified this session (statute walk + full-library audit; content itself unchanged WY added 2026-08-21 (full-library cross-check pass): generic mechanics, no CO-specific statutory language or number, confirmed no conflict with WY findings from this project. | NE added (session 1): Neb. Rev. Stat. §76-1437(3) allows up to 3x periodic rent or 3x actual damages for willful bad-faith holdover — higher than this clause's double-rent figure, so the clause still holds up in NE without an override (per Taylor's read, Flag 6). See edu-holdover-ne for the full NE figure and a note to revisit the double-rent baseline once more states are surveyed. | MN extended (Minnesota session, whole-library audit): generic mechanics, already vetted against KS/NE's prohibited-lease-provisions statutes (the strictest bar found in this project to date) since this clause was already tagged KS;NE; no MN-specific statutory language or number identified in this session's statute walk that conflicts. No exculpatory/liability-waiver language present. | Cross-state plain-language cleanup (Minnesota session, follow-up to MN's plain-language audit): long compound sentence split into shorter ones, no substantive change. Not a legal requirement for this clause's other tagged states (only MN's Plain Language Contract Act, Minn. Stat. §325G.31, was confirmed to apply this project) — done as a general readability improvement since the pattern was found library-wide, not MN-specific. | SHARED-CLAUSE PASS 2026-09-03 (§5a.1). EDIT: removed the hardcoded 'double the Monthly Rent ... or the maximum amount allowed under applicable law, if less' and replaced it with a pure deferral to the statutory maximum. §5a.1 JUDGMENT: **STATE-DRIVEN** — the holdover figure genuinely differs per state — but the EDIT itself is uniform-safe and no per-state override is required, because each state's figure is already carried by its own education row. WHY THE OLD TEXT WAS WRONG IN BOTH DIRECTIONS, which is why leaving it was not an option: (1) OVER-PROMISED in MN — Minnesota has NO holdover multiplier at all (§504B.141 and the eviction chapter, confirmed at MN re-audit), so 'double the Monthly Rent' described a remedy that does not exist; the self-limiting tail made it lawful but misleading. (2) UNDER-CLAIMED in NE — Nebraska allows three months' periodic rent or threefold actual damages, whichever is greater, PLUS statutory attorney fees (§76-1437(3)), all of which EXCEED double monthly rent. The old 'or the maximum allowed ... if less' language could only ever cap DOWNWARD, so a Nebraska landlord relying on the clause would recover materially less than the statute allows. A ceiling-only formulation silently forfeits recovery in any state whose statutory figure is higher than the hardcoded one. KS is unaffected either way (1.5x cap under K.S.A. 58-2570(c), already below double, per edu-holdover-ks). GAP SURFACED, NOT CLOSED: CO and WY have NO holdover-damages education row and their statutory figures have never been verified in this project. The 'double' figure appears to have originated as Colorado's, but that has not been confirmed against C.R.S. Recommend verifying CO and WY holdover figures and adding edu-holdover-co / edu-holdover-wy, matching KS/NE/MN. | FOLLOW-UP 2026-09-03: the gap flagged in the shared-clause pass is now closed, and the answer is worse than expected. THE 'DOUBLE THE MONTHLY RENT' FIGURE HAD NO STATUTORY BASIS IN ANY OF THE FIVE TAGGED STATES. CO: no multiplier, damages = reasonable rental value (§13-40-123, Behr v. Burge). WY: no multiplier, actual damages plus 10% interest (§1-21-1211(b), provisional). KS: 1.5x cap, BELOW double (K.S.A. 58-2570(c)). NE: three months' periodic rent or threefold actual plus attorney fees, ABOVE double (§76-1437(3)). MN: no multiplier at all. So the number was wrong in every direction simultaneously — too high in three states, too low in one, and baseless in the two where it was assumed to have originated. The shared-clause pass hypothesized it 'appears to have originated as Colorado's'; that hypothesis is now DISPROVED. It appears to be generic template boilerplate that entered the library before any state research and was never questioned, and it survived four state re-audits. Removing it was correct. Recording the provenance because it is the clearest example in the project of an unsourced number propagating through a shared clause: nothing in the library ever asserted where 'double' came from, and every state's own research quietly contradicted it. | FL: Applies as written (tag-first screen, instruction 26). The referent exists: Fla. Stat. §83.58 lets the landlord recover double the rent for the period a tenant holds over without permission (last amended s. 10, ch. 2013-136). holdover-ca NOT tagged: it would give up the double-rent recovery (K.3, ceiling-only). §83.575(3): a tenant who stays with permission after termination without §83.57(3) notice owes one additional month's rent; statutory, no lease text needed. s5a.1: states-only change, no propagation owed. | AZ: Applies as written. The referent exists: A.R.S. §33-1375(C) - if the holdover is willful and not in good faith, the landlord may recover up to the greater of two months' periodic rent or twice actual damages; if the landlord consents in writing to continued occupancy, §33-1314(D) makes it month-to-month. holdover-ca NOT tagged: its actual-damages measure would give up the statutory recovery (K.3). The "for each day" wording does not match Arizona's lump-sum measure but does not cap it. s5a.1: states-only change, no propagation owed.

title: Month-to-Month Termination Notice
bodyText: Either party may terminate a month-to-month tenancy by written notice served as provided in Code of Civil Procedure section 1162 or by certified or registered mail. Tenant must give notice at least as long as the period of the tenancy (30 days for a month-to-month tenancy), regardless of how long Tenant has resided at the property. Landlord must give at least 60 days' written notice, except that 30 days' notice is sufficient if Tenant has resided at the property for less than one year, or if the conditions in Civil Code section 1946.1(d) are met (unit separately alienable, sold to a natural-person bona fide purchaser in escrow, notice given within 120 days of escrow, no prior notice given, and purchaser intends to reside there at least one year). Landlord's notice must include the statutory abandoned-property statement required by Civil Code section 1946.1(h). Where this property is subject to Civil Code section 1946.2, notice alone is not sufficient: after the qualifying occupancy period Landlord must also state a just cause for termination.
notes: CA: REWRITTEN 2026-09-19 from primary text of Civ. Code s1946.1. The pre-existing dormant row was defective in four ways: (1) it applied the 30/60 split to BOTH parties - s1946.1(b) imposes 60 days on the OWNER only; a tenant's notice is one tenancy period regardless of occupancy length, so the old text bound a long-term tenant to a 60-day duty CA law does not impose, while reciting 'as required by California law'; (2) it omitted the s1946.1(d) bona-fide-purchaser 30-day path entirely; (3) it omitted the s1946.1(h) abandoned-property statement the owner's notice must contain; (4) it was silent on the s1946.2 just-cause overlay, so for a covered unit it told the tenant the tenancy could be ended on notice alone, which is false. Same error shape as the CO entry-notice 'as required by Colorado law' correction.

title: Use of Property & Common Areas
bodyText: Tenant will not, without Landlord's written consent, drill holes, use nails, hooks, or screws on the property, or fasten anything to its fixtures, appliances, or interior or exterior surfaces. Tenant will comply with any weight restrictions on balconies or porches and will not use them to store personal belongings without Landlord's consent. Tenant will not keep a waterbed or other water-filled furniture at the property, or any item (such as a piano or safe) whose weight Landlord has not agreed is reasonable for the floor, without Landlord's prior written consent. Tenant will not burn wax candles at the property. Tenant will not post or display any sign, banner, or advertisement visible from outside the property without Landlord's consent. Nothing in this Section restricts any display that applicable law entitles Tenant to make, such as the display of the flag of the United States or of religious or cultural items, subject to any lawful limits on its size, placement, and manner.

title: Bed Bug Disclosure
bodyText: Information about Bed Bugs. Bed bug Appearance: Bed bugs have six legs. Adult bed bugs have flat bodies about 1/4 of an inch in length. Their color can vary from red and brown to copper colored. Young bed bugs are very small. Their bodies are about 1/16 of an inch in length. They have almost no color. When a bed bug feeds, its body swells, may lengthen, and becomes bright red, sometimes making it appear to be a different insect. Bed bugs do not fly. They can either crawl or be carried from place to place on objects, people, or animals. Bed bugs can be hard to find and identify because they are tiny and try to stay hidden. Life Cycle and Reproduction: An average bed bug lives for about 10 months. Female bed bugs lay one to five eggs per day. Bed bugs grow to full adulthood in about 21 days. Bed bugs can survive for months without feeding. Bed bug Bites: Because bed bugs usually feed at night, most people are bitten in their sleep and do not realize they were bitten. A person's reaction to insect bites is an immune response and so varies from person to person. Sometimes the red welts caused by the bites will not be noticed until many days after a person was bitten, if at all. Common signs and symptoms of a possible bed bug infestation: • Small red to reddish brown fecal spots on mattresses, box springs, bed frames, mattresses, linens, upholstery, or walls. • Molted bed bug skins, white, sticky eggs, or empty eggshells. • Very heavily infested areas may have a characteristically sweet odor. • Red, itchy bite marks, especially on the legs, arms, and other body parts exposed while sleeping. However, some people do not show bed bug lesions on their bodies even though bed bugs may have fed on them. For more information, see the Internet Web sites of the United States Environmental Protection Agency and the National Pest Management Association. Tenant shall report any suspected bed bug infestation to Landlord promptly and in writing, using the following procedure: {{bed_bug_reporting_procedure}}.
notes: CA: REWRITTEN 2026-09-19 against Civ. Code s1954.603 (primary text supplied by Taylor). Statute requires the information 'in substantially the following form' and in AT LEAST 10-POINT TYPE - shipped effectively verbatim because 'substantially' is not a licence to compress. THIRD type-size floor found in CA (8-point at s2079.10a, 10-point here, 12-point at s1946.2(f)(3)); the schema still cannot express any of them. The prior dormant row was a four-line paraphrase and had two substantive defects beyond omitting the entire prescribed block: (1) it promised 'Landlord's process for investigating a suspected infestation' - s1954.603(b) requires the opposite, the procedure for the TENANT TO REPORT to the landlord, which is why this row now carries a landlord-supplied {{bed_bug_reporting_procedure}} field; (2) it asserted the notice covers 'the danger of self-treating with pesticides' - NO SUCH ELEMENT EXISTS in s1954.603. That element appears in other states' bed-bug statutes, so this is the Instruction 18 error shape (another state's architecture imported as fact) sitting inside a shipped CA row. Timing: duty attaches on and after 2017-07-01 prior to creating a NEW tenancy. The separate one-time catch-up duty to notify all existing tenants by 2018-01-01 is spent and is deliberately not modelled. s1954.601 defines 'pest control operator' as a Branch 2 licensee of the Structural Pest Control Board. The chapter is 6.9.1, not 6.9.2 as I guessed. Five defects in the prior dormant row. (1) TRIGGER WRONG: the row keyed off 'an order prohibiting occupancy due to methamphetamine contamination that has not been satisfied'. The statute keys off a REMEDIATION ORDER under ss25400.22/25400.25, and the duty runs until the owner receives a s25400.27 notice that the property requires NO FURTHER ACTION. An occupancy prohibition is not the trigger. (2) FENTANYL OMITTED: the chapter has covered methamphetamine OR FENTANYL since AB 1596 took effect 2020-01-01. The row was meth-only and is retitled - six years stale. (3) TIMING: s25400.28(b) attaches the duty to all prospective tenants WHO HAVE COMPLETED A RENTAL APPLICATION, earlier than lease signing. The row modelled it purely as a lease disclosure, so the duty could be missed entirely for an applicant who never reaches signature. (4) FREE TEXT IS NOT COMPLIANCE: the statute requires four mechanical things - written notice, A COPY OF THE ORDER provided, the tenant's WRITTEN ACKNOWLEDGMENT before signing, and the notice ATTACHED to the rental agreement. The old '[describe any known contamination order]' bracket satisfies none of them. This is document assembly, not clause text - same class of problem as the s1632 translation duty. (5) REMEDY OMITTED: if the owner does not comply with (b), THE PROSPECTIVE TENANT MAY VOID THE RENTAL AGREEMENT. Severe, and absent from the old row. OUT OF SCOPE, flagged not resolved: s25400.28(c) is a separate stricter regime for a mobilehome, manufactured home or recreational vehicle subject to an order - it may not be sold, rented OR OCCUPIED until notice of all meth or fentanyl laboratory activities and any remediation is given, with notice and order attached to the rental agreement, and (c)(4) gives the same void right. Other limbs read and captured for whenever it does commence: (b) no duty to conduct air or surface testing; (c)(1) disclosure to prospective tenants before entering the agreement and (c)(2) to current tenants in affected units as soon as reasonably practical; (d) exemption where the mold was remediated per the s26130 guidelines. NOTE the (a) trigger reaches mold 'both visible and invisible or hidden'. SEPARATE AND UNREAD: Civ. Code s1941.1(a)(7) is reported to place visible mold in the habitability list, which would make mold actionable in CA regardless of s26147's status. Not read this pass - pull it before concluding CA has no mold obligation. CORRECTION 2026-09-19: my earlier pointer to Civ. Code s1941.1(a)(7) as the mold limb was WRONG - (a)(7) is garbage and rubbish receptacles. The real route is the OPENING WORDS of s1941.1(a), read section-open: a dwelling is untenantable if it substantially lacks the listed characteristics OR IS A RESIDENTIAL UNIT DESCRIBED IN H&S s17920.3 OR s17920.10. That incorporation is confirmed from the text. Whether s17920.3 actually lists visible mold growth as a substandard condition is NOT confirmed - s17920.3 has not been read. NEEDED: H&S s17920.3. The supplied s1941.1 text also stopped at (a)(7), so (a)(8) onward is unread. RESOLVED 2026-09-19 on the habitability limb: H&S s17920.3(a)(13) (read section-open; amended by Stats. 2024 ch. 487 (SB 1465), eff. 2025-01-01) DOES list 'Visible mold growth' as a substandard condition, and Civ. Code s1941.1(a) incorporates s17920.3 by reference. So California DOES have a live mold obligation - it is a HABITABILITY duty, not a disclosure duty. This row is a disclosure clause and stays INACTIVE: the s26147 disclosure duty remains contingent under s26147(e) and the only question left on it is factual, whether the department ever adopted the s26103/s26105 standards and s26130 guidelines. Two limits on the habitability route that matter and are easy to overstate: (1) visible mold growth must be 'as determined by a health officer or a code enforcement officer, as defined in Section 829.5 of the Penal Code' - it is NOT self-executing on a tenant's or landlord's own assessment; (2) it EXCLUDES mold that is minor and found on surfaces that can accumulate moisture as part of their properly functioning and intended use (shower surrounds and the like). The s17920.3 preamble adds a further threshold: the condition must exist to an extent that endangers life, limb, health, property, safety or welfare. s17920.10, the OTHER s1941.1(a) incorporation, READ 2026-09-19 - it governs lead hazards, not mold, so it does not affect this row. See edu-lead-hazards-ca. FACTUAL QUESTION RESOLVED 2026-09-19: the s26147(e) predicate standards were NEVER ADOPTED. Primary source: CDPH's own 2005 Report to the Legislature on implementing the Toxic Mold Protection Act concluded that science-based permissible exposure limits for indoor mold could not be established, and CDPH's 2017 Statement on Indoor Dampness and Mold confirms the scientific basis for that conclusion had not changed as of 2015 and that no federal or state policy sets safe exposure limits. The SB 655 (2015) Senate floor analysis quotes the same CDPH position. Consistent secondary sources through 2026 report no PELs adopted. So s26147 has NEVER COMMENCED and this row correctly stays INACTIVE - now VERIFIED as not in force, the same posture as foreclosure-disclosure-ca. WORTH NOTING: at least one 2026 secondary source describes s26147 as operative with a 'practical trigger' of visible mold - the exact misreading s26147(e) forecloses. Another secondary-source error of the kind this project was built to catch. Residual limit: CDPH's primary statements run to 2017; post-2017 status rests on consistent secondary reporting and the absence of any contrary source.

title: Flood Disclosure
bodyText: Flood Hazard Disclosure. [If Landlord has actual knowledge that the property is located in a special flood hazard area or an area of potential flooding, state that fact here; otherwise state 'Landlord has no actual knowledge that the property is located in a special flood hazard area or an area of potential flooding.'] Tenant may obtain information about hazards, including flood hazards, that may affect the property from the Internet Web site of the Office of Emergency Services, including the MyHazards tool at {{myhazards_url}}. Landlord's insurance does not cover the loss of Tenant's personal possessions, and it is recommended that Tenant consider purchasing renter's insurance and flood insurance to insure Tenant's possessions from loss due to fire, flood, or other risk of loss. Landlord is not required to provide additional information concerning the flood hazards to the property, and the information provided pursuant to Government Code section 8589.45 is deemed adequate to inform Tenant.
notes: CA: REWRITTEN 2026-09-19 against Gov. Code s8589.45 (primary text supplied by Taylor, current as of 2026-01-01). STRUCTURAL DEFECT CORRECTED - rule_type moved CONDITIONAL -> REQUIRED. The prior dormant row treated the WHOLE disclosure as conditional on the property being in a flood zone. It is not: s8589.45(a) requires the disclosure in EVERY residential lease entered into on or after 2018-07-01, and only element (a)(1) carries the 'if the owner has actual knowledge' qualifier. Elements (a)(2), (3) and (4) are unconditional. As previously modelled, a non-flood-zone CA property would have received NO disclosure at all. Four further defects in the old text: (1) it omitted element (a)(2) entirely, including the statutory requirement that the disclosure CONTAIN the MyHazards Internet Web site address; (2) it omitted element (a)(4), the landlord safe harbour; (3) it narrowed element (a)(3) to 'renter's insurance covering flood damage' - the statute requires stating that the owner's insurance does not cover the tenant's possessions AND recommending both renter's and flood insurance against fire, flood or other risk of loss; (4) it glossed the trigger as a 'special flood hazard area as designated by the Federal Emergency Management Agency' - the statute says 'special flood hazard area OR AN AREA OF POTENTIAL FLOODING' and never mentions FEMA, so the row imported a narrower federal definition the statute does not use. ACTUAL KNOWLEDGE is defined, not left at large - s8589.45(a)(1)(A)-(C): written notice from any public agency, the mortgage holder requiring flood insurance, or THE OWNER CURRENTLY CARRYING FLOOD INSURANCE. The third is the one landlords overlook: carrying the policy is itself actual knowledge. This belongs in the builder as a question, not as landlord free text. Prescribed floor: NO SMALLER THAN EIGHT-POINT TYPE. s8589.45(b) subjects the disclosure to Civ. Code s1632 - SECOND statute in CA carrying the translation duty after s1946.2(f)(3). OPEN: {{myhazards_url}} is an app-config value, not landlord input. The statute requires the address to appear; the current CalOES MyHazards address has NOT been verified from primary source this pass and must be confirmed and maintained at sync - a hardcoded URL is exactly the kind of value that rots silently.

Code ch. 92 read in full, section-open, 2026-09-25 (Justia '2025 Texas Statutes' host copy supplied by Taylor; per-section history lines checked - latest amendments 89th Leg., R.S.
