title: Pet Policy
bodyText: Tenant may keep only pets identified in writing to and approved by Landlord. Tenant will pay Landlord a pet deposit, if applicable, and pet rent of {{pet_rent_amount}} per month. Tenant is responsible for all damage, waste removal, odor, and disturbance caused by a pet. Landlord may revoke approval of a pet that becomes a nuisance or safety concern, and may enter the property and remove a pet if the pet becomes vicious or displays symptoms of severe illness, or if Tenant dies, becomes incapacitated, or is otherwise unable to care for the pet and Landlord believes in good faith that the pet is being abused or neglected.
notes: K.S.A. 58-2547(a)(4). Full-library liability audit (session 5): drops two separate exposures — the generic's 'will indemnify Landlord from claims arising from Tenant's pet(s)' sentence (K.S.A. 58-2547(a)(4) bars indemnification obligations for either party's liability, not just landlord exculpation, so this direction is exposed too) and the 'without liability to Tenant' pet-removal language. Conservative fix, same rationale as the other KS overrides above — no obvious statutory exception fits either sentence.

title: Pet Policy
bodyText: Tenant may keep only pets identified in writing to and approved by Landlord. Tenant will pay Landlord a pet deposit, if applicable, and pet rent of {{pet_rent_amount}} per month. Tenant is responsible for all damage, waste removal, odor, and disturbance caused by a pet, and will indemnify Landlord from claims arising from Tenant's pet(s), except to the extent the claim arises from Landlord's own negligence. Landlord may revoke approval of a pet that becomes a nuisance or safety concern, and may enter the property and remove a pet, without liability to Tenant except to the extent caused by Landlord's gross negligence or willful misconduct, if the pet becomes vicious or displays symptoms of severe illness, or if Tenant dies, becomes incapacitated, or is otherwise unable to care for the pet and Landlord believes in good faith that the pet is being abused or neglected.
notes: Neb. Rev. Stat. §76-1415(1)(d). Full-library liability audit (session 5): the tenant-indemnifies-Landlord sentence is left unchanged — it covers the tenant's own pet's actions, not Landlord's negligence, so Nebraska's negligence-specific ban doesn't reach it. Only the pet-removal 'without liability to Tenant' sentence is narrowed to exclude Landlord's own gross negligence or willful misconduct, same pattern as tenants-property-insurance-ne. | NE RE-AUDIT 2026-08-31 — INDEMNITY NARROWED. §76-1415(1)(d) read from primary source. It reaches indemnification, but only indemnification of the landlord 'for THAT liability arising due to active and actionable negligence' — i.e. the landlord's OWN negligence. The original NE session left this sentence untouched on the reasoning that it 'covers the tenant's own pet's actions, not Landlord's negligence.' That was directionally right but INCOMPLETE: 'claims arising from Tenant's pet(s)' was UNQUALIFIED, so a claim in which the landlord was itself actively negligent (e.g. knew a pet was vicious and failed to act) would still 'arise from Tenant's pet' and be swept in — reaching exactly what (d) prohibits. The clause was overbroad at the margin, not prohibited at its core. Fix is a carve-out, not deletion. CONTRAST WITH KANSAS, and this is why the two rows must stay separate: K.S.A. 58-2547(a)(4) bars indemnifying EITHER PARTY, so pet-policy-ks correctly removed the indemnity outright. Nebraska's (d) is landlord-only and negligence-gated, so Nebraska keeps the indemnity with a carve-out. Do not merge.

title: No General Prohibited-Lease-Provisions Statute in Wyoming
bodyText: Unlike Colorado (C.R.S. §38-12-801), Kansas (K.S.A. 58-2547), and Nebraska (§76-1415), Wyoming has no equivalent statute banning categories of lease provisions outright — no attorney-fee-shifting ban, no confession-of-judgment ban, no exculpation/liability-limitation ban. All 11 sections of Article 12 (W.S. 1-21-1201–1211) were read directly from primary source during Wyoming's original verification pass, and no such section exists. This means the liability-disclaimer exposure found for Kansas and Nebraska in `tenants-property-insurance`, `services-utilities-provided`, `parking`, `storage-space`, and `pet-policy` doesn't apply to Wyoming — those clauses' generic language is safe to keep as-is for WY leases.
notes: W.S. 1-21-1201–1211 (full text read directly from primary source, WY session 3). Genuine confirmed absence, not merely unchecked — closes the question raised by the cross-state liability audit (sessions 5–6 of the Nebraska work) for Wyoming specifically.

title: No Immigration-Status Inquiry Prohibition
bodyText: Wyoming has no statute prohibiting landlords from inquiring about immigration status. Only California, Illinois, and Colorado have been found to have a dedicated statute of this kind.
notes: Confirmed absent — consistent with the KS and NE findings on this same item; multiple independent Wyoming landlord-tenant law overviews consistently describe protected classes as federal-only with no state additions, and none mention immigration status. Closes the last open state for this checklist item (CO: present/standing rule, WY/KS/NE: confirmed absent).

title: No State-Level Right-to-Call-Police Statute
bodyText: Wyoming has no state-level statute establishing a non-waivable tenant right to call police or emergency services. Any protection here would exist, if at all, at the municipal level — not audited here, consistent with how this category of question has been treated for other states in this project.
notes: Confirmed absent at the state level — consistent with the KS and NE findings, though this rests on absence-of-mention across multiple general-overview sources rather than an explicit 'no such law' statement, the same weaker-evidence caveat already flagged for the equivalent KS/NE findings. Closes the last open state for this checklist item.

title: No Dedicated Tenant-Screening Fairness Act
bodyText: Wyoming has no rental-application or tenant-screening fairness statute — application fees are uncapped, with no requirement that the fee track the actual cost of a background/credit check. Landlords do not need tenant consent to run background and credit checks. Federal Fair Credit Reporting Act obligations still apply regardless of state law.
notes: Confirmed absent with reasonable confidence — Landlord Studio's WY guide explicitly states 'despite there being no statute' regarding application fees, an affirmative statement rather than mere silence. Closes the last open state for this checklist item (CO: deferred, WY: confirmed absent, KS: not yet checked, NE: confirmed absent).

title: Returned Check Fee Cap
bodyText: Wyoming caps the fee a landlord can collect for a dishonored check at $30, on top of the check's face value, after making written demand for payment (Wyo. Stat. §1-1-115(b)). This is a general bad-check statute, not landlord-tenant-specific, but it applies to a bounced rent check the same as any other dishonored check. The `returned-payments` clause doesn't hardcode a dollar figure, so it isn't in conflict — just be aware the fee you actually set for a Wyoming lease is capped at $30 by this statute, regardless of what the lease might otherwise allow.
notes: Wyo. Stat. §1-1-115(b). Confirmed via 7+ independent sources all citing the same statute, including one (iPropertyManagement) quoting the operative statutory language directly — a materially stronger evidence base than the misattributed $15 NE returned-check figure rejected during the Nebraska liability audit (that one turned out to govern payday-loan licensees only). This is a real, general Wyoming statute, correctly attributed.

title: Landlord's Right of Entry
bodyText: Landlord may enter the property only for a reasonable business purpose, and will make a good faith effort to give Tenant notice of the intent to enter of not less than 24 hours in advance, unless Tenant permits entry with less notice. Any notice will specify a time or window of entry, and Landlord will enter only between 8:00 a.m. and 8:00 p.m., unless Landlord and Tenant agree to a different time. However, Landlord may enter without prior notice if Landlord reasonably believes immediate entry is necessary to prevent injury to persons or property, to determine Tenant's safety, or to comply with local ordinances regarding unlawful activity on the property. If Landlord enters while Tenant is not present and prior notice was not given, Landlord will leave written disclosure of the entry in a conspicuous place on the property.
notes: MN added (Minnesota session, statute walk + supersedes generic landlords-access): Minn. Stat. § 504B.211. 24-hour notice IS statutorily required in MN (contrast with CO, where it is not) with additional detail the generic clause doesn't capture: mandatory 8am-8pm entry window (subd. 2), 9 enumerated reasonable-business-purpose categories (subd. 3, paraphrased here rather than listed exhaustively — full list in edu-entry-notice-content-mn), and 3 specific no-notice emergency exceptions (subd. 4). Non-waivable. Penalty: rent reduction up to full lease rescission, deposit recovery, up to $500 civil penalty per violation, attorney fees. Does not apply to manufactured home parks (subd. 7) — flag as a property-type exception to revisit if Steinoak ever supports MHP listings. | MN plain-language pass (Minnesota session): replaced 'Notwithstanding the foregoing' with 'However' — same meaning, everyday wording, per Minn. Stat. § 325G.31's 'common and everyday meanings' requirement.

title: Return of Security Deposit
bodyText: Within three weeks after termination of this Lease, and after receiving Tenant's mailing address or delivery instructions, Landlord will return the Security Deposit, together with simple interest as required by Minnesota law, or will provide Tenant a written statement showing the specific reason for withholding the deposit or any portion of it. Landlord may withhold only amounts reasonably necessary to remedy a Tenant default in the payment of rent or other funds due under this Lease, or to restore the property to its condition at the commencement of the tenancy, ordinary wear and tear excepted.
notes: MN added (Minnesota session, statute walk + supersedes generic security-deposit-return): Minn. Stat. § 504B.178. Return window is 3 weeks (21 days) — shorter than CO's 30/60-day pattern, longer than KS/NE's 14-day pattern. Deposit accrues simple noncompounded interest at 1%/year (subd. 2) — this project has not yet built an interest-tracking mechanism into the product; flagging as a product gap, not just a clause gap, since the clause can promise interest but Steinoak doesn't yet calculate or disclose an amount anywhere. Bad-faith retention carries punitive damages up to $500 (subd. 7) in addition to the doubling-type damages under subd. 4 — not restated in the clause text itself, kept as landlord-facing awareness only, consistent with prior sessions' pattern of not larding lease clauses with penalty language the tenant doesn't need to see. | MN re-audit 2026-09-03, canvass pass 2: §504B.178 read IN FULL. Numbers previously verified all hold (three weeks; 1% simple noncompounded; $500 bad-faith punitive). FOUR ELEMENTS THE CLAUSE DOES NOT CAPTURE, surfaced rather than silently left: (1) subd. 3(c) — 'In any action concerning the deposit, the burden of proving, by a fair preponderance of the evidence, the reason for withholding all or any portion of the deposit shall be on the landlord.' The burden is on the LANDLORD, which is landlord-facing knowledge worth having and is not in any MN row. (2) subd. 3(a)(2) — a separate FIVE-DAY return window where the tenant leaves due to legal condemnation of the building for reasons not caused by the tenant's willful, malicious, or irresponsible conduct. The clause states only the three-week track. Not added to body text because the condemnation scenario is narrow and the clause already defers to law, but FLAGGED for Taylor as a possible addition. (3) subd. 2 — interest of less than $1 is excluded entirely, a de minimis rule relevant to the not-yet-built deposit-interest calculation feature. (4) subd. 7 — bad-faith retention is PRESUMED where the landlord failed to comply with subd. 3 or 5, unless the deposit is returned within two weeks after an action for recovery is commenced. That presumption, not just the $500 figure, is the operative risk. Also confirmed: subd. 3(b) mailing-compliance safe harbor (first class, prepaid, proper return address, correctly addressed, within the time required); subd. 10 waiver void; subd. 11 estates at will deemed renewed each rental period.

title: Termination of Lease Upon Death of Tenant
bodyText: If Tenant dies during the term of this Lease (or, if there is more than one Tenant, upon the death of all Tenants), either Landlord or the personal representative of Tenant's estate may terminate this Lease upon at least two months' written notice, effective on the last day of a calendar month, delivered by hand or by first-class prepaid mail to the address of the other party. Termination under this section does not relieve Tenant's estate of liability for rent or other sums owed before or during the notice period, or for amounts necessary to restore the property to its condition at the commencement of the tenancy, ordinary wear and tear excepted.
notes: MN added (Minnesota session, statute walk): Minn. Stat. § 504B.265. First state in this library where death-of-tenant is an affirmative statutory termination right built into the lease relationship (2-month notice, either party may invoke) rather than only a prohibition on penalty clauses. This is architecturally different from CO's edu-death-of-tenant-co (which is a PROHIBITED-framed education entry warning against penalty clauses under Letty's Act) — MN needed an actual REQUIRED LEASE_CLAUSE instead, since the statute contemplates the lease itself accommodating the mechanism. Does not apply to tenancies at will (subd. 1). Non-waivable and cannot be shortened by lease, though parties may otherwise agree to modify the specific provisions of the section (subd. 4) — kept the clause at the statutory floor rather than trying to draft optional modifications. | MN re-audit 2026-09-03 — HARD-NUMBER RE-VERIFICATION, full section read from revisor.mn.gov. CONFIRMED CORRECT on every operative element: two months' written notice (subd. 2); effective on the last day of a calendar month; hand delivered or mailed postage prepaid first class to the other party's address; either the landlord OR the personal representative of the estate may invoke it; applies to leases 'other than a lease at will' (subd. 1); estate remains liable for rent and other sums owed prior to or during the notice period and for restoration. Subd. 4 waiver rule also confirmed as the clause's notes described it: any attempted waiver of the right of termination is void, AND any lease provision requiring a LONGER notice period than the statute is void, but the parties may otherwise agree to modify the section's specific provisions. No error found. NOT CAPTURED, minor and landlord-facing only: subd. 2's last sentence lets the landlord satisfy the notice requirement by delivering or mailing to the premises formerly occupied by the tenant — practically useful where the estate's address is unknown. VERSION CHECK: SF 3492 (2024) proposed adding a subd. 5 remedies provision to this section and restructuring §504B.271. Neither appears in the current 2025 statutes; §504B.271's history line runs 1999 c 199 and 2010 c 315 only. The bill was not enacted in that form, so both clauses are current.

title: Termination of Lease Upon Infirmity of Tenant
bodyText: If Tenant (or, if there is more than one Tenant, all Tenants) has been found by a medical professional to need to move into a nursing home, a boarding care home, a supervised living facility, an assisted living facility, or any other facility or accessible unit qualifying under Minnesota law, Tenant or Tenant's authorized representative may terminate this Lease before it expires. This Section does not apply, and Tenant may not terminate under it, where Tenant requires an accessible unit and Landlord can provide an accessible unit in the same complex in which Tenant currently resides that is available within two months of Tenant's request. Tenant must give at least two months' written notice, effective on the last day of a calendar month, delivered by hand or by first-class prepaid mail. The notice must include a copy of the medical professional's written documentation of the need to relocate, along with documentation that Tenant has been accepted as a resident, or has a pending application, at the facility. Termination under this section does not relieve Tenant of liability for rent or other sums owed before or during the notice period, or for amounts necessary to restore the property to its condition at the commencement of the tenancy, ordinary wear and tear excepted.
notes: MN added (Minnesota session, statute walk): Minn. Stat. § 504B.266. Genuinely new named-topic not previously seen in CO, WY, KS, or NE — a tenant-initiated early-termination right tied to a medical need to move into a care facility (requires assistance with ADLs/IADLs, meets a nursing-facility level-of-care criterion, or has a qualifying disability/functional impairment per § 245.462, subd. 11a). Documentation requirements are substantive (medical professional's written finding + proof of acceptance or pending application at the receiving facility) — kept in the clause since the statute makes them conditions of the notice itself, not separate landlord-side procedure. FLAG FOR TAYLOR: recommend adding 'tenant-initiated infirmity/medical-facility termination' to the named-topic checklist so future states get checked for an equivalent provision — this was not on the canvass list built from CO/WY/KS/NE. | MN plain-language pass (Minnesota session): split a 99-word sentence into three shorter ones, no substantive change, per Minn. Stat. § 325G.31's 'clear and coherent' requirement. | MN re-audit 2026-09-03 — TWO ERRORS FOUND on full primary read of §504B.266; both corrected in body text. (1) MISSING LANDLORD RIGHT: subd. 2(b) provides that where the tenant requires an accessible unit as defined in §363A.40 subd. 1, and the landlord can provide an accessible unit in the SAME COMPLEX available within two months of the request, 'the provisions of this section do not apply and the tenant may not terminate the lease.' The shipped clause granted the termination right unconditionally and never mentioned this defeasance — a real, valuable landlord right that was simply absent. (2) OVER-GRANTED TRIGGER: the shipped clause said 'need to move into a medical care facility,' a generic phrase. The statute does not use an open category — subd. 2 enumerates specific licensed facility types (nursing home; boarding care home licensed under ch. 144; supervised living facility; assisted living facility per §144G.08 subd. 7; accessible unit per §363A.40 subd. 1(b); state facility per §246.50 subd. 3; adult foster care program per §245A.02 subd. 6c; intensive residential treatment services per §245I.23). A generic 'medical care facility' grants tenants a termination right BROADER than Minnesota law requires, at the landlord's expense. Body text now references the statutory list rather than restating it, so the clause cannot drift from the enumeration as facility-licensing statutes are amended. [RESOLVED 2026-09-03 at RA-15 — Taylor chose the hybrid: four common types named inline plus an open catch-all, in house style with no section number in body text. Original flag retained below for traceability.] PRIOR-FLAG TEXT (superseded): restating the ten enumerated facility types inline is the alternative — more transparent to the tenant, but goes stale. Reference chosen for durability, consistent with the approach taken for §504B.216's apportionment formulas. Say the word if you prefer inline. Two months' notice, last-day-of-calendar-month effectiveness, and hand-delivery-or-first-class-mail all CONFIRMED correct against subd. 3. | MN re-audit 2026-09-03, FACILITY-LIST REVISION per Taylor: adopted the hybrid — four common facility types named inline, open catch-all for the rest. Rationale accepted that the threshold question gets answered in real time when a termination notice arrives, so the four cases that actually arise should be readable off the lease, while the less common types (state facility per §246.50, adult foster care per §245A.02 subd. 6c, intensive residential treatment per §245I.23, accessible unit per §363A.40) stay covered by the catch-all without going stale. HOUSE-STYLE CORRECTION made at the same time: the prior revision cited 'Minnesota Statutes, section 504B.266' in tenant-facing body text. A library-wide scan found this was the ONLY clause of ~190 doing so — every other clause defers generically ('as required by Colorado law', 'specified by applicable law'). Catch-all rephrased to 'qualifying under Minnesota law' to match house convention. Taylor's instruction was to follow suit if other states had anything similar; the scan found NO analog anywhere — ~70 clauses defer to statute but always for a NUMBER or TIMELINE, and the 6 clauses with inline enumerations are DUTY lists (tenant-duties-ks/ne, renter-duties-wy, habitability-baseline-ne), not qualifying-category lists. No hybrid existed in any state. This clause therefore SETS the pattern rather than following one — flagged so future states with a qualifying-category list can inherit it deliberately: name the common cases inline, catch-all the rest, no section numbers in body text.

title: Property Abandoned After Termination
bodyText: If Tenant abandons the property, Landlord may take possession of Tenant's personal property remaining on the property and will store and care for it. Landlord has a claim against Tenant for the reasonable costs and expenses of removing, storing, and caring for the property. Landlord may sell or otherwise dispose of the property 28 days after Landlord receives actual notice of the abandonment, or 28 days after it reasonably appears to Landlord that Tenant has abandoned the property, whichever is later. Before selling the property, Landlord will make reasonable efforts to notify Tenant of the sale at least 14 days in advance, by personal service or by first-class and certified mail to Tenant's last known address, and by posting notice of the sale in a conspicuous place on the property at least two weeks before the sale. Landlord may apply a reasonable amount of the sale proceeds to the removal, storage, and care costs described above, or to any amount properly withheld from the Security Deposit.
notes: MN added (Minnesota session, statute walk): Minn. Stat. § 504B.271. 28-day hold before disposal (longer than KS/NE/WY's shorter windows — worth a cross-state comparison note but not a conflict), plus a separate 14-day advance sale notice requirement layered on top. Non-waivable (subd. 4). Note the statute's dual-track notice for the sale itself (personal service OR mail AND posting — 'and' language, not 'or', similar in structure to KS's dual-requirement approach flagged in that state's decision log, not WY's either/or approach) — worth double-checking wording precision if this clause is revised later. | MN re-audit 2026-09-03 — HARD-NUMBER RE-VERIFICATION, full section read from revisor.mn.gov. CONFIRMED CORRECT: 28-day disposal window (subd. 1(b), running from actual notice OR when abandonment reasonably appears, whichever occurs LAST — the clause's 'whichever is later' is accurate); 14-day pre-sale notice (subd. 1(d)); and the conspicuous-posting requirement, which I suspected on entry might be cross-state contamination imported from KS and specifically checked — subd. 1(d) does require posting 'in a conspicuous place on the premises at least two weeks prior to the sale,' in ADDITION to personal service or first-class-and-certified mail. The clause is right and the suspicion was wrong; recorded so it is not re-litigated. NOT CAPTURED, minor: subd. 1(d)'s rule that where notice is mailed, the 14-day period is deemed to start on the day the notices are deposited in the U.S. mail. Left out of tenant-facing text deliberately; landlord-facing timing detail. NEW GAP FOUND, see edu-abandoned-property-retake-duty-mn: subd. 2's 24-hour/48-hour retake-on-demand duty and punitive damages were captured nowhere in the library. Subd. 3: a landlord who unlawfully took possession pays removal/storage/care costs. Subd. 4: non-waivable, and extends to occupants and owners in post-redemption foreclosure or contract-for-deed cancellation. | MN re-audit 2026-09-03 — SECOND TRACK CONFIRMED against primary text (§504B.365 read in full, revisor.mn.gov PDF). The secondary-source claim flagged at RA-12 is CORRECT. Minnesota has two abandoned-property routes and the tripwire is only WHERE the property is stored after a writ is executed: §504B.365 subd. 3(d) — property stored ON the premises — states 'Section 504B.271 applies to personal property removed under this paragraph,' i.e. this clause's 28-day/14-day track; §504B.365 subd. 3(a)-(c) — property moved OFF the premises — instead gives the plaintiff a LIEN for removal/storage costs, enforceable by detaining the property, with a public sale under §§514.18-514.22 permitted if no payment is made for 60 days after execution of the order to vacate. Same eviction, same day, different statute and a 60-day rather than 28-day clock. SCOPE DECISION: this clause is left covering the §504B.271 voluntary-abandonment route only, which is what it is titled for and what a lease clause can properly address. The post-writ duties are landlord procedure, not lease terms — logged as edu-writ-execution-property-duties-mn per the project's standing pattern for procedural obligations. FLAGGED FOR TAYLOR: the lease builder cannot express the storage-location fork; if the legal tracker ever handles evictions, this is a genuine branch point.

title: Shared-Metered Utility Billing
bodyText: If the property is part of a shared-metered residential building, Landlord will remain the bill payer and customer of record for utility service to the building. Landlord will not apportion or bill Tenant for electricity usage; electricity may only be submetered in accordance with applicable law. If Landlord apportions natural gas or water and sewer service to Tenant, Landlord will do so only using the method required by Minnesota law, will bill Tenant no less frequently than Landlord is billed by the utility, and will provide Tenant, upon request, copies of the underlying utility bills being apportioned. Any administrative billing charge will not exceed $8 per billing period, and any late payment charge for utilities billed separately from rent will not exceed $5 per month and will not compound. If Tenant vacates before Landlord receives the actual utility bill for the final period, Landlord may issue an estimated final utility bill calculated as permitted by applicable law, based on the immediately preceding billing period and prorated to the date Tenant vacates, without additional fees or charges beyond those applicable law allows. Landlord will not disconnect or cause the disconnection of Tenant's utility service for nonpayment of utility charges.
notes: MN added (Minnesota session, statute walk): Minn. Stat. § 504B.216 — by far the most prescriptive utility statute encountered in this project to date; the generic utilities-* clauses were extended to MN for directly-metered situations, but this dedicated CONDITIONAL clause is needed for shared-metered buildings specifically. Key constraints: electricity apportionment is flatly PROHIBITED (subd. 5(a)) — submetering only; gas apportionment must use the square-footage formula and water/sewer must use the occupant-count formula (subds. 6-7), not restated verbatim in the clause to avoid the clause becoming stale if the formula changes, but the underlying statute is the authority; $8 admin fee cap and $5 non-compounding late fee cap (subds. 8-9); disconnection ban (subd. 12) with cold-weather/heat-emergency/medical-emergency carve-outs layered into MN's eviction-for-nonpayment procedure rather than into a lease clause. IMPORTANT — this clause alone is NOT sufficient for compliance: § 504B.216, subd. 10 requires a specific, close-to-verbatim disclosure attachment in any lease where gas or water is apportioned. See edu-utility-disclosure-attachment-mn for the required text; this needs to become an actual generated lease attachment, not just clause language, when the lease builder reaches that feature. FLAG FOR TAYLOR: property attribute 'shared-metered building' (vs. directly metered) is a strong candidate for an auto-trigger field, alongside the existing HOA/pre-1978/utility-metering trigger candidates already noted for the product. | GAP-DISCOVERY BACKFILL 2026-09-27 (instruction 36, sources 2-4; not a re-audit): CHANGED -- ONE SENTENCE ADDED, AND A MAJOR ADJACENT REGIME CROSS-REFERENCED. What was verified and found CORRECT (checked before changing anything, per Addendum K.3): this row already states the electricity-apportionment prohibition, the $8 administrative billing charge cap, the $5 non-compounding late-fee cap and the disconnection ban accurately, and Minn. Stat. Sec. 216B.023 subd. 2(a)(1) independently confirms the electricity ban. No error found. WHAT WAS MISSING: Laws 2024, ch. 107 REPEALED Sec. 504B.215 (the revisor page now reads 'MS 2022 [Repealed, 2024 c 107 s 9]') and split the shared-metered regime between Sec. 504B.216 and three NEW sections in the Public Utilities chapter -- Sec. Sec. 216B.022, 216B.023 and 216B.024. MN's pass captured the Sec. 504B.216 half and never reached the Ch. 216B half of the same act: submeter ANSI and accuracy standards, PUC jurisdiction over a submetering landlord, an express lease-content requirement for billing timing, eight mandatory bill-content items, a billing- error refund duty, a six-month undercharge cap, mandatory payment plans, and a consumer-affairs referral duty. Those are now in edu-submetering-billing-duties-mn, and the lease-side billing-timing requirement is in the new utility-billing-schedule-mn row. BODY CHANGE: one sentence added giving the landlord the estimated-final-bill right created by Laws 2026, ch. 81 -- s 4 adds Sec. 504B.216 subd. 7a for APPORTIONED service and s 1 adds Sec. 216B.023 subd. 3a for SUBMETERED service, in identical terms. Both take the default August 1, 2026 effective date (neither section carries its own EFFECTIVE DATE clause; ch. 81 signed 2026-05-12), so both are in force. The sentence is landlord-favourable and would otherwise be a forfeited opt-in right (instruction 30). Note subd. 7a is NOT in the 2025 compilation of Sec. 504B.216 -- it was read from the session law (instruction 34/35). MN-only row: no Sec. 5a.1 propagation owed. The Sec. 504B.216 subd. 10 verbatim attachment obligation in edu-utility-disclosure-attachment-mn is unaffected and still outstanding as a product item.

title: Required Utility Disclosure Attachment for Apportioned Billing
bodyText: If you apportion natural gas or water/sewer costs to tenants in a shared-metered building, Minnesota law (Minn. Stat. § 504B.216, subd. 10) requires you to attach specific disclosure language to leases entered into or renewed on or after January 1, 2025, explaining how the bill is calculated, what tenants are and aren't charged for, the fee caps, and tenants' right to a payment plan and to dispute resolution through the Public Utilities Commission. This is close to a verbatim statutory text requirement, not just a general-content requirement — using your own paraphrase instead of the statute's language creates real compliance risk. This is a lease-attachment feature, not lease clause text; flag for the lease builder when attachments are supported.
notes: MN added (Minnesota session, statute walk): companion to utility-apportionment-mn. Full statutory text captured in the statute walk this session and available on request when Taylor is ready to build the attachment feature — not reproduced here to keep this education entry focused on the compliance obligation rather than duplicating the exact wording in two places in the library.

title: What Minnesota's Entry Notice Must Include
bodyText: Minnesota's entry-notice statute (Minn. Stat. § 504B.211) is more prescriptive than most states: notice must be at least 24 hours in advance, must specify a time or window, and entry is restricted to 8:00 a.m.-8:00 p.m. unless you and the tenant agree otherwise. 'Reasonable business purpose' is not open-ended — the statute lists nine specific categories (showing the unit to prospective tenants/buyers/insurers, maintenance, code inspections, tenant-caused disturbance, reasonable suspicion of a lease violation, prearranged housekeeping in qualifying senior housing, reasonable belief of unauthorized occupancy, and after the tenant has vacated). Emergency entry without notice is allowed only for injury/security/law-enforcement necessity, tenant-safety checks, or compliance with local unlawful-activity ordinances — and if you enter without the tenant present and without prior notice, you must leave written disclosure of the entry in the unit. One more thing that trips landlords up: the notice right is doubly protected. The tenant cannot waive it in advance, AND you cannot require the tenant to waive it as a condition of signing or keeping the lease. A lease paragraph saying 'Landlord may enter at any time for inspection' is not just unenforceable — putting it in the lease and asking for a signature is itself the conduct the statute prohibits. What IS allowed is real-time consent: a tenant may let you in on shorter notice in the moment if they want to. And the $500 civil penalty attaches per violation, so a pattern of unannounced entries compounds rather than capping out.
notes: MN added (Minnesota session, statute walk): companion to landlords-access-mn. Full 9-category purpose list and 3-category emergency-exception list confirmed directly from Minn. Stat. § 504B.211, subds. 3-5. | MN re-audit 2026-09-03: §504B.211 subd. 2 non-waiver language read directly. DOUBLE BAR confirmed — 'A residential tenant may not waive and the landlord may not require the residential tenant to waive the residential tenant's right to prior notice of entry under this section as a condition of entering into or maintaining the lease.' Two distinct prohibitions: prospective tenant waiver is void, AND landlord conditioning lease formation OR continuation on waiver is itself prohibited conduct. The prior version of this row stated the notice requirement but not the non-waiver, so a landlord could have read it and still believed a broad access clause was merely unenforceable rather than affirmatively violative. Real-time tenant consent to shorter notice remains permitted and is already reflected in landlords-access-mn. Penalty is per-violation, not per-tenancy.

title: Never Waive a Tenant's Right to Call Police
bodyText: Minnesota has a standalone statute (Minn. Stat. § 504B.205) prohibiting any lease provision, policy, or penalty that bars or limits a tenant's right to call police or emergency assistance, including in response to domestic abuse or a mental-health or health crisis. The right is explicitly non-waivable, and this is one of the more directly codified versions of this rule seen across the states checked so far — Minnesota gives tenants a private right of action for $250 or actual damages plus attorney fees, and the attorney general has independent enforcement authority.
notes: MN added (Minnesota session, statute walk): satisfies universal standing rule #1 (never waive tenant's right to call police) directly and explicitly — Minnesota is the first state in this project where the right is its own dedicated statute rather than inferred from a broader prohibited-provisions list (CO) or confirmed absent (WY/KS/NE).

title: Attorney Fee Mutuality Is Automatic Under Minnesota Law
bodyText: If your lease lets you recover attorney's fees from the tenant under certain circumstances, Minnesota law (Minn. Stat. § 504B.172) automatically gives the tenant the same right against you, to the same extent, if the tenant prevails in the same type of action. This happens by operation of law regardless of what the lease says — unlike Colorado, where the lease itself must be drafted to say fees are mutual, or Kansas, where fee-shifting is flatly prohibited. You don't need special mutuality language in a Minnesota lease for this protection to apply, but you also can't draft around it.
notes: MN added (Minnesota session, statute walk): third distinct pattern for this topic seen across the project — CO requires mutual drafting, KS flatly prohibits fee-shifting, MN makes mutuality automatic by statute regardless of lease language. No lease clause change needed; pure landlord-facing awareness.

title: Minnesota's Applicant Screening Fee Rules
bodyText: Minnesota law (Minn. Stat. § 504B.173) restricts when and how you can charge and keep an applicant screening fee: you can't charge one if you know no unit is or will reasonably soon be available, you must give a written receipt on request, and you can't cash or deposit the fee until all earlier applicants have been screened and rejected or offered the unit. You must return the fee if you reject the applicant for a reason not disclosed in advance, if an earlier applicant gets the unit instead, or for any portion not actually used for screening. You must disclose your screening service and criteria in writing before accepting the fee, and notify a rejected applicant within 14 days of the criteria they failed to meet. You also can't deny an application based on a pending eviction case, a sealed/expunged court file, or an eviction that didn't end in a writ of recovery.
notes: MN added (Minnesota session, statute walk): pre-lease/application-stage requirement, not lease clause text — logged as landlord education per this project's established pattern for procedural obligations that precede lease signing. | GAP-DISCOVERY BACKFILL 2026-09-27 (instruction 36, sources 2-4; not a re-audit): CROSS-REFERENCE ADDED -- A NEIGHBOURING SECTION WAS MISSING FROM THE LIBRARY. This row covers Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.173 (applicant screening fee). The very next section, Sec. 504B.175 (PRELEASE DEPOSIT), had no row anywhere in the library and is now covered by edu-prelease-deposit-mn and prelease-deposit-application-mn. The two are deliberately separate bodies of money: Sec. 504B.175 subd. 1 expressly excludes 'the payment of a reasonable applicant screening fee used to conduct a background check' from the definition of 'prelease deposit'. So a landlord taking money at the application stage may be holding two regulated things at once, governed by different rules and different remedies -- a screening fee under Sec. 504B.173, and anything beyond it as a prelease deposit requiring a conspicuous written agreement and 7-day return under Sec. 504B.175, with a penalty of the deposit plus one-half. Recorded here so the pairing is visible from whichever row a reader reaches first. bodyText unchanged. Note this is the same adjacency failure as Sec. Sec. 504B.195 and 504B.204: MN's statute walk read a section and moved past its immediate neighbour.

title: Minnesota's Total Monthly Payment Disclosure Requirement
bodyText: Minnesota law (Minn. Stat. § 504B.120) requires you to disclose all nonoptional fees in the lease, and to state the sum of rent plus nonoptional fees as the 'Total Monthly Payment' on the first page of the lease. Any unit advertisement must also disclose nonoptional fees and whether utilities are included. This is a formatting/placement requirement as much as a content requirement — violating it carries treble damages plus possible attorney fees. FLAG FOR TAYLOR: this is a product-level requirement (first-page placement, specific 'Total Monthly Payment' label) rather than something a lease clause alone can satisfy — relevant to the lease builder's layout for MN leases, not just its clause selection.
notes: MN added (Minnesota session, statute walk): flagged as a product/UI implication, not just a content gap, consistent with how utility-apportionment-mn's disclosure attachment was also flagged. Recommend Taylor track these lease-formatting requirements (MN's page-1 placement, MN's verbatim utility attachment) somewhere the lease-builder team will see them, separate from pure clause content.

title: Tenants Have a Statutory Right to Organize
bodyText: Minnesota law (Minn. Stat. § 504B.212) gives tenants the right to form and operate a tenant association, and requires you to allow tenants and tenant organizers to distribute information in common areas and to individual units, contact tenants by mail/phone/electronically, and convene meetings in a space at the building. You are not required to hand over tenant contact information, and a tenant association must stay independent of ownership/management (your representatives can't attend meetings unless invited). This isn't lease clause content to include or exclude — it's a landlord conduct restriction that exists regardless of what the lease says, and there's no lawful way to draft around it.
notes: MN added (Minnesota session, statute walk): genuinely new named-topic, not present in CO/WY/KS/NE or the existing checklist. Effective Jan 5, 2025 per session law. Recommend adding 'tenant right to organize' to the named-topic checklist for future states, alongside infirmity termination.

title: Tenant's Property Insurance
bodyText: Landlord's insurance does not cover loss or damage to Tenant's personal property. Except for loss or damage caused by Landlord's own gross negligence or willful misconduct, Landlord is not liable, including for ordinary negligence, for loss or damage to Tenant's personal property. Tenant will obtain and maintain renter's insurance covering Tenant's personal property and liability throughout the Term, with liability coverage of at least {{tenant_insurance_minimum}}, and will provide Landlord with evidence of coverage upon request.
notes: MN added (Minnesota session, exculpatory-clause follow-up): Minnesota has no statute voiding landlord liability-waiver language (unlike CO/KS/NE). Instead, courts apply common-law strict construction per Justice v. Marvel, LLC, 979 N.W.2d 384 (Minn. 2022), extending Dewitt v. London Rd. Rental Ctr., Inc., 910 N.W.2d 412 (Minn. 2018): a clause releasing a party from its own negligence is enforceable only if it 'clearly and unequivocally' says so; broad unqualified 'not liable' language (as in the generic clause) risks being read as failing that standard and providing no real protection. No exculpatory clause, however drafted, can bar claims for intentional, reckless, or willful/wanton conduct, so this clause carves those out explicitly rather than attempting (and failing) to cover them. Taylor reviewed and approved this draft language before it was committed to the library. GROUP NORMALISED 2026-09-19: 'Insurance & Liability' -> 'Notices & General' (session drift; 12 canonical groups are used by all nine states).

title: Pet Policy
bodyText: Tenant may keep only pets identified in writing to and approved by Landlord. Tenant will pay Landlord a pet deposit, if applicable, and pet rent of {{pet_rent_amount}} per month. Tenant is responsible for all damage, waste removal, odor, and disturbance caused by a pet, and will indemnify Landlord from claims arising from Tenant's pet(s). Landlord may revoke approval of a pet that becomes a nuisance or safety concern, and may enter the property and remove a pet if the pet becomes vicious or displays symptoms of severe illness, or if Tenant dies, becomes incapacitated, or is otherwise unable to care for the pet and Landlord believes in good faith that the pet is being abused or neglected. Except for loss caused by Landlord's own gross negligence or willful misconduct, Landlord is not liable, including for ordinary negligence, for any resulting loss to Tenant. A service animal or support animal that Tenant or an Occupant needs as a reasonable accommodation for a disability is not a pet under this Lease, and Minnesota law prohibits Landlord from requiring any additional fee, charge, or deposit for such an animal. Tenant remains responsible for any damage to the property caused by a service or support animal.
notes: MN added (Minnesota session, exculpatory-clause follow-up): Minnesota has no statute voiding landlord liability-waiver language (unlike CO/KS/NE). Instead, courts apply common-law strict construction per Justice v. Marvel, LLC, 979 N.W.2d 384 (Minn. 2022), extending Dewitt v. London Rd. Rental Ctr., Inc., 910 N.W.2d 412 (Minn. 2018): a clause releasing a party from its own negligence is enforceable only if it 'clearly and unequivocally' says so; broad unqualified 'not liable' language (as in the generic clause) risks being read as failing that standard and providing no real protection. No exculpatory clause, however drafted, can bar claims for intentional, reckless, or willful/wanton conduct, so this clause carves those out explicitly rather than attempting (and failing) to cover them. Taylor reviewed and approved this draft language before it was committed to the library. | CORRECTION 2026-09-07 (cross-state core-obligations canvass, run during the SD re-audit). **This clause was non-compliant with a mandatory Minnesota lease-content requirement.** Minn. Stat. S504B.113 subd.3(b): 'If a landlord requires an additional fee, charge, or deposit pursuant to a pet policy, the landlord **must disclose in the lease** the prohibition on additional fees, charges, or deposits for service or support animals under this section.' This clause requires a pet deposit and pet rent - so the trigger was met - and carried **no mention of service or support animals at all**. CONSEQUENCE OF THE OMISSION: S504B.113 subd.3(c) gives the tenant a **private right of action to recover pet fees paid** where the landlord omitted the disclosure and the tenant shows they would have requested and would likely have received an accommodation. The defect was therefore not merely technical - it created a recovery route against any MN landlord using this clause. HOW IT WAS FOUND: the core-obligations canvass, not the exotic-topic canvass. S504B.113 was read in full while filling MN's assistance-animal cells; the subd.3(b) lease-disclosure mandate is a lease-CONTENT rule hiding inside an animal-accommodation statute, which is why a topic-driven pass that treated assistance animals as a LANDLORD_EDUCATION subject never reached it. History of S504B.113: 1Sp2021 c 8 art 2 s 10; 2024 c 118 s 6 - so the duty has been in force since at least 2021 and was amended in 2024. S5a.1: pet-policy-mn is an MN-only override (the generic `pet-policy` is CO;WY;ND and is untouched), so no other state's rendering changes and **no propagation is owed**. Note the parallel: SD's `pet-policy-sd` was created in this same session for a different state-law reason, and KS and NE also carry their own overrides - four of seven states now diverge from the generic on this clause. NOT CHANGED, and flagged: the clause retains its indemnity and its entry-and-remove language. MN's own limits on those were not examined in this pass.

title: Storage Space
bodyText: Tenant is assigned the following storage space for Tenant's exclusive use during the Term: [identify storage space/location here]. Tenant will not store any hazardous, flammable, or perishable materials in the storage space. Except to the extent applicable law does not allow Landlord's liability to be limited, and except for loss or damage caused by Landlord's own gross negligence or willful misconduct, Landlord is not liable, including for ordinary negligence, for damage to or theft of items stored there.
notes: MN added (Minnesota session, exculpatory-clause follow-up): Minnesota has no statute voiding landlord liability-waiver language (unlike CO/KS/NE). Instead, courts apply common-law strict construction per Justice v. Marvel, LLC, 979 N.W.2d 384 (Minn. 2022), extending Dewitt v. London Rd. Rental Ctr., Inc., 910 N.W.2d 412 (Minn. 2018): a clause releasing a party from its own negligence is enforceable only if it 'clearly and unequivocally' says so; broad unqualified 'not liable' language (as in the generic clause) risks being read as failing that standard and providing no real protection. No exculpatory clause, however drafted, can bar claims for intentional, reckless, or willful/wanton conduct, so this clause carves those out explicitly rather than attempting (and failing) to cover them. Taylor reviewed and approved this draft language before it was committed to the library. GROUP NORMALISED 2026-09-19: 'Storage' -> 'Parking & Storage' (session drift; 12 canonical groups are used by all nine states). | GAP-DISCOVERY BACKFILL 2026-09-27 (instruction 36, sources 2-4; not a re-audit): CHANGED -- BODY NARROWED, AND THIS IS A JUDGMENT CALL FOR TAYLOR TO CONFIRM. The liability sentence previously read 'Except for loss or damage caused by Landlord's own gross negligence or willful misconduct, Landlord is not liable, including for ordinary negligence, for damage to or theft of items stored there.' A statutory carve-out has been added in front of it, matching the pattern already used in services-utilities-provided-mn. WHY: Minnesota's self-service storage facility act, Minn. Stat. Sec. 514.975 subd. 1, provides that 'A rental agreement may not exempt an owner from liability for damages to an occupant's personal property caused by the owner's negligence.' Sec. 514.971 subd. 2(a) defines 'self-service storage facility' as 'real property designed and used for the purpose of renting or leasing individual storage space to occupants who are to have access for the purpose of storing and removing personal property', and its only exclusions are financial-institution vaults, warehouses issuing documents of title, and commercial short-term parking -- there is NO exclusion for lockers in an apartment building, and Sec. 514.971 subd. 3 defines 'owner' to include a lessor. WHAT IS UNRESOLVED: whether a locker supplied as an incident of a dwelling lease is within the act. The better reading is that it is not, because such property is not 'designed and used for the purpose of renting or leasing individual storage space'. But a landlord who rents lockers for a SEPARATE FEE, to tenants or the public, is squarely at risk, and in that case the old sentence was VOID rather than merely weak. No Minnesota case law was searched, and the statutory text does not settle it -- so rather than assert an answer, the clause is made self-limiting so it is correct either way, and the full analysis with both readings is in the new edu-self-storage-act-scope-mn row. TAYLOR: if you would rather leave the original sentence and rely on the education row, say so and this change can be reverted -- the clause was not wrong for the ordinary apartment-locker case. State-driven, MN-only row: no Sec. 5a.1 propagation owed. Found by the instruction-28 typography sweep ('bold type', 'underlined'), not by a storage search -- Sec. 514.975 subd. 2 conditions a stored-property value limit on bold or underlined printing.

title: Services & Utilities Provided by Landlord
bodyText: Landlord will provide only the services and utilities expressly specified in this Lease, and as otherwise required by applicable law. Except for interruptions or insufficiencies caused by Landlord's own gross negligence or willful misconduct, Tenant waives all liability of Landlord, including for ordinary negligence, for any interruption or insufficiency of a service or utility resulting from causes beyond Landlord's reasonable control. Nothing in this Section waives, limits, or modifies any right or remedy Tenant has under Minnesota Statutes sections 504B.221, 504B.225, or 504B.231, or under any other provision of Minnesota law that may not be waived by a tenant.
notes: MN added (Minnesota session, exculpatory-clause follow-up): Minnesota has no statute voiding landlord liability-waiver language (unlike CO/KS/NE). Instead, courts apply common-law strict construction per Justice v. Marvel, LLC, 979 N.W.2d 384 (Minn. 2022), extending Dewitt v. London Rd. Rental Ctr., Inc., 910 N.W.2d 412 (Minn. 2018): a clause releasing a party from its own negligence is enforceable only if it 'clearly and unequivocally' says so; broad unqualified 'not liable' language (as in the generic clause) risks being read as failing that standard and providing no real protection. No exculpatory clause, however drafted, can bar claims for intentional, reckless, or willful/wanton conduct, so this clause carves those out explicitly rather than attempting (and failing) to cover them. Taylor reviewed and approved this draft language before it was committed to the library. | CORRECTED (MN re-audit 2026-09-03): added a statutory-rights carve-out. Minn. Stat. §504B.221(b), read directly from revisor.mn.gov, provides 'Any provision, whether oral or written, of any lease or other agreement, whereby any provision of this section is waived by a tenant, is contrary to public policy and void,' and gives the tenant treble damages or $500, whichever is greater, plus attorney fees for landlord-caused interruption of electricity, heat, gas, or water. Parallel non-waiver language appears in §504B.225 and §504B.231. The clause's ordinary-negligence waiver for 'interruption ... of a service or utility' overlapped this non-waivable zone. The original MN exculpatory analysis (MN log §11) reached the correct conclusion that MN has no CONSOLIDATED prohibited-provisions statute, but never enumerated the ~18 scattered per-section non-waiver rules, so this overlap was missed. State-driven fix, MN-only row — no propagation owed.

title: Habitability Baseline
bodyText: Landlord will keep the property and all common areas fit for the use intended by the parties and in reasonable repair. This includes maintaining heat at a minimum of 68 degrees Fahrenheit in all places intended for habitation, including kitchens and bathrooms, from October 1 through April 30, unless a utility company requires and instructs that the heat be reduced. It also includes extermination of insects, rodents, vermin, or other pests. These duties do not apply where the disrepair is caused by Tenant's own willful, malicious, or irresponsible conduct or that of a person under Tenant's direction or control. Landlord will keep the property and common areas in compliance with applicable health and safety laws, including any applicable local rental-licensing ordinance. Landlord will make the property and common areas reasonably energy efficient where doing so is cost-effective under applicable law. Tenant will notify Landlord promptly in writing of any condition requiring repair, and Landlord will undertake required repairs within a reasonable time, consistent with applicable law.
notes: MN added (Minnesota session, CO;WY-scoping resolution, supersedes generic landlord-maintenance): Minn. Stat. § 504B.161. Follows the established WY/KS/NE pattern (habitability-baseline-wy/ks/ne) of building a dedicated clause once a state's habitability covenant carries specifics the generic doesn't capture. MN's specifics: the 68°F Oct 1–Apr 30 heat minimum (already reflected in services-utilities-provided's note but not previously in a maintenance-duty clause), an explicit extermination duty, and a cost-effectiveness-gated energy-efficiency duty — none of which the generic landlord-maintenance clause states. Non-waivable except for a narrow tenant-delegation option (§504B.161, subd. 2) requiring adequate consideration and a conspicuous writing, which cannot waive common-area maintenance — not built into this clause as an option this session, flagged for a future session if Taylor wants to offer it. | MN re-audit 2026-09-03: confirmed Minn. Stat. §504B.161 subd. 1(b) makes these covenants NON-WAIVABLE — 'The parties ... may not waive or modify the covenants imposed by this section.' Subd. 2 allows a narrow exception: the landlord and tenant may agree in writing that the TENANT will perform specified repairs or maintenance, but only if supported by adequate consideration AND set forth in a conspicuous writing, and such an agreement may not waive subd. 1 or relieve the landlord of the duty to maintain COMMON AREAS. The original MN session did not record this. No body-text change made — the clause already states the duties affirmatively and does not attempt a waiver — but FLAGGED FOR TAYLOR: if Steinoak ever offers a tenant-performs-maintenance option for MN, it must carry adequate consideration, conspicuous formatting, and a common-areas carve-out, or it is void. | MN re-audit 2026-09-03, canvass pass 2: 'habitability operational duties' canvass topic resolved for MN — PRESENT and covered by this clause plus edu-renters-insurance-limits-mn. Enforcement mechanics confirmed as living outside this clause by design: rent escrow (§504B.385), tenant remedies action (§504B.395), emergency relief (§504B.381), and the code-violation notice track (§504B.185). Those are tenant-side procedures, not lease terms, consistent with the project's treatment of remedies elsewhere. | GAP-DISCOVERY BACKFILL 2026-09-27 (instruction 36, sources 2-4; not a re-audit): CHANGED -- BODY REFINED TO MATCH THE CURRENT TEXT OF Sec. 504B.161 subd. 1, WHICH WAS AMENDED TWICE IN 2025. The revisor's Recent History for Sec. 504B.161 shows 'Subd. 1 Amended 2025 c 11 s 1' AND 'Subd. 1 Amended 2025 c 32 art 4 s 4' (on top of 2024 c 118 s 11 and 2023 c 52 art 19 s 91). Read section-open, the current subd. 1 contains two elements this row's body did not carry: (a)(5) requires heat at 68 degrees Fahrenheit 'in all places intended for habitation including kitchens and bathrooms ... unless a utility company requires and instructs the heat to be reduced', and (a)(4) requires compliance with health and safety laws 'including ordinances regulating rental licensing'. Both are now in the body. THE ROW WAS NOT WRONG: it already carried the 68-degree minimum and the October 1 - April 30 window correctly, and omitting the utility-instruction carve-out stated the duty more strictly than the statute -- i.e. it under-claimed a landlord protection rather than over-claiming a landlord right. That is the safe direction, but it is the same shape as the holdover-figure problem in reverse, so it is fixed rather than left. rule_type, content_type and states unchanged. MN-only row: no Sec. 5a.1 propagation owed. NOT RESOLVED: which of the two 2025 chapters made which change was not traced to the session laws -- the current consolidated text was read and is what the row now reflects; flagged if Taylor wants the provenance split. The subd. 1(b) non-waivability and subd. 2 (adequate consideration plus a conspicuous writing, no common-area waiver) findings already in these notes were re-confirmed against the current text and are unchanged. PLAIN-LANGUAGE FIX applied in the same pass: my first draft of this refinement folded the heat minimum, the utility carve-out, the extermination duty and the tenant-conduct exception into a single 93-word sentence. Minnesota's Plain Language Contract Act (Minn. Stat. Sec. 325G.31) applies to this library and the project has already run a cross-state long-sentence cleanup, so lengthening a MN clause was a regression. Split into five sentences with no change in meaning: the duties, the exception and the compliance obligations are all identical to the statute. Caught by this pass's own sentence-length screen, not by review.| INSTRUCTION 29 FINDING, CORRECTED BEFORE SHIPPING: the full History line reads '... 2025 c 32 art 4 s 4; 1Sp2025 c 11 s 1'. The second 2025 amendment is from a SPECIAL SESSION (1Sp2025), and the revisor's Recent History SIDEBAR renders it as plain '2025 c 11 s 1', which hides that fact. Minnesota therefore held a 2025 special session that amended the habitability covenant. Instruction 29 requires asking whether a special session has met since the last regular one -- for Minnesota the answer is YES for 2025, and the sidebar will not tell you. Read the full History line at the foot of the section, not the sidebar, when session provenance matters. The substantive text read and reflected in this row's body is the current consolidated text either way.

title: Assistance Animal Accommodation
bodyText: A service animal or other assistance animal that Tenant or an Occupant needs as a reasonable accommodation for a disability is not considered a pet under this Lease, regardless of any pet policy, breed, weight, or size restriction stated elsewhere in this Lease. Landlord will not charge a pet deposit, pet rent, or other pet-related fee for a qualifying assistance animal. If the disability or the disability-related need for the animal is not readily apparent, Landlord may request documentation from a licensed professional confirming the disability and the need for the animal, as permitted under Minnesota law. Tenant remains responsible for any damage to the property caused by the animal beyond ordinary wear and tear. Misrepresenting a disability or an animal's status as a service or support animal may result in denial of Tenant's application or request.
notes: MN added (Minnesota session, CO;WY-scoping resolution): supersedes the generic assistance-animal-accommodation clause (currently KS;NE) for Minnesota specifically. Minn. Stat. § 504B.113 is materially more detailed than the generic FHA-baseline version: it defines a specific closed list of 'licensed professional' categories eligible to provide documentation (subd. 2), requires the lease to disclose the fee-prohibition if the landlord otherwise charges pet fees (subd. 3(b), already reflected in the fee-prohibition sentence here), and creates an application-denial remedy for misrepresentation (subd. 4-5, cross-referenced from the criminal-statute scope caveat logged separately this session — MN's criminal service-animal-misrepresentation statute, § 609.833, likely does not reach this housing scenario, so this lease-remedy sentence is the operative protection, not the criminal statute). | MN re-audit 2026-09-03: §504B.113 subd. 3(b) read in full — CONDITIONAL LEASE-DISCLOSURE DUTY confirmed. 'If a landlord requires an additional fee, charge, or deposit pursuant to a pet policy, the landlord must disclose in the lease the prohibition on additional fees, charges, or deposits for service or support animals under this section.' Subd. 3(c) gives the tenant an action to RECOVER pet fees paid where the landlord omitted the disclosure and the tenant shows they would have requested and likely received an accommodation. PRODUCT IMPLICATION, FLAGGED FOR TAYLOR: this clause is not merely available for MN leases — it becomes MANDATORY whenever the landlord charges any pet fee, deposit, or pet rent. Since pet-policy-mn carries {{pet_rent_amount}} and a pet deposit, any MN lease selecting pet-policy-mn must also force-include this clause or the landlord is exposed to fee recovery. The current builder lets the user pick clauses manually, so nothing enforces the pairing. This is a concrete instance of the REQUIRED-clause enforcement gap already flagged in the architecture review.

title: Tenants' Right to Legally Possess Cannabis and Hemp Products
bodyText: Minnesota law (Minn. Stat. § 504B.171(c)) prohibits you from banning a tenant's legal possession of cannabis products, lower-potency hemp edibles, or hemp-derived consumer products, or their use of cannabinoid or hemp-derived products — this right is non-waivable. You can still prohibit consumption by combustion or vaporization (smoking or vaping) specifically, which is exactly what Steinoak's Smoking Policy clause does — it doesn't touch possession or non-smoking use, so it stays compliant. Where landlords get this wrong is writing a broader 'no marijuana' or 'no cannabis' clause instead of a smoking/vaping-specific one — that broader version would violate this statute.
notes: MN added (Minnesota session, CO;WY-scoping resolution follow-up): companion education entry for the finding logged in §18 of the decision log. Checked directly against `smoking-policy` (already MN-tagged) — confirmed no conflict, since that clause is scoped to smoking/vaping only. This entry exists specifically to prevent a landlord from drafting a broader custom clause that would violate the statute.

title: Minnesota's Plain-Language Lease Requirement
bodyText:
If your lease term is three years or less, Minnesota's Plain Language Contract Act (Minn. Stat. §§ 325G.29-.37) applies to it, separately from the landlord-tenant code. It requires the lease to be written in clear and coherent language using words with common, everyday meanings, and to be appropriately divided and captioned. A violation is treated as a violation of law under Minn. Stat. § 8.31, which brings attorney general enforcement and a private right of action, and a court may reform or limit an offending provision to avoid an unfair result — rewriting the term rather than just reading it against you — where a material provision violates the Act, the tenant was substantially confused about rights, obligations, or remedies, and financial detriment resulted or is likely.

The limits matter as much as the rule. Making a good faith and reasonable effort to comply is a defense to civil penalties, and a landlord who made that effort may not be assessed attorney's fees or investigation costs at all — so a sincere attempt at plain drafting is a real safe harbor, not just mitigation. A tenant may recover actual damages only if the violation left them substantially confused. Class action fees against one landlord are capped at $10,000 total. Claims must be raised within six years of the tenant signing. Most importantly for you: a violation of this Act is NOT a defense to a claim arising from the tenant's own breach, and NOT a defense to an eviction action — a tenant cannot escape nonpayment by pointing at your lease's prose. Reformation relief is also unavailable once the lease's obligations have been fully performed, so the exposure is during the tenancy, not years after it ends. One timing note for month-to-month landlords: for purposes of this Act, periodic tenancies renew at the commencement of each rental period.
notes: MN added (Minnesota session, CO;WY-scoping resolution follow-up): companion education entry for the finding logged in §22 of the decision log (Minn. Stat. § 325G.30, subd. 2(3) defines 'consumer' to include anyone leasing residential premises for a term not exceeding three years, pulling most MN leases into this Act's coverage). This entry documents the obligation; it does NOT constitute an audit of Steinoak's clause library against § 325G.31's specific drafting requirements. FLAG FOR TAYLOR: a full plain-language audit of the library's drafting style is a separate, substantial future undertaking, not completed this session, and potentially relevant beyond Minnesota if other states have similar consumer-contract statutes not yet discovered. | CORRECTED 2026-09-03, same session: §325G.33 and §325G.37 read from primary text (revisor.mn.gov). THE PRIOR VERSION MISSTATED THE REMEDY. It said a violating lease 'isn't automatically void, but a court will construe any resulting ambiguity against you' — that is contra proferentem, a general contract doctrine, and is NOT what the statute provides. §325G.33 actually provides: (1) 'Any violation of section 325G.31 is a violation of a law under section 8.31, subdivision 1' — pulling in AG enforcement AND §8.31 subd. 3a's private-attorney-general right of action with costs and attorney fees, limited per §325G.34; and (2) 'In addition to the remedies provided in section 8.31, a court reviewing a consumer contract may reform or limit a provision so as to avoid an unfair result' on a three-part test — material provision violates §325G.31, the violation caused the consumer to be SUBSTANTIALLY CONFUSED about rights/obligations/remedies, and it has caused or is likely to cause FINANCIAL DETRIMENT. The court 'shall also make orders necessary to avoid unjust enrichment.' Bringing such a claim does not let the tenant withhold performance of an otherwise valid obligation. Judicial REFORMATION is a materially stronger remedy than adverse construction and the row understated it. NEW FINDING from §325G.37: 'For the purposes of this section periodic tenancies renew at the commencement of each rental period' — so a month-to-month lease is renewed monthly and re-subjected to the Act each period. Relevant to the Act's own grandfathering (contracts executed before 1983-07-01 are exempt, but renewals after that date are covered). STILL UNREAD, FLAGGED: §325G.34 'Limits on Remedies' — its text was not reached. The row references the limits' existence without characterizing them. Read before relying on the remedy description. §325G.35 (AG review) and §325G.16 (confession of judgment, previously resolved as scoped to consumer credit sales of personal property and not reaching real property leases) also remain unread in full. | COMPLETED 2026-09-03: §325G.34 'Limits on Remedies' read in full from revisor.mn.gov — the item flagged as unread in the previous note is now discharged, and the limits are substantial enough that omitting them made the row alarmist. Subd. 1: good faith and reasonable effort to comply is a DEFENSE to civil penalties. Subd. 2: a party who made that effort 'shall not be assessed attorney's fees or costs of investigation' — a genuine safe harbor, not merely mitigation. Subd. 3: class-action attorney fees and investigation costs against one person capped at $10,000 across any class action or series of class actions arising from a particular contract. Subd. 4: 'Violation of section 325G.31 is not a defense to a claim arising from a consumer's breach of a consumer contract or to an action for eviction' — LANDLORD-FAVORABLE AND IMPORTANT, a tenant cannot use lease prose to defeat a nonpayment eviction; and actual damages are recoverable only where the violation caused substantial confusion. Subd. 5: six-year statute of limitations running from the date the consumer executes the contract. Also captured from §325G.33 subd. 2's final sentence, missed in the prior pass: 'No relief shall be granted pursuant to this subdivision unless the claim is brought before the obligations of the contract have been fully performed' — reformation is a during-tenancy remedy only. NET EFFECT ON THE EARLIER RECOMMENDATION: the library-wide plain-language audit flagged at MN §27 item 5 and RA-9 item 2 remains worth doing, but its urgency drops — good-faith drafting effort is an affirmative defense to penalties and fees, and the Act cannot be used to defeat an eviction. Downgrading from a compliance risk to a quality issue. Still unread: §325G.35 (AG review) and §325G.16 (confession of judgment, previously resolved as not reaching real property leases).

title: Reserve Your Rights Every Time You Accept Late Rent
bodyText: Minnesota follows a common-law rule: if you accept rent knowing the tenant has already breached the lease, you waive your ability to EVICT for that particular past breach. What survives is broader than most landlords assume — the late fee, the rent itself, damages, your right to insist on timely payment going forward, and eviction for any later or repeated breach all remain available. The doctrine reaches only past breaches you already knew about when you accepted payment. If the tenant repeats the conduct, you may bring a new eviction action. Two practical points from the Minnesota Supreme Court's September 2025 decision in Hook & Ladder Apartments v. Nalewaja: first, what matters is your objective conduct, not what you privately intended, and simply receiving a payment and doing nothing counts as accepting it. Second, you can avoid acceptance by acting promptly — telling the tenant (or the housing agency) that you do not accept the payment, attempting to return it, segregating it, placing it in escrow, or not spending it. Whether a standing non-waiver clause in your lease defeats the doctrine is an OPEN question in Minnesota — the Supreme Court expressly declined to decide it and sent it back to the district court. Do not rely on lease boilerplate alone; act promptly at the time of acceptance.
notes: MN CORRECTED (MN re-audit 2026-09-03). Prior version was wrong in BOTH directions, the same failure shape the NE re-audit found, because it was inherited from NE reasoning rather than researched on Minnesota law (see MN log §5a.1 propagation note). (1) OVERSTATED the loss: prior text said the landlord waives the right to evict 'or otherwise act on that specific breach.' Hook & Ladder Apartments, L.P. v. Nalewaja, A23-1048 (Minn. Sept. 24, 2025), full opinion read directly, confirms the doctrine bars only eviction for that past known breach; footnote 5 expressly limits it to evictions for material breach and distinguishes the separate waiver rules for holdover and nonpayment. Gluck v. Elkan (1886) and Zotalis v. Cannellos (1917): waiver of a past breach does not relieve future performance or bar eviction for repeated breaches. (2) UNDERSTATED/OVERSTATED certainty on the fix: prior text asserted flatly that 'this isn't something a standing lease clause can fix.' That is NOT settled Minnesota law — Hook & Ladder squarely raised the lease's non-waiver clause and the Court said 'We decline to address this issue, which should be decided in the first instance by the district court.' Minnesota's answer to the KS-style standing-clause question is genuinely OPEN, exactly as MN §16 originally left it. RULE TYPE: common law, not statutory — differs from NE (§76-1433) and confirms MN never had a statutory analog. Hook & Ladder also overruled Westminster Corp. v. Anderson (Minn. App. 1995), extending the doctrine to Section 8 / public-housing-agency payments. NOTE ON TIMING: this decision issued 2025-09-24, ELEVEN MONTHS BEFORE MN's original session (2026-08-23) — a research miss, not a currency lapse.

title: Delayed Occupancy Due to New Construction
bodyText: If the property is new construction, including a new building, rehabilitation, reconstruction, or an addition, and Landlord knows the property will not be ready for occupancy by the Start Date, Landlord will notify Tenant in writing at least seven days before the Start Date. The notice will offer Tenant a choice of: (1) alternative housing provided by Landlord, reasonably equivalent in size, amenities, and location, until the property is ready; (2) a payment from Landlord equal to the Rent, to help cover the cost of alternative housing Tenant arranges; or (3) the right to terminate this Lease. If Tenant chooses option (1) or (2) and the property is still not ready within 90 days of the original Start Date, Tenant may then terminate this Lease.
notes: MN added (Minnesota session, non-blocking item follow-up): dedicated CONDITIONAL clause for the narrower statutory scenario flagged in §27, item 2. Minn. Stat. § 504B.153 — applies specifically when the property is 'new construction' (statutory definition: new building, rehabilitation, modification, reconstruction, or addition). Non-waivable (subd. 3). Landlord's violation remedy: greater of one month's rent, $1,000, or actual damages, plus attorney fees (subd. 4) — not restated in the tenant-facing clause, kept as landlord-facing awareness consistent with this project's established pattern. This clause supplements, not replaces, the generic `possession-delay` clause already extended to MN — that clause remains the default for ordinary (non-new-construction) delivery delays; this one applies specifically when the new-construction trigger is present. No `supersedes` set, since both can coexist depending on property type.

title: Return of Security Deposit
bodyText: Within thirty days after termination of this Lease and delivery of possession of the property -- or, where North Dakota law sets a different trigger for the start of that period, within thirty days after that trigger -- Landlord will deliver or mail to Tenant the Security Deposit, together with any interest required by North Dakota law, less any lawful deductions, along with a written itemization of any amounts withheld. If the Security Deposit remains unclaimed by Tenant for one year after termination of this Lease, Landlord will report and remit it as required by North Dakota's unclaimed property law.
notes: N.D.C.C. § 47-16-07.1(1),(3),(4). Interest owed only if occupancy was 9+ months per statute; not restated as a condition in the clause text itself. Same product gap as Minnesota: Steinoak doesn't yet calculate or disclose a deposit-interest amount anywhere in the builder — recommend a single shared fix covering both states rather than two separate ones. | § 47-30.2-04 VERIFIED FROM PRIMARY 2026-09-06 (ndlegis.gov/cencode/t47c30-2.pdf), previously cited but never read. Subsection (15) expressly enumerates 'A security deposit, including interest on the security deposit, made in advance by a person to secure an agreement for rights of services, less any lawsuit deductions, which remains unclaimed by the owner for more than one year after termination of the agreement' -- the one-year figure in this clause is confirmed and security deposits are a named category, not a residual catch-all. CAUTION ON THE CROSS-REFERENCE: § 47-16-07.1(3) sends the reader to '§ 47-30.2-04' for 'the reporting requirements', but 47-30.2-04 is the PRESUMPTION section and contains no reporting duty at all. The actual holder duties sit at §§ 47-30.2-21 through 47-30.2-32. The statute's own cross-reference is imprecise; a reader following it lands on a section that does not say what the referring statute claims. Duties now captured at edu-unclaimed-deposit-holder-duties-nd. Note also ch. 47-30.1 (the prior Uniform Unclaimed Property Act) was repealed by S.L. 2021 ch. 337 § 22 and replaced by ch. 47-30.2 effective 2021-07-01 -- any pre-2021 secondary source on ND deposit escheat is superseded. | AMENDED 2026-09-06 at Taylor's direction. The clause promised return within thirty days of termination-and-delivery-of-possession without qualification. N.D.C.C. § 47-16-17.1(8) does not change the thirty days; it REPLACES THE TRIGGERING EVENT in a domestic violence termination -- (a) sole victim tenant: the first day of the month following vacatur; (b) co-tenants still bound: expiration of the lease. On a 14-month lease where the victim leaves in month three, (b) lands roughly eleven months later than the unqualified clause promised. WHY THIS MATTERED DESPITE RUNNING TENANT-FAVOURABLE: a lease term more generous than statute is enforceable AS A CONTRACT TERM, so a landlord following the clause pays out far earlier than required, and a landlord following the statute breaches their own lease. The generated document was manufacturing that bind. WORDING CHOSEN DELIBERATELY NEUTRAL ('where North Dakota law sets a different trigger') rather than naming domestic violence, so a routine deposit clause does not surface DV to every tenant. The specifics stay in edu-dv-deposit-timing-nd, which is where a landlord looks when it is actually relevant. The neutral phrasing also captures any future statutory trigger substitution without a further edit.

title: Security Deposit Amount Limits
