title: Water Submeter Billing Disclosure
bodyText: Water Submeter Billing. [Include this section only if Landlord will bill Tenant for water service separately from Rent through a submeter. It must be given in at least 10-point type before this Lease is executed.] Tenant will be billed for water service separately from Rent. Landlord estimates the monthly bill for water service for dwelling units at the property at {{water_bill_estimate}}, based on {{water_bill_estimate_basis}}. Bills are due {{water_bill_due_dates}} and are paid as follows: {{water_bill_payment_procedure}}. Tenant may contact Landlord or Landlord's billing agent with questions about water service billing at {{water_billing_address}}, {{water_billing_email}} and {{water_billing_phone}}. The monthly bill for water service may include only the following charges: the amount due for the usage measured by the submeter, charged at allowable rates; a portion of the fixed fee charged by the water purveyors for water service; a fee for Landlord's or the billing agent's costs; and any late fee, with the amounts and times assessed. Tenant shall notify Landlord of any leaks, drips, water fixtures that do not shut off properly, including a toilet, or other problems with the water system, including problems with water-saving devices, and Landlord is required to investigate and, if necessary, repair these problems within 21 days. Tenant may report any leaks, drips or water fixtures that do not shut off properly to Landlord or Landlord's agent at {{water_repair_address}}, {{water_repair_email}} and {{water_repair_phone}}. Landlord will provide any of the following if Tenant asks: the location of the submeter, the calculations used to determine a monthly bill, and the date the submeter was last certified for use together with the date it is next scheduled for certification. If Tenant believes that the submeter reading is inaccurate or the submeter is malfunctioning, Tenant shall first notify Landlord in writing and request an investigation. This disclosure is only a general overview of the laws regarding submeters, and those laws can be found at Chapter 2.5 (commencing with Section 1954.201) of Title 5 of Part 4 of Division 3 of the Civil Code.
notes: CA: NEW 2026-09-28, gap-discovery source 2 (real-lease comparison). Civ. Code s1954.204, read section-open on leginfo 2026-09-28; the ten subdivisions were also taken verbatim from a FindLaw reproduction before the leginfo read, and the two agree. THE MISS: the whole of Chapter 2.5 (commencing with s1954.201) was flagged as UNREAD in landlord-entry-ca's own notes - s1954(a)(5) names it as an entry ground and the CA pass identified it as the water submetering chapter but never read its substance. A CA landlord who submeters water and bills separately therefore got NO disclosure at all from this library. Surfaced by both professional leases: the CAA form's water-conservation section and the C.A.R. RPOD's water-submeter item. PRESCRIBED FORM, s1954.204: the disclosure must be made BEFORE EXECUTING the rental agreement, IN WRITING, in AT LEAST 10-POINT TYPE, and the statute expressly says it 'may be incorporated into the rental agreement' - which is why this ships as a lease clause rather than education. That is the fifth prescribed type-size floor in the CA set. All ten items are mandatory: (a) separate billing; (b) an estimate computed EITHER from the average or median bill for comparative units at the property over any three of the past six months OR from average indoor use by a family of four of approximately 200 gallons per day plus all other monthly charges - the builder must ask which basis was used and record it; (c) due dates and payment procedures; (d) a mailing address, an email address AND a toll-free or local telephone number for billing questions; (e) the closed list of permitted charges; (f) the tenant's notification duty and the landlord's 21-DAY investigate-and-repair duty; (g) a second set of contact details, for leaks - the statute requires contact details TWICE, for billing and for leaks, and they may differ; (h) three items supplied on request, including the submeter's last and next certification dates; (i) the write-first-and-request-an-investigation route; (j) the pointer to the chapter, which the statute effectively dictates. CLASSIFIED CONDITIONAL, not REQUIRED: the duty is unconditional once the landlord elects to bill separately through a submeter, but that election is the landlord's, so the clause is included only when it applies - the same shape as ordnance-demolition-meter-disclosures-ca and unbundled-parking-ca. SCOPE, s1954.202: 'submeter' is a device measuring an individual rental unit's consumption in a multiunit residential or mixed-use structure, owned and operated by the landlord or the landlord's agent; 'property' is real property of two or more dwelling units served by a single master meter; 'landlord' excludes a tenant subletting to subtenants and excludes a common interest development. OPERATIVE 2018-01-01 by s1954.218. Distinct from Civ. Code s1940.9, the SHARED-METER disclosure in ordnance-demolition-meter-disclosures-ca: s1940.9 is about the tenant's meter serving areas outside the unit; this is about the landlord submetering and reselling. NOT READ: ss1954.207 to 1954.212, 1954.215 to 1954.217 and 1954.219, and the Water Code s537 et seq. multiunit-structure install mandate found by the same search. See edu-water-submeter-billing-ca for the billing, late-fee and termination rules.

title: Billing tenants for water through a submeter
bodyText: If you submeter water and bill tenants separately from rent, California regulates the bill itself, not just the disclosure. You may bill only for the volume measured by the submeter at allowable rates, a share of the fixed charge the water purveyor bills the property, a fee for your own or your billing agent's costs, and a late fee. Submeters must be read within three days of the same point in each billing cycle, payments must be due at the same point in each cycle, and the bill must separately set out the beginning and ending readings and dates, the consumption in gallons, the rates, any amounts carried over, any late fee, the total, the due date and how to reach you with questions. A tenant cannot be required to pay electronically. A late fee may not be imposed until 25 days after the bill is sent, and is capped at seven dollars on the first bill and ten dollars on each later bill, with all late fees in any twelve-month period limited to ten percent of the unpaid amount; partial payments go against the oldest outstanding bill. Two rules matter most. Water service charges are not rent, so unpaid water is never a pay-or-quit matter: once a bill is 180 days overdue or the unpaid amount reaches two hundred dollars, the route is a three-day notice to perform conditions or covenants or quit. And you may not shut off or interfere with water service for any reason, including nonpayment.
notes: CA: NEW 2026-09-28, gap-discovery source 2. Civ. Code ss1954.205, 1954.206, 1954.213 and 1954.214 read section-open on leginfo 2026-09-28. Companion to water-submeter-disclosure-ca. s1954.205(a) is a CLOSED LIST of billable items, with three alternative volumetric calculations - (A) the tenant's submeter share of the purveyor's usage dollars, (B) for a tiered rate schedule, either method (A) or dividing each tier's volume evenly among the dwelling units and applying each block's rate, (C) the purveyor's exact per-unit rates where it charges per dwelling unit - plus a share of recurring fixed charges computed either proportionally to volumetric use or by dividing them equally among all residential and nonresidential units, plus an administrative fee under (a)(3). s1954.206: three-day read window, same-point due dates, written consent for electronic bills which the tenant may rescind at any time with 30 days for the landlord to comply, NO requirement to pay electronically, and an eleven-item bill-content list. s1954.213 is the one that will surprise landlords: (a) no late fee until 25 days after mailing or other transmittal, with a business-day rollover; (b)(1) $7 first, $10 each subsequent; (b)(2) all late fees in any 12-month period capped at 10 PERCENT of the unpaid amount, excluding the s1954.205(a)(3) administrative fee; (b)(3) partial payments credited to the OLDEST outstanding bill; (c) at 180 days overdue OR $200 unpaid the landlord may terminate under CCP s1161 with a THREE-DAY NOTICE TO PERFORM CONDITIONS OR COVENANTS OR QUIT; (d) water service charges DO NOT CONSTITUTE RENT; (e) the landlord may not shut off or otherwise interfere with water service FOR ANY REASON, INCLUDING NONPAYMENT. Three consequences for existing rows. (1) late-fee-safe-harbor-ca: this is the only residential late-fee CAP in California, and it applies to water bills, not rent - see that row's revised notes. (2) The s1954.213(c) route is NOT a pay-or-quit, because (d) takes water out of rent; edu-three-day-notice-ca's s1161(3) limb is the applicable one. (3) s1954.213(e) is ABSOLUTE and carries NO intent element, unlike Civ. Code s789.3 in edu-self-help-eviction-ban-ca, which requires intent to terminate the occupancy - so a submetered-water shutoff is unlawful even where s789.3 would not reach it. s1954.214 preserves local ordinances adopted before 2013-01-01 on submeter approval, installation, maintenance, reading, billing and testing, so the municipal layer is live here too (edu-municipal-layer-ca). ALSO FOUND, NOT READ: PUC s739.5 (master-meter rate treatment) and Water Code ss537-537.5 (multiunit-structure submeter install mandate). The application-of-payments shared row is NOT in conflict: it orders payments of rent and lease charges, while s1954.213(b)(3) orders water bills among themselves, and water is not rent.

title: Mold Booklet Delivery
bodyText: Dampness and Mold. Before signing this Lease, Landlord gave Tenant the consumer-oriented booklet on dampness and mold for renters published by the California Department of Public Health, which describes the potential health risks and the health impact that may result from exposure to mold, and Tenant acknowledges receiving it. Landlord is not required to conduct air or surface testing of the unit or the building for mold. Tenant will promptly notify Landlord of any dampness, water intrusion, leak or visible mold in the unit.
notes: CA: NEW 2026-09-28, gap-discovery source 2 (real-lease comparison). H&S s26148 read section-open on leginfo 2026-09-28. THIS ROW EXISTS BECAUSE edu-mold-disclosure-contingency-ca WAS WRONG - see that row's correction. s26148(a): 'Residential landlords SHALL provide written disclosure to prospective tenants of the potential health risks and the health impact that may result from exposure to mold by distributing a consumer-oriented booklet developed and disseminated by the department.' (b) before entering the rental or lease agreement. (c) the requirements do not apply until the first January 1 or July 1 at least six months after the department APPROVES THE BOOKLET. TWO DIFFERENT CONTINGENCIES IN ONE ARTICLE, and that is the whole point: s26147(e) is contingent on CDPH adopting s26103/s26105 permissible exposure limits and s26130 remediation guidelines, which it has NEVER done; s26148(c) is contingent only on CDPH APPROVING A BOOKLET, which it HAS done. So s26147 is still suspended and s26148 is live. OPERATIVE DATE: CDPH's own Indoor Air Quality mold page states 'As of Jan. 1, 2022, California rental housing providers are required to provide this mold booklet to prospective tenants.' The booklet is 'Information on Dampness and Mold for Renters in California' (CDPH, dated 2021-05-12), which is consistent with a 2022-01-01 operative date under (c). EVIDENTIARY LIMIT, stated rather than glossed: the statute is read from the official revisor site, but the operative date rests on CDPH'S OWN STATEMENT of the requirement, not on a located approval instrument; the formal approval date was not found, and the CDPH page does not cite s26148. If the approval date were shown to be different the operative date could shift, but not the existence of the duty. This is the same class of administrative fact the sibling row already relies on for the s26103 non-adoption. THE DUTY IS DELIVERY, NOT DRAFTING: s26148 requires distributing the booklet, so this clause is the acknowledgment, and the app must actually deliver the current CDPH booklet - a lease recital with no booklet is not compliance. Both professional leases screened do exactly this (C.A.R. RLMM 12/24 paragraph 38A; CAA CA-041 12/24 section 33). The no-testing sentence restates s26147(b), which binds regardless of the (e) suspension. BUILDER: the booklet is a CDPH-hosted PDF that is revised - treat its URL and edition as a maintained app-config value on the legal watch, like the MyHazards address in flood-disclosure-ca. NOT DONE: no check of whether CDPH has issued a later edition than 2021-05-12.

title: Towing a vehicle from the property
bodyText: A lease clause saying you may tow is not enough in California. Unless the parcel is improved with a single-family dwelling, you may only have a vehicle removed without the vehicle owner's consent if a sign at least 17 by 22 inches, with lettering at least one inch high, is displayed in plain view at ALL entrances to the property, prohibiting public parking, stating that vehicles will be removed at the owner's expense, and giving the telephone number of the local traffic law enforcement agency together with the name and telephone number of every towing company you have a written general towing authorization agreement with. Two other routes exist: 96 hours after a parking-violation notice has been issued, or, for a vehicle missing a major part needed to operate safely, 24 hours after you notify local traffic law enforcement. If you have a vehicle removed without meeting one of those conditions, you are liable for DOUBLE the towing or storage charges. Separately, the towing company may not start a tow without your written authorization, and whoever authorizes it must normally be present and verify the violation. There is one exception built for small landlords: if the property has 15 or fewer units with no onsite owner, agent or employee, the tenant may verify the violation and request the tow from that tenant's own assigned space, giving you a signed request or email either up front or within 24 hours of calling, which you pass to the towing company within 48 hours.
notes: CA: NEW 2026-09-28, gap-discovery sources 2 and 3. Veh. Code s22658 read section-open on leginfo 2026-09-28 (subdivisions (a), (e)(1) and (l)(1)(A) quoted; the section runs about 23,000 characters and was NOT read in full - the storage-facility, notice, lien, release and enforcement limbs in (b)-(d), (f)-(k) and (m)-(n) were not read). Surfaced twice: the CAA CA-041 12/24 form cites s22658, and the landlord-scenario screen's 'car towed from the lot' scenario had no row - the same gap Arizona's screen found (edu-towing-az). s22658(a): the owner or person in lawful possession, INCLUDING a common interest development association, may cause removal under (a)(1) signage, (a)(2) 96 hours after a parking-violation notice, (a)(3) 24 hours after notifying local traffic law enforcement about a vehicle lacking an engine, transmission, wheels, tires, doors, windshield or other major part needed to operate safely, or (a)(4) where the parcel is improved with a SINGLE-FAMILY DWELLING, which needs no sign. The sign content is prescribed and includes the NAME AND TELEPHONE NUMBER OF EACH TOWING COMPANY party to a written general towing authorization agreement - so changing tow companies means changing every sign. s22658(e)(1): liability for DOUBLE the storage or towing charges for failing to comply with (a)(1), (2) or (3), or for failing to state the grounds for removal when the vehicle's legal or registered owner asks. s22658(l)(1)(A): no tow without the property owner's or lessee's WRITTEN AUTHORIZATION, and the authorizing person must be present at the time of removal and verify the alleged violation, EXCEPT for a residential rental property of 15 OR FEWER UNITS with no onsite owner, owner's agent or employee where the tenant verifies the violation and requests the tow FROM THAT TENANT'S ASSIGNED PARKING SPACE with a signed request or email, provided within 24 hours if the request was by phone, which the owner or agent gives the towing company within 48 hours; the request must carry the tenant's name and address and the date and time of the request. (l)(1)(E)(i) bars a general authorization to tow at the towing company's discretion except for fire hydrant and fire lane violations. NO CLAUSE CONFLICT: parking-ks-oh-ca and assigned-parking-space defer to law and do not promise a towing right. NOT READ: Veh. Code ss22651 and 22853, local towing ordinances, and the CID towing provisions cross-referenced from s22658(a).

title: Selling the property with a tenant in place
bodyText: Selling a tenanted California property triggers four separate duties. First, showings: entry to exhibit the unit to prospective or actual purchasers needs the ordinary written notice, but if you have given the tenant written notice within the previous 120 days that the property is for sale and that you or your agent may contact the tenant to arrange showings, you may then give ORAL notice a reasonable period before entry, and you must leave written evidence of the entry inside the unit. Second, the deposit: on transferring your interest you must either hand the remaining deposit to the buyer and then notify the tenant in writing of the transfer, the claims made against the deposit, the amount held and the successor's name, address and telephone number, or return it to the tenant with a full accounting. Before a voluntary transfer you must also give the buyer a written statement of the deposit remaining, an itemisation of lawful deductions and which of the two routes you chose. Get this wrong and you and the buyer are jointly and severally liable. Third, the identity disclosure must be kept current and runs against the new owner or manager, who has 15 days to comply and may not serve a nonpayment notice for rent that accrued while out of compliance. Fourth, nothing in California law obliges a tenant to sign an estoppel certificate or a certification of lease terms for your lender or buyer; that is a matter of contract only.
notes: CA: NEW 2026-09-28, gap-discovery sources 2 and 3. The scenario 'owner sells the property with a tenant in place' had no row, the same gap Arizona's screen found (edu-selling-rented-property-az), and both professional leases carry a sale provision: C.A.R. RLMM 12/24 paragraph 21 (for-sale signs) and paragraph 33 (tenant estoppel certificate, C.A.R. Form TEC, three days to return), and CAA CA-041 12/24 section 42 (Resident's Certification of Terms, Form CA-160, ten days). SOURCES, all previously read in this project rather than newly: Civ. Code s1954(d)(2) for the 120-day for-sale written notice and the oral-notice and written-evidence-of-entry mechanics, which landlord-entry-ca's notes deliberately left out of body text and flagged as 'a conditional landlord right worth its own row' - this is that row; s1950.5(i) transfer or return election and the tenant notice; s1950.5(j) the pre-transfer written statement to the successor; s1950.5(k) joint and several liability, with the s1950.5(k)(3) good-faith-belief shelter for a successor; s1962(c) currency of the identity disclosure, the successor's 15 days and the bar on serving a CCP s1161(2) notice for rent accrued during noncompliance. ESTOPPEL CERTIFICATES: 'estoppel certificate' and 'tenant estoppel' each return ZERO sections in the official leginfo full-text search across all codes (run 2026-09-28) - confirmed absent statute-wide. A tenant may refuse, and the deemed-acknowledgment device both forms use is a contract term whose enforceability was not researched; note also that a certificate purporting to waive s1950.5 or s1954 rights would run into Civ. Code s1953(a). FOR-SALE SIGNS: 'for sale sign' returns only Civ. Code s2079.26, not a landlord-tenant duty, so the landlord's right to post one is contract plus the s1954 showing ground. NOT INCLUDED: whether the lease binds the buyer, which is common law and not researched; Civ. Code s1946.1(d)'s 30-day notice on a sale to a natural-person owner-occupier buyer, which is already in month-to-month-notice-ca; and foreclosure, which is edu-no-foreclosure-disclosure-ca and tenant-forward-proceedings-ca. 'prospective purchasers' returned 113 sections and was NOT exhaustively reviewed - that term was not used for any absence claim here.

title: Holding deposits and money taken before the lease
bodyText: California has no holding-deposit statute, which is exactly why this is a trap. If you take money from an applicant to hold a unit, it is almost certainly security: the deposit statute defines security as any payment, fee, deposit or charge imposed at the beginning of the tenancy to reimburse you for processing a new tenant or as an advance payment of rent, used for any purpose, however denominated. Security counts toward the one-month cap and is refundable, so calling money a non-refundable holding fee does not make it one. The single exception is the application screening fee, which the statute expressly says is not security and not an advance fee, and which has its own cap, receipt and refund rules. Practical consequence: keep the screening fee separate and documented, and treat anything else you collect before move-in as refundable deposit money, or as first month's rent if that is what it is. Whether a true pre-tenancy holding deposit can be forfeited when an applicant backs out is unsettled in the statutes; the safest course is a short written agreement signed before the money changes hands that says what happens if either side walks away.
notes: CA: NEW 2026-09-28, gap-discovery sources 2 and 3. CONFIRMED ABSENT CODE-WIDE by the official leginfo full-text search across all codes, run 2026-09-28: 'holding deposit' returns 4 sections, none landlord-tenant (SHC 31151, MVC 490.5, MVC 1006.6, WAT 11706); 'application deposit' 0; 'reservation deposit' 1 (FIN 17312, not landlord-tenant). Arizona's screen produced the same shape (edu-holding-deposit-az), which is why this was screened for CA. The substantive content rests on sections already read in the CA pass: Civ. Code s1950.5(b), security defined as any payment 'however denominated' imposed at the beginning of the tenancy, whether to cover the cost of processing a new tenant or as an advance payment of rent; s1950.5(c)(1) one-month cap; s1950.5(n), a lease may not characterise security as non-refundable; and s1950.6(k), the application screening fee is NOT 'security' under s1950.5 and not an 'advance fee' - see edu-screening-fee-ca, and note s1950.6(j) includes GUARANTORS AND COSIGNERS in 'applicant', so a cosigner can be charged a screening fee. Surfaced by the C.A.R. RLMM 12/24 'MOVE-IN COSTS RECEIVED/DUE' paragraph, which collects money before the lease runs. OPEN, and the row says so rather than guessing: whether s1950.5(b) reaches money taken BEFORE a tenancy begins at all, since its own words are 'at the beginning of the tenancy' - the statutes do not settle it and no case was read. due-at-signing-ca already blocks the overcollection at signing; this row covers the money taken earlier.

title: No Liens for Tenant Improvements
bodyText: The interest of Landlord in the property will not be subject to liens for improvements made by Tenant, whether or not Landlord has consented to the improvements. Before any work begins, Tenant will notify every contractor, subcontractor and supplier that makes or furnishes any improvement to the property for Tenant of this provision.
notes: FL: Lead from the Florida Realtors Residential Lease for Single Family Home or Duplex (RLHD-3x Rev 7/16, (c)2022 Florida Realtors; approved by the Supreme Court of Florida 2010-04-15), gap-discovery source 2 (FL log, gap-discovery backfill). Primary text read section-open 2026-09-27 from the official 2026 Florida Statutes (flsenate.gov), with history line. Opt-in landlord right (instruction 30). Controlling text: Fla. Stat. §713.10 (s. 5, ch. 2023-226 latest). Why it matters: under §713.10(1), when a lessee makes an improvement 'in accordance with an agreement between such lessee and her or his lessor, the lien shall extend also to the interest of such lessor'. no-alterations (tagged FL) has the landlord consenting to alterations, which can create that agreement. §713.10(2)(a): when the lease 'expressly provides that the interest of the lessor shall not be subject to liens for improvements made by the lessee', the lessee must notify the contractor, and a knowing or willful failure makes the contract voidable at the contractor's option. FULL PROTECTION NEEDS RECORDING (§713.10(2)(b)): the lessor's interest is not subject to such liens when the lease terms expressly prohibit it AND either (1) the lease or a short form or memorandum containing the specific prohibiting language is recorded in the county before a notice of commencement, or (2) a parcel-wide notice (lessor's name, legal description, the specific lease language, and a statement that all or a majority of leases on the parcel prohibit such liability) is recorded before a notice of commencement. Contractor demand: a lessor who does not serve a verified copy of the lease provision within 30 days after a contractor's written demand, or serves a false copy, is subject to the lien (§713.10(3)). Landlord steps are in edu-construction-liens-fl. Builder: include by default in FL leases; prompt the landlord about recording. Library-wide question for Taylor (not acted on): whether other states' leases need a similar clause.

title: Tenant Improvements and Construction Liens
bodyText: In Florida, when a tenant makes improvements under an agreement with the landlord, a contractor's lien can reach the landlord's interest in the property. A lease can prevent this, but only if the lease expressly says the landlord's interest is not subject to liens for the tenant's improvements and the landlord also records, in the county's official records before the contractor records a notice of commencement, either the lease (or a short form or memorandum containing that language) or a notice covering the parcel that states the lease language and that all or most leases on the parcel contain it. The tenant must tell its contractors about the provision. If a contractor sends the landlord a written demand for a copy of the lease provision, the landlord must serve a verified copy within 30 days; failing to respond, or sending a false copy, exposes the property to the contractor's lien.
notes: FL: Lead from the Florida Realtors Residential Lease for Single Family Home or Duplex (RLHD-3x Rev 7/16, (c)2022 Florida Realtors; approved by the Supreme Court of Florida 2010-04-15), gap-discovery source 2 (FL log, gap-discovery backfill). Primary text read section-open 2026-09-27 from the official 2026 Florida Statutes (flsenate.gov), with history line. Controlling text: Fla. Stat. §713.10(1)-(3). Verification under §92.525 (not read). Notice of commencement and notice to owner: §§713.13, 713.06 (not read; L.5). Lease clause: no-liens-fl.

title: Association Approval of This Lease
bodyText: [Use only if the property is in a condominium, cooperative or homeowners' association whose governing documents require the association to approve a lease or a tenant.] This Lease is contingent on the association's approval. Tenant will apply promptly, give the association the information it reasonably requires, and cooperate in the approval process. The association's application fee will be paid by {{association_fee_payer}}. If approval has not been given by {{association_approval_deadline}}, either party may end this Lease by written notice to the other before approval is given, and Landlord will then return all amounts Tenant has paid under this Lease. Tenant will not owe Rent for any period before approval during which Tenant is not permitted to take possession. Any security deposit the association requires of Tenant is separate from the Security Deposit under this Lease.
notes: FL: Lead from the Florida Realtors Residential Lease for Single Family Home or Duplex (RLHD-3x Rev 7/16, (c)2022 Florida Realtors; approved by the Supreme Court of Florida 2010-04-15), gap-discovery source 2 (FL log, gap-discovery backfill). Primary text read section-open 2026-09-27 from the official 2026 Florida Statutes (flsenate.gov), with history line. The lead: both Supreme Court-approved Florida leases carry an association-approval contingency (single-family form §16; multi-family form §XX). Association approval itself comes from the association's governing documents, not statute; the clause handles the lease mechanics. Statutory limits: Fla. Stat. §718.112(2)(k) (condominiums; s. 8, ch. 2025-175 latest): no fee for a lease or sublease unless the association must approve it and the documents provide a fee; fee may not exceed $150 per applicant (spouses, or a parent and dependent children, count as one), adjusted every 5 years by CPI as published by DBPR; no charge for a renewal with the same lessee; if the documents authorize it, the association may require a prospective lessee to escrow a security deposit of up to 1 month's rent, protecting common elements and association property, with interest, claims, refunds and disputes handled as under Part II of ch. 83. Cooperatives: §719.106 has a parallel rental deposit (abstract only, not read). Homeowners' associations: §720.306(1)(h) (read) limits which owners a post-2021-07-01 rental restriction binds. Rent abatement before possession is consistent with possession-delay (tagged FL). Deposit returned on termination follows security-deposit-return-fl. Builder: show when the landlord indicates an association requires approval.

title: Condominium and HOA Rules for Renting
bodyText: Florida condominium and homeowners' associations can affect a rental in three ways. First, approval: if the association's documents require it to approve leases, a condominium association may charge an approval fee only if its documents provide for one, capped at $150 per applicant (adjusted for inflation every 5 years) and not charged for a renewal with the same tenant; it may also require the tenant to put up a deposit of up to one month's rent to protect the common areas, handled like a landlord's deposit. Second, rental restrictions: a homeowners' association rule adopted after July 1, 2021 that prohibits or regulates rentals binds only owners who buy after it is adopted or who consent to it, except that any association may regulate leases shorter than 6 months and limit rentals to three times a year. Third, rent demands: if the owner of a condominium unit or of a home in a homeowners' association falls behind on association charges, the association can demand in writing, using a notice form set by statute, that the tenant pay the rent to the association until the owner's debt is paid. The tenant must then pay the association and is immune from the landlord's claim for the rent paid to it. For a condominium, the tenant also gets credit against the rent owed to the landlord, and the association can serve Chapter 83 notices and evict the tenant for not paying it. A landlord may not retaliate against a tenant for paying rent to an association on its demand.
notes: FL: Gap found by the landlord-scenario screen (gap-discovery source 3, FL log, gap-discovery backfill). Primary text read section-open 2026-09-27 from the official 2026 Florida Statutes (flsenate.gov), with history line. Controlling text: Fla. Stat. §718.112(2)(k) (approval fee, lessee deposit); §720.306(1)(h)1-5 (HOA rental restrictions after 2021-07-01; s. 22, ch. 2021-99); §718.116(11)(a)-(f) (condominium rent demand: prescribed notice to the tenant, notice to the owner, receipts, tenant immunity, liability capped at rent owed, landlord credit, association may use §83.56 notices and §§83.59-83.625 eviction but has no §83.51 duties, receiver may supersede; s. 19, ch. 2023-203 latest); §83.64(1)(e) (retaliation). HOA rent demand: Fla. title: Removing Squatters (Unauthorized Occupants)
bodyText: A Florida property owner can ask the sheriff to remove squatters from a residential property without going to court if all of these are true: the owner or the owner's agent makes the request; the property includes a dwelling; the people entered unlawfully and are still there; the property was not open to the public when they entered; the owner told them to leave; they are not current or former tenants under a written or oral rental agreement the owner authorized; they are not the owner's immediate family; and there is no pending lawsuit about the property between the owner and them. The owner files a sworn complaint with the sheriff, who then serves a notice to vacate immediately and puts the owner back in possession; the sheriff may charge for standing by while locks are changed and belongings removed. A person wrongly removed can be restored to possession and recover actual damages, statutory damages of three times the fair market rent, costs and attorney's fees. This procedure cannot be used against a tenant or a former tenant, including one who stays after the lease ends; that requires an eviction.

title: Sales Tax on Short Rentals
bodyText: Florida charges a 6 percent state tax on rent for living quarters in a hotel, apartment house, rooming house, tourist or trailer camp, mobile home park, recreational vehicle park, condominium or timeshare resort. The tax does not apply to a tenant with a bona fide written lease longer than 6 months for continuous residence, to a tenant who has lived continuously in the same place for more than 6 months and has already paid the tax for the first 6 months, or to rentals in buildings intended primarily as people's permanent residence. Full-time postsecondary students and active-duty military are also exempt. A lease of 6 months or less can therefore carry sales tax, and county tourist taxes may apply as well. Whether the tax reaches a single-family house is not settled by this statute's list of facility types.

title: Uncashed Deposit Refunds
bodyText: If a tenant never cashes a Florida landlord's deposit refund, the money does not become the landlord's. Under Florida's unclaimed property law, intangible property a business holds or owes is presumed abandoned after a dormancy period, generally 5 years from when it became payable unless another period is specified by law, and must then be reported and delivered to the state. A landlord should keep records of the refund and the tenant's last known address.

title: Towing Tenants' and Guests' Vehicles
bodyText: A Florida property owner, a tenant of the property, or someone either authorizes (including a condominium association's representative) may have a vehicle parked without permission towed by a regular towing business, without paying for the tow. Except for property that is part of a single-family residence, or when the vehicle's owner is told in person that the space is reserved, the owner must first post permanent signs at each driveway entrance: within 10 feet of the road, with light-reflective letters at least 2 inches high stating that unauthorized vehicles will be towed at the owner's expense, the words "tow-away zone" in letters at least 4 inches high, the tower's name and phone number, mounted 3 to 6 feet above the ground, and in place at least 24 hours before any tow. The tower must store the vehicle nearby, notify the police within 30 minutes, release it within 1 hour of request, and stop and release it for half the posted rate if the owner arrives during the tow. A person who improperly causes a tow is liable for the removal and storage costs, damages, attorney's fees and court costs. Counties and cities may add rules and set maximum towing rates.

title: Removing a Squatter Without an Eviction Action (2026 Act)
bodyText: Kansas enacted a removal of squatters act in 2026 (L. 2026, ch. 56; H.B. 2378). It lets the owner of a dwelling unit, or the owner's agent, have a squatter removed by law enforcement instead of filing an eviction case. A squatter is a person occupying a dwelling who is not entitled to occupy it under a lease or rental agreement and is not authorized to occupy it by a tenant. The owner submits a notarized affidavit to local law enforcement stating six things: that the affiant is the owner or the owner's agent; that the person entered and remains unlawfully; that the person was not authorized to enter; that the person is not a tenant or a holdover tenant; that the affiant asked the person to leave and the person refused; and that the person is not an immediate family member. Law enforcement verifies the affiant's ownership and apparent entitlement to relief, and no sooner than 24 hours after receiving the affidavit an officer serves a notice to vacate immediately, either by hand or by posting it on the front door or entrance. Occupancy by a squatter is excluded from the Kansas Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, and removing a squatter does not require an eviction action under that Act. Three limits make this a poor tool to reach for casually. A current or former tenant is not a squatter, and a holdover tenant is expressly excluded, so a tenant who overstays still goes through the Chapter 61 eviction process. An immediate family member cannot be removed this way; the act's list runs to spouse, child, grandchild of any degree, parent, mother-in-law, father-in-law and grandparent, among others. And the downside is severe: a false affidavit is a class A nonperson misdemeanor, and a person wrongly removed may recover possession, actual costs and damages, treble the fair market rent as punitive damages, court costs and attorney fees. Use this only where you are certain there is no tenancy and no family relationship. Anything short of that belongs in an eviction action.

title: Abandonment Ends the Lease Unless You Try to Re-Rent
bodyText: If a Kansas tenant abandons the dwelling unit, you must make reasonable efforts to rent it at a fair rental (K.S.A. 58-2565(c)). This is not only a duty to mitigate damages — the statute attaches a consequence that ends the lease. If you re-rent for a term beginning before the original rental agreement would have expired, the agreement is deemed terminated as of the date the new tenancy begins. And if you fail to use reasonable efforts to re-rent at a fair rental, or you accept the abandonment as a surrender, the rental agreement is deemed terminated by you as of the date you had notice of the abandonment. Either way rent stops accruing from that date, so a landlord who leaves an abandoned unit sitting and later sues for the balance of the term will find the claim cut off at the notice date rather than running to the end of the lease. Two practical consequences. Document the re-letting effort — when it was listed, at what rent, showings, applications, why any applicant was turned down — because that record is what preserves a rent claim past the abandonment date. And note that the statute deems the termination to be by the landlord, which matters anywhere your rights or a tenant's turn on which party ended the tenancy.

title: What You Can Sue For When the Lease Ends
bodyText: On termination of the rental agreement, K.S.A. 58-2568 gives you a claim and lets you file an action for possession, for rent, or for both. It also gives you a separate claim for actual damages for breach of the rental agreement, and that damages action may be filed before the rental agreement's termination date — you do not have to wait for the term to run out to sue on a breach. Two things follow. Possession and money are not alternatives in Kansas: suing for possession does not make you give up the rent claim, and you can combine them. And because the damages claim is for actual damages, it is bounded by the other Kansas limits already in this library — the re-letting duty on abandonment, which cuts rent off at the notice date (K.S.A. 58-2565(c)), and the holdover cap of one and one-half times periodic rent or actual damages (K.S.A. 58-2570(c)). Kansas gives you no statutory right to accelerate the remaining rent, and no right to recover attorney fees, because K.S.A. 58-2547(a)(3) voids a lease fee-shifting provision outright.

title: Tenant Counterclaims and Rent Paid Into Court
bodyText: In a Kansas action for possession based on nonpayment of rent, or an action for rent where the tenant still occupies the premises, the tenant must raise any counterclaim for amounts recoverable under the rental agreement or applicable law in that action or forfeit the right to bring it (K.S.A. 58-2561(a)). The court may order the tenant to pay accrued and future rent into court and then determine each party's net obligation; the party owed money is paid first out of the funds on deposit, with any remainder paid by the other party. Where no rent remains due after that netting, the tenant may prevail in the possession action. If the tenant has already vacated and you are suing only for rent, the tenant may still counterclaim but is not required to deposit rent into court (58-2561(b)). What this means in practice is that a habitability or deposit counterclaim normally lands inside your own eviction case rather than arriving as a separate suit later, and the rent on deposit is the fund your judgment gets paid from — so expect the case to turn on the net number, not on possession alone.

title: Remedies When Entry Is Refused — and When You Enter Wrongly
bodyText: Kansas attaches remedies to entry in both directions (K.S.A. 58-2571). If the tenant refuses to allow lawful access to the dwelling unit, you may obtain injunctive relief to compel access or terminate the rental agreement, and in either case recover actual damages. If you make an unlawful entry, or a lawful entry in an unreasonable manner, or make repeated demands for entry that are otherwise lawful but have the effect of harassing the tenant, the tenant may obtain injunctive relief or terminate the rental agreement, and recover actual damages. Read this with the entry standard itself: Kansas requires only reasonable notice at reasonable hours, with no fixed number of hours, so what counts as a lawful entry is judged against that standard rather than against a statutory clock. The practical point for a landlord is that refusal of access is a remedy you have to go get — Kansas gives you an injunction or termination, not a right to let yourself in — and that a pattern of entry demands can itself be the violation even when each individual entry would have been lawful.

title: The Kansas Eviction Process, Step by Step
bodyText: A Kansas eviction runs as a limited-actions case under Chapter 61, Article 38, and it is separate from the notice the lease and the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act require. Before filing, you must give a notice to leave the premises at least three days before starting the lawsuit (K.S.A. 61-3803). That three-day period is counted as three consecutive 24-hour periods, intermediate weekends, legal holidays and days the clerk's office is closed are included in the count, and if you mail the notice you add two days. It may be delivered to the other party, left with a person over 12 years of age at the premises, posted in a conspicuous place, or mailed to the premises. The statute allows this notice to be combined with a notice under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, so one properly drafted notice can serve both purposes rather than requiring two. You then file a petition, and the court sets the appearance date in the summons: not less than three nor more than 14 days after the summons issues (K.S.A. 61-3805). After a judgment for possession the court issues a writ of restitution at your request, and the writ must be executed within 14 days after the person named in it receives it (K.S.A. 61-3808). If an appeal stay is entered, execution stops immediately, and if possession has already been restored to you it goes back to the tenant. Nothing in this process lets you shortcut the Act's own notice-and-cure periods, which run first.

title: When a Tenant's Unpaid City Utility Bill Can Become a Lien on Your Property
bodyText: In Kansas, unpaid fees for utility service supplied by a municipally owned utility can become a lien on the property served, certified to the county clerk and collected on the tax roll with the usual tax penalties (K.S.A. 12-808c). One subsection decides who carries that risk in a rental: "A lien shall not attach to property for unpaid utility fees or charges, when the utility service has been contracted for by a tenant and not by the landlord or owner of the property." So whose name is on the utility account is not an administrative detail — it determines whether the city can put the tenant's unpaid water, sewer, trash, gas or electric bill on your tax bill. If the tenant contracts for the service, no lien attaches to your property. If you keep the account in your own name for convenience, for a master-metered building, or because the tenant could not get service, the exception does not apply and the lien can attach. The practical rule is to require tenant-name accounts wherever the service is separately metered, and to treat any account you hold yourself as your own credit exposure rather than the tenant's. Note the limit: this concerns municipally owned utilities. Investor-owned utilities and rural water districts are outside it, and a rural water district's own collection remedies are a separate question.

title: A Deposit Refund the Tenant Never Cashes Is Not Yours
bodyText: When you mail a security deposit refund and the tenant never cashes it, the money does not revert to you. Under the Kansas Disposition of Unclaimed Property Act it becomes presumed abandoned and has to be reported and delivered to the state. A refund owed to a former tenant falls in the Act's catch-all category, "all other property, five years after the owner's right to demand the property or after the obligation to pay or distribute the property arises, whichever first occurs" (K.S.A. 58-3935(a)(16)). A holder of property presumed abandoned reports it to the state administrator before November 1 each year, covering the 12 months ending the preceding July 1 (K.S.A. 58-3950). There is a small-holder exemption: no report is required if you have no individual item over $100 and your aggregated total is under $250, unless the administrator requires otherwise — which will not cover most deposit refunds, since a typical Kansas deposit is capped at a month's rent and exceeds $100. Two practical points. Keep the unclaimed refund in a form you can still deliver five years later rather than writing it back into income. And this is separate from the deposit return rules themselves: complying with K.S.A. 58-2550's 14-day and 30-day deadlines is what avoids the 1.5-times penalty, while this Act governs what happens to the money afterwards.

title: Holding Deposits Sit Outside the Deposit Cap — Until the Lease Names Them
bodyText: Kansas defines a security deposit as "any sum of money specified in a rental agreement, however denominated, to be deposited with a landlord by a tenant as a condition precedent to the occupancy of a dwelling unit" (K.S.A. 58-2543(m)). Two limits in that sentence matter. It is denomination-blind, so calling money a fee, a reservation charge or a last-month payment does not keep it out — if the lease specifies it and occupancy depends on it, it is a security deposit and the K.S.A. 58-2550 cap, retention rules and return deadlines apply. But it is also agreement-scoped: money taken at application, before any rental agreement exists, is not specified in a rental agreement. A true pre-lease holding deposit therefore sits outside the deposit statute — which also means the tenant does not get 58-2550's remedies for it, and Kansas does not otherwise regulate the rental application process. The trap is the handoff. The moment the signed lease recites the holding money, or credits it toward the deposit or first month's rent, it becomes money specified in a rental agreement, counts against the cap, and starts the return clock. Decide up front which of the two you are taking, say so in writing to the applicant, and if you intend it to become part of the deposit, count it against the cap from the start.

title: Nobody Can Collect the Rent Free of the Habitability Duties
bodyText: Kansas law provides that "A rental agreement, assignment, conveyance, trust deed or security instrument may not permit the receipt of rent free of the obligation to comply with subsection (a) of K.S.A. 58-2553" (K.S.A. 58-2549). Subsection (a) of 58-2553 is the landlord's habitability duty — codes materially affecting health and safety, common areas, the electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating and air-conditioning systems, trash removal, running water and reasonable hot water and heat. What the section does is close the gap between who takes the rent and who owes the duties. An assignment of rents to a lender, a deed, a trust deed or a security instrument cannot be drafted so that the party receiving rent escapes the habitability obligation, and neither can the lease itself. This matters in three ordinary situations: financing that assigns rents as collateral, a receiver or lender collecting rents during a default, and a sale where rent is directed to a new party. In each case the duty travels with the rent. Check any rent-assignment language in your loan documents against this section rather than assuming the lease is the only place the problem could arise.

title: No Kansas Foreclosure Notice or Lease-Survival Statute for Tenants
bodyText: Kansas has no state statute requiring a landlord to disclose a pending foreclosure to a tenant or applicant, and no state statute governing whether a lease survives a foreclosure sale. Several states in this library do have one; Kansas does not. What governs instead is Kansas's judicial foreclosure process, including the redemption period in K.S.A. 60-2414, and the federal Protecting Tenants at Foreclosure Act, which requires a successor in interest to honor an existing bona fide lease and to give a bona fide tenant at least 90 days' notice to vacate. Two practical consequences. If you are selling or losing a tenanted property, Kansas law gives you no disclosure obligation to the tenant, but the tenancy is not yours to terminate merely because the property is in foreclosure. And if you are buying at a Kansas foreclosure sale, expect to inherit the tenancy rather than an empty unit, and expect the federal 90-day floor to apply before you can require the tenant to leave.

title: No Foreign-Adversary Property Ownership Restriction in Kansas
bodyText: Kansas has no statute restricting the ownership of real property by foreign adversaries or by entities tied to designated countries. The legislature passed one in 2024 — House Substitute for Senate Bill 172 — and the Governor vetoed it on May 10, 2024. The veto was not overridden: the bill appears in the 2024 session laws only as a governor's veto message, with no session-law chapter number, and no Kansas enactment on the subject followed in 2025 or 2026. So a Kansas landlord selling to, buying from, or leasing to an entity with foreign ownership faces no state-law ownership restriction or registration duty of this kind. Federal rules still apply on their own terms, including CFIUS review of certain real estate transactions near sensitive sites and the federal agricultural foreign-investment reporting requirement, neither of which this Kansas absence affects.

title: No State Towing Rules for Your Parking Lot
bodyText: Kansas does not regulate towing from private rental property the way some states do. There is no state statute requiring signs at the entrances to your lot, no requirement that you sign a written authorization for each tow, and no state cap on what a towing carrier may charge the vehicle's owner. What Kansas does have is an abandoned-vehicle route and a tower's lien. Under K.S.A. 8-1102, where a vehicle is abandoned on private property the public agency for that jurisdiction may remove and dispose of it "upon request of the owner or occupant of such real property" — a request, not a written authorization — and whoever removes the vehicle at that agency's request has a possessory lien on it for the costs of removing, towing and storing it. K.S.A. 8-1103 carries the related lien provisions. The practical upshot is that the lease clause and your own arrangement with the towing company are doing most of the work here, because no state signage or authorization statute backs them up. Two cautions: Kansas cities have home-rule authority and many do regulate towing by ordinance, and the Kansas Corporation Commission regulates motor carriers — neither was researched, so check the ordinance for each property's city before relying on this.

title: No State Pool Barrier Requirement for Rental Property
bodyText: Kansas has no state statute imposing a pool fence, barrier, gate or safety-notice requirement on a residential landlord. The Kansas pool rules that do exist sit in the Department of Health and Environment's child care regulations — K.A.R. 28-4-129 for child care centers and K.A.R. 28-4-594 for family child care homes — and they apply because of the licensed child care activity, not because the property is rented. Pool barrier requirements in Kansas therefore come from whichever building or pool code the city or county has adopted, which varies from place to place. Two things follow for a landlord. Check the local adopted code for each property with a pool rather than assuming a statewide rule exists, since the absence of a state statute is not the absence of a requirement. And note the overlap with the residential-use clause: if a tenant runs a licensed child care operation out of the home, the K.A.R. 28-4 pool and fencing rules start applying to your property through the tenant's license, which is one more reason the residential-use-only restriction is worth enforcing.

bodyText: If Tenant paid Landlord any money to hold the property before this Lease was signed, Landlord will apply that money to Tenant's security deposit or to Rent. Landlord will not keep it as a separate charge and will not treat it as a nonrefundable fee.

title: Taking Money to Hold a Unit: Minnesota's Prelease Deposit Rules
bodyText: If you take money from a prospective tenant before a lease is signed, Minnesota law (Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.175) lets you accept it only under a conspicuous WRITTEN agreement that states the circumstances in which you will return it, and states that you must return it within seven days of one of those circumstances occurring. 'Return' means postmarked within seven days, though the applicant may instead ask you to destroy the payment or hold it for pickup. If the applicant does sign a lease, you must apply the money to their security deposit or rent -- you cannot keep it as a fee. Get the return conditions in writing before you take the money: the penalty is the full amount of the deposit plus another one-half of it, and there is no cure once you have taken money with no written agreement. A reasonable applicant screening fee is NOT a prelease deposit and is governed separately.
notes: MN added (gap-discovery backfill 2026-09-27, checklist instruction 36 -- sources 2, 3 and 4 only; not a re-audit). Official Minnesota Revisor full-text search of the 2025 Minnesota Statutes (api.revisor.mn.gov search service, exact-phrase with word variants), every landlord-relevant hit read section-open on revisor.mn.gov. Subd. 2(b) defines 'return' as postmarked within seven days, with an applicant-requested alternative of destruction or retrieval. Subd. 4: liability is the deposit plus one-half as a penalty, 'in addition to any other remedies'. History: 1999 c 97 s 1; 1999 c 199 art 1 s 174 -- no recent amendment (Recent History block empty). title: Submetering and Separate Utility Billing: The Rules Outside Chapter 504B
bodyText: If you submeter electricity or natural gas, or apportion gas, in a shared-metered residential building, Minn. Stat. Sec. Sec. 216B.022 to 216B.024 impose a compliance regime separate from Sec. 504B.216, and it puts you under the Public Utilities Commission's authority. The main duties: submeters installed on or after January 1, 2025 must meet ANSI standards, and every submeter, whenever installed, must measure accurately. You may not apportion electricity at all -- electricity may only be submetered. Charge only for what the tenant's own unit used, never for common areas or space you use yourself; divide fixed and non-usage charges equally among the units; and pass through each unit's equal share of any bill credit. Every submetered bill must show the present and previous readings, the reading date, your rate and the utility's rate to you, the tenant's share of taxes and surcharges, any credit, any administrative billing charge, the total, and the due date and late-fee date and amount. If you overcharge, refund promptly; if you undercharge, you may bill back only six months, and you must offer a no-interest, no-fee payment plan where the tenant was not at fault. You must offer a payment plan for any overdue utility bill, and if you cannot agree, tell the tenant they can go to the Commission's consumer affairs office and give them its current phone number and email. When a tenant moves out before the real bill arrives, you may issue an ESTIMATED final bill based on the previous billing period, prorated to the move-out date, with no extra charges beyond the administrative billing charge and a late fee limited to the prior period.

title: You Must Hand Over Outstanding Inspection and Condemnation Orders
bodyText: Minnesota law (Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.195) makes you give out copies of certain code-enforcement paperwork, and the duty runs to APPLICANTS as well as tenants. If a citation has been issued on an inspection order that the housing inspector marks as threatening a tenant's health or safety, or if there is an outstanding condemnation order or declaration that the premises are unfit for human habitation, you must deliver or mail a copy: to an existing tenant within 72 hours of the citation; to any person BEFORE they sign a lease or pay rent or a security deposit for a new tenancy; and to anyone before they take over ownership. If the order does not involve a health-or-safety violation, you instead post a summary in a conspicuous place in each affected building, together with notice that you will make the order available for review on request by a tenant or prospective tenant, and you must actually provide it when asked. You are not in violation if you have only an initial repair order, if the repair deadline and any extension have not expired, if fewer than 60 days have passed since the deadline expired with no citation issued, or if you finish the repairs in time. Proving you disclosed is an affirmative defense. The tenant's remedy runs through the private attorney general statute, so damages, costs and attorney fees are available, and the duty cannot be waived by the lease.

Subd. 1(a) the three recipients and the 72-hour clock; note (2) is triggered by signing OR paying rent OR paying a security deposit, whichever comes first. Subd. 1(b) the conspicuous-posting alternative for non-health/safety orders plus the on-request production duty. Subd. 2 remedies via Sec. 8.31 subd. 3a plus equitable relief. Subd. 3 the four exceptions. Subd. 4 affirmative defense. Subd. 5 remedies are additional and any lease waiver is 'contrary to public policy and void'. title: Never Accept Rent or a Deposit After a Condemnation or Vacate Order
bodyText: Minnesota law (Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.204) flatly bars you from accepting rent or a security deposit once the premises have been condemned or declared unfit for human habitation, ordered vacated for violating a housing, health or fire code or a rental licensing ordinance, or ordered vacated under a government taking. If you take money anyway you owe the tenant actual damages PLUS three times everything you collected after the date of the order, plus costs and attorney fees -- and the violation also breaches the statutory habitability covenant, which opens up the tenant-remedies machinery on top. The statute says it must be construed liberally in the tenant's favour, and no lease term can waive it. Practically: the moment a vacate or condemnation order lands, stop collecting, and do not accept a payment a tenant offers voluntarily.

Sec. 504B.385 and 504B.395. Paragraph (b): remedies are additional and any lease waiver is void. bodyText: Between November 15 and April 15, if Tenant removes from, abandons, or vacates the property or any part of it while the Term is still running, Tenant will first give Landlord at least three days' written notice of Tenant's intention to do so. This Section does not apply where the tenancy is ending. Tenant understands that the property contains plumbing and other pipes that can be damaged by freezing, and that Minnesota law makes failure to give this notice a criminal offense.

title: The Unlawful-Activities Covenant Is in Every Minnesota Lease Whether You Write It or Not
bodyText: Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.171 writes a covenant into every Minnesota residential lease, oral or written, so you do not need a crime-free clause to have one. Both you AND the tenant covenant not to allow controlled substances in violation of the criminal drug chapter, prostitution or prostitution-related activity, unlawful use or possession of a firearm, or stolen or robbery-obtained property -- and the covenant reaches the common area and curtilage, not just the unit. The covenant is not broken by a third party's conduct unless you or the tenant knew or had reason to know of it, so what matters in practice is what you did once you found out. The tenant separately covenants not to commit domestic-abuse-type acts against another tenant or authorized occupant. A breach voids the tenant's right to possession. Two limits worth knowing: you cannot prohibit a tenant from legally possessing cannabis products, lower-potency hemp edibles or hemp-derived consumer products, and the tenant cannot waive that right -- but smoking or vaping them is outside the protection, so a smoke-free policy is still enforceable. And because the covenant binds you too, allowing the conduct is your own breach, not merely a ground against the tenant.

title: A Nuisance Notice Can Close Your Building for a Year, and Evicting the Tenant Is the Way Out
bodyText: This is the largest landlord-side risk in Minnesota law that has nothing to do with Chapter 504B. Under Minn. Stat. Sec. Sec. 617.80 to 617.87, a prosecuting attorney who believes a nuisance is being maintained in your building must first serve written notice on ALL owners, by personal service or certified mail. A nuisance can be established by a single incident of prostitution-related activity, or by two or more incidents of certain other offences within the previous 12 months, anywhere within the building. The notice tells you what kind of nuisance is alleged, summarises the evidence and dates, and warns that if you do not abate it or otherwise resolve matters with the prosecutor within 30 DAYS, a district court complaint may follow that can enjoin the use of your building FOR ANY PURPOSE FOR ONE YEAR. Your way out is Sec. 617.85: as the owner you may file a motion in that same abatement proceeding to cancel the offending tenant's lease and recover the premises, and maintaining a nuisance is an additional ground for eviction beyond the ordinary grounds. Two features make this genuinely protective. It is no defence that your lease does not list this ground, so a thin lease does not cost you the remedy. And the court must not order abatement of the premises where it cancels that tenant's lease and grants you restitution AND finds both that the acts were committed by that tenant and that the tenant was NOT acting in conjunction with you or under your control. Read that second condition carefully: evicting the tenant protects the building only if you were not party to the conduct, so a landlord who knew and did nothing cannot evict his way out of an abatement order. Do not let the 30 days run.

Subd. 4(b)(3): failure to abate or resolve within 30 days of service may lead to a complaint that 'could, among other remedies, result in enjoining the use of the building for any purpose for one year or, in the case of a tenant, lessee, or occupant, could result in cancellation of the lease'. Sec. 504B.281 to 504B.371; 'It is no defense ... that the lease or other agreement controlling the tenancy or leasehold does not provide for eviction or cancellation of the lease upon the ground provided in this section'; on a finding the court SHALL cancel and grant restitution; and the court 'must not order abatement of the premises' where it cancels the lease, grants restitution of that portion, and finds the acts were committed by that tenant. title: Minnesota's Expedited Eviction Track Changed on August 1, 2026
bodyText: Minnesota has a fast eviction track, and Laws 2026, ch. 81 widened it as of August 1, 2026. Under Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.321 subd. 2 you may seek an expedited hearing where the case is brought on the unlawful-activities covenant, or where the tenant seriously endangers other residents' safety, intentionally and seriously damages property -- and now also where the tenant ASSAULTS you, your employees or your contractors, using the criminal code's definition of assault. You must file an affidavit stating specific facts and instances explaining why expedition is required; a referee or judge screens it, and the hearing is set no less than five and no more than seven days from issuance of the summons, which must be served within 24 hours unless the court orders otherwise. Two cautions. The penalty for seeking expedition without sufficient basis rose from $500 to $750 in the same 2026 act. And -- this part is not new, it has been in the statute since 2023 -- the court may consider ONLY the expedited allegations and may NOT consolidate them with anything else, including breach of lease, holdover, or nonpayment of rent. So if you want unpaid rent as well, that is a separate action; do not bundle it in and expect the court to hear it.

title: If Your Online Rent Portal Goes Down, Minnesota Law Is Now Against You
bodyText: Laws 2026, ch. 81 rewrote Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.118 -- now titled PAYMENT OF RENT -- and added digital-payment rules effective August 1, 2026. A 'digital payment platform' is any electronic application or system under your direct control, or run by a vendor under contract with you, that lets a user conduct financial transactions. If you require or permit tenants to pay through one, then whenever it is not functioning you must offer an alternative way to pay, and you may NOT charge any fee for using that alternative. If you know the platform is down you must either restore access or offer an alternative as soon as practicable. And if a tenant fails to pay because BOTH the platform and the alternative you provided are not working for them, you may not take any adverse action -- the statute names filing an eviction and assessing late fees specifically. The teeth are in the next subdivision: the tenant has an affirmative defence to a nonpayment eviction if you violated the section, and on a showing that you did, the eviction action MUST BE DISMISSED and the tenant gets reasonable attorney fees plus any other equitable relief. Keep dated records of outages and of the alternative you offered. The cash-receipt duty is unchanged and is now subdivision 2.

title: Never Name a Tenant's Child as a Defendant in an Eviction
bodyText: New Minn. Stat. Sec. 504B.2136, effective August 1, 2026, says a residential landlord shall not list the minor child of a residential tenant as a defendant in an eviction action complaint against that tenant. The only exception is where a minor is the only person renting the unit from you -- then you may name the minor. The rule cannot be waived or modified by the parties, and any lease provision purporting to waive it is contrary to public policy and void. The tenant recovers actual damages or $300, whichever is greater, for a violation. This is easy to breach by accident: if your process is to name every occupant on the complaint, change it now. It applies to eviction actions filed on or after August 1, 2026.

Paragraph (a) the prohibition and the sole-minor-tenant exception; paragraph (b) non-waivable, any waiver 'contrary to public policy and void'; paragraph (c) 'actual damages or $300, whichever is greater'. EFFECTIVE DATE clause read in full: 'This section is effective August 1, 2026, and applies to eviction actions filed on or after that date.' Signed 2026-05-12; in force as of this pass. NOT A NEW TOPIC LIBRARY-WIDE -- CORRECTED BEFORE SHIPPING. My first draft of this row asserted that no state had a row on who may be named as an eviction defendant. That was wrong, and the topic_key alignment check caught it: Ohio already carries edu-minor-tenant-filing-oh on topic_key 'minor-tenant-filing'. Ohio's rule is stronger in remedy and narrower in target -- naming a minor TENANT alongside a parent or adult guardian means the court SHALL dismiss without prejudice AND SHALL order the landlord to pay the minor tenant's reasonable attorney fees, and Ohio defines 'minor tenant' as an unemancipated tenant under 18. Minnesota's Sec. 504B.2136 instead bars naming the minor CHILD of a tenant (whether or not the child is a tenant), is expressly non-waivable, and fixes damages at actual or $300, whichever is greater. So the two are genuinely different rules on the same topic and both belong. This row shares Ohio's topic_key. The topic IS still missing from the named-topic checklist, which is a real gap -- two of fourteen states now have a rule and no canvass row asks about it. Because the section is brand new it will not appear in the 2025 compilation's chapter index at all, which is instruction 35's trap running in the opposite direction (a section IN FORCE but MISSING from the compilation). Recommended as a new named-topic checklist row: every future state should be asked whether it restricts who may be named as a defendant. title: Towing From Your Lot: Posting Is What Makes It Lawful
bodyText: Minnesota's towing rules live in Minn. Stat. ch. 168B, not in the landlord-tenant chapter, and the timeframes turn on what kind of property you have. A vehicle left unattended may be impounded from private property IMMEDIATELY where the property is single-family or duplex residential, and immediately from ANY residential property that is properly posted. Non-residential private property gets immediate removal if properly posted and 24 hours if not. Read that list carefully: the 24-hour fallback is non-residential ONLY, so a multi-unit residential lot that is NOT posted has no timeframe available to it under that provision. If you manage anything larger than a duplex, post the lot. Two further points. Sec. 168B.035 is about towing by government towing authorities from public property, and it expressly preserves a private property owner's authority to authorize a tow under ch. 168B -- so that section's rules are not your rules. And the statutory lien that a tow operator gets for towing and storage arises on a tow requested by a LAW ENFORCEMENT OFFICER, so a tow you order yourself does not create it; settle who pays with your towing company in your contract. Chapter 168B does not define 'properly posted', so follow your city's sign requirements.

title: Methamphetamine Contamination: No Disclosure Duty, but an Occupancy Ban and a Recorded Affidavit
bodyText: Minnesota has no statute requiring a landlord to disclose that a property was once a clandestine drug lab. What it has instead is Minn. Stat. Sec. 152.0275 subd. 2, and the practical consequences are bigger than a disclosure duty. A county or local health department or sheriff SHALL order that any property found to be a clandestine lab site and contaminated be prohibited from being occupied or used until it has been assessed and remediated under the Department of Health's cleanup guidelines, and the remediation must be done by a contractor who then verifies the work to you and to the authority within five days; the authority vacates its order after that. If a contractor certifies work that did not meet the guidelines, the contractor is liable to you for the extra remediation cost and your attorney fees, with a six-year limit. Public-health nuisance abatement procedures apply on top. The disclosure happens without you: the authority records an affidavit with the county recorder or registrar of titles naming the owner, describing the property and mapping the contaminated area, expressly to disclose the history 'to any potential transferee', and the recorder must record it so it turns up in an ordinary title search. Affidavits can be filed to show remediation and to vacate the order, after which they stop being notice. Local community health services administrators also keep records of affected properties. So: check the title and the local administrator before you buy, and expect an occupancy prohibition rather than a disclosure form if it happens to you.

title: A Deposit Refund the Tenant Never Cashed Is Not Yours to Keep
bodyText: When you send a security-deposit refund and the former tenant never cashes it, the money does not become yours after a while. Under Minnesota's unclaimed property act (Minn. Stat. Sec. 345.39 subd. 1) intangible personal property held in the ordinary course of your business that stays unclaimed by the owner for more than THREE YEARS after it became payable is presumed abandoned, and the listed examples include customer overpayments, credit balances and miscellaneous outstanding checks. A stale refund check or an uncollected credit balance sits squarely in that category. Do not write it back to income: track it, and when the dormancy period runs, report and remit it to the state. Charges you may lawfully withhold are excluded from the calculation, so what is at issue is the net amount you actually owed the tenant.

title: Renting Storage Lockers Separately Can Pull You Into the Self-Service Storage Act
bodyText: If you rent storage space to tenants, check whether Minnesota's self-service storage facility act (Minn. Stat. Sec. Sec. 514.970 to 514.979) applies before you rely on your storage clause. A 'self-service storage facility' is real property designed and used for renting or leasing individual storage space to occupants who have access to store and remove personal property; the only exclusions are financial-institution vaults, warehouses that issue documents of title, and commercial short-term parking. There is NO exclusion for storage lockers in an apartment building. If the act applies, Sec. 514.975 imposes real requirements on the rental agreement: it must disclose your lien rights including the right to deny access, and the extent and limits of your insurance on the occupant's property; it must let the occupant name an optional alternate contact person, with a space they initial if they decline; any cap on the value of stored property is effective ONLY if printed in bold type or underlined, and may not be set below $1,000; and there is a uniformed-services disclosure. Most importantly, a rental agreement 'may not exempt an owner from liability for damages to an occupant's personal property caused by the owner's negligence' -- so a negligence disclaimer is void where the act applies. The safer reading is that a locker thrown in with a dwelling at no separate charge is not a self-service storage facility, because the property is not designed and used for renting storage space. But if you rent lockers for a separate fee, to your tenants or to the public, assume the act applies and drop the disclaimer.

title: No Rekeying or Lock-Hardware Duty in Minnesota
bodyText: Minnesota imposes no statutory duty to rekey or change locks between tenancies, and no deadbolt or lock-hardware requirement for rental housing. Locks are a matter for your lease and any local housing code. The one statutory lock rule runs the other way and is already covered in the library: a tenant who is a victim of violence has a right to have the locks changed. Rekeying at turnover is good practice, not a legal obligation, so if you want it as an obligation on the tenant's side, put it in the lease.

title: No Fire-Sprinkler Duty for Private Rental Housing
bodyText: Minnesota's only retrofit sprinkler mandate does not reach private landlords. Minn. Stat. Sec. 299F.48 requires automatic sprinkler systems in existing PUBLIC HOUSING buildings, and the section defines that term narrowly: housing for low-income persons and households financed by the federal government and owned and operated by the public housing authorities and agencies formed by cities and counties, in which at least one story used for human occupancy is 75 feet or more above the lowest level of fire department vehicle access. Compliance is due by August 1, 2033. If you are a private owner, none of that applies to you. New construction and remodelling are still governed by the State Building Code and State Fire Code, which Sec. 299F.48 expressly does not supersede.

title: Selling With a Tenant in Place: No Minnesota Statute Beyond the Deposit Handover
bodyText: Minnesota has no general statute governing what you owe a tenant when you sell a tenanted property, and no release-on-sale provision of the kind some states have. What Minnesota does regulate is the money: the security-deposit transfer and successor-liability rules, which are covered separately in the library. Beyond that, selling with a tenant in place is governed by your lease, by common-law rules about whether the buyer takes subject to the tenancy, and by the ordinary entry-notice rules when you show the unit. There is also no statutory requirement to notify tenants that you have sold, and no statutory right of first refusal for residential tenants. So put what you need into the lease and the purchase agreement, because the statute will not supply it.
