title: What North Dakota Law Will Not Let the Lease Do
bodyText: North Dakota has no list of prohibited residential lease terms inside its landlord-tenant chapter, and it is easy to conclude from that the lease can say whatever you want. That is wrong. Five sections of Chapter 9-08 void whole categories of contract term, and a lease is a contract like any other. A provision is unlawful if it is contrary to an express provision of law, contrary to the policy of express law though not expressly prohibited, or otherwise contrary to good morals (§ 9-08-01). A provision whose object is, directly or indirectly, to exempt anyone from responsibility for their own fraud, for willful injury to another person or their property, or for violation of law -- whether the violation is willful or negligent -- is against the policy of the law (§ 9-08-02). Penalties imposed by contract for nonperformance are void outright (§ 9-08-03). A clause fixing damages in advance is void to that extent, unless it would be impracticable or extremely difficult to fix the actual damage (§ 9-08-04). And a clause that restricts a party from enforcing its rights by the usual legal proceedings in the ordinary tribunals, or that shortens the time in which it may enforce them, is void unless a North Dakota statute specifically permits it (§ 9-08-05). What this means in practice: a flat "Landlord is not liable" sentence will not protect you where the loss came from your own violation of a statute or building code; a flat early-termination, short-notice, or administrative fee is exposed as a contractual penalty rather than a damages estimate; and Chapter 47-16's own unconscionability section (§ 47-16-13.3) sits on top of all of it as a case-by-case backstop.

The checklist's own topic row L642 'Lease-content restrictions (state-wide, not just the LT chapter)' recorded ND as 'Outside the chapter: NOT CANVASSED' -- this row is that canvass. Found via the gap-discovery source 3 scenario screen, prompted by flat non-liability and indemnification clauses in a real North Dakota lease (source 2). | SCOPE DISCIPLINE -- what § 9-08-02 does NOT say: it does not void an exemption from ordinary negligence as such. Its three targets are fraud, WILLFUL injury, and violation of law (willful or negligent). A disclaimer is therefore exposed where the loss traces to the landlord's breach of a statute or code (§§ 47-16-13.1, 23-13-15, fair housing), not merely to carelessness. title: The Tenant Can Repair and Deduct, or Just Leave
bodyText: North Dakota gives a tenant three routes when you do not repair, and none of them requires going to court first. If, within a reasonable time after the tenant's notice of dilapidations that you ought to repair, you neglect to do so, the tenant may repair the premises and deduct the expense of the repair from rent; recover that expense from you in any other lawful manner; or vacate the premises -- and a tenant who vacates on that ground is discharged from further payment of rent and from performing the lease's other conditions (§ 47-16-13). There is no escrow mechanism, no statutory dollar cap on the deduction, no requirement that the tenant get your approval of the repair or the contractor, and no notice period fixed in days. Two consequences to plan around. First, a deduction properly made under this section is not unpaid rent, so treating it as a nonpayment default and filing on it is a real risk. Second, on any claim under §§ 47-16-13.1 through 47-16-13.6 the court may award reasonable attorney's fees to the prevailing party (§ 47-16-13.6), so a small repair dispute can carry your opponent's fees. Answering a written repair request promptly, in writing, with a date, is the only reliable way to keep this section from being used against you.

Plus § 47-16-13.6' -- and no CSV row existed for it. title: Selling a Property With a Tenant in It
bodyText: North Dakota imposes no duty to tell your tenant you are selling, and no statutory notice period before a sale -- but four other things bind you. The security deposit and accrued interest must be transferred to the buyer; you are not released from liability until that transfer actually happens, and the buyer is bound by North Dakota's deposit rules even though the buyer never received the deposit (§ 47-16-07.1(5)). The buyer steps into your rent remedies (§ 47-16-28), your tenant's remedies under the lease run against the buyer (§ 47-16-29), and your remedies run against anyone the tenant assigned to, for claims accruing while they held the assignment -- except where the assignment was security for a loan and was not accompanied by possession (§ 47-16-30). Separately, selling triggers seller-disclosure duties in Chapter 47-10 that have nothing to do with the lease. For a residential dwelling of four or fewer units you must give the buyer a written disclosure of all material facts you are aware could adversely and significantly affect an ordinary buyer's use and enjoyment, before final acceptance of the purchase agreement -- and that applies whether or not a real estate licensee is involved, subject to nine exemptions including foreclosure, fiduciary and immediate-family transfers (§ 47-10-02.1). Since 2025 you must also disclose in writing any knowledge you have of radon concentrations, give the buyer the prescribed radon warning to acknowledge by signature, and hand over any prior test results and evidence of mitigation reasonably available to you; comply and you are immune from radon-based claims (§ 47-10-02.2). And if the property sits in a homeowners' association or condominium project, you have ten days from executing the agreement to deliver the association's governing documents, budgets, assessments, litigation and violation history -- and if you do not, the buyer may void the purchase contract until they are delivered and for five days afterwards (§ 47-10-02.3).

title: No Radon Disclosure Duty When You Rent -- But There Is One When You Sell
bodyText: North Dakota requires no radon disclosure, testing, or warning from a landlord to a tenant, even though the EPA places the whole state in its highest-risk zone. The one mandatory disclosure at the start of a North Dakota tenancy is the signed condition statement (§ 47-16-07.2), and it says nothing about radon. The picture changes the moment you sell rather than rent: since 2025 a seller of residential real property must disclose any knowledge of radon concentrations in writing, give the buyer a prescribed radon warning to acknowledge by signature, and provide any prior test results and evidence of mitigation (§ 47-10-02.2). Testing and disclosing voluntarily to a tenant is still worth considering, since a habitability claim under § 47-16-13.1 does not require a disclosure statute to exist.

title: No Mold Disclosure Duty
bodyText: North Dakota has no mold disclosure requirement, no statutory mold standard, and no remediation timeline. Mold is not therefore risk-free: visible mold or the water intrusion behind it can put you in breach of the duty to keep the premises fit and habitable and to comply with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety (§ 47-16-13.1(1)(a)-(b)), and a tenant who gives you notice and gets no repair in a reasonable time can repair and deduct, or vacate and stop paying rent (§ 47-16-13). Treat a moisture complaint as a habitability matter on a clock rather than a disclosure question.

title: No Bed Bug Disclosure or Treatment Rule
bodyText: North Dakota imposes no bed bug disclosure duty, no treatment timeline, and no allocation of treatment cost between landlord and tenant. An infestation is handled under the general duties instead: your obligation to keep the premises fit and habitable and to comply with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety (§ 47-16-13.1(1)(a)-(b)), against the tenant's obligation to keep the occupied part of the premises as clean and safe as its condition permits (§ 47-16-13.2(2)). Because nothing divides the cost by statute, whatever your lease says about pest treatment is what will govern -- so say it.

title: No Duty to Change the Locks for a Domestic Violence Victim
bodyText: North Dakota's domestic violence tenancy statute gives a victim one thing: the right to terminate the lease early on written notice, without penalty, paying the month of termination plus one additional month's rent subject to your duty to mitigate (§ 47-16-17.1). It does not give the tenant a right to require you to change the locks, and it does not give you a deadline, a cost allocation, or any immunity for doing so. If a tenant asks, you are deciding under the lease and under your own judgment, not under a statute -- and you still owe every remaining tenant on that lease quiet possession (§ 47-16-08) and the confidentiality duty in § 47-16-17.1(4), which bars you from disclosing the documentation the tenant gave you and carries statutory damages of $1,000 plus actual damages, fees and costs.

title: No Late Fee Cap -- But Do Not Read That as No Limit
bodyText: North Dakota sets no dollar or percentage cap on late fees, and no statutory grace period. It has also declined to set one three times: bills to cap late rent fees were introduced in 2021 (HB 1440, HB 1442) and again in 2025 (SB 2236, which would have amended § 47-16-20 to cap a late fee at eight percent of the overdue rent). None became law. The absence of a cap is not the absence of a limit. Two general contract sections reach a late fee directly: penalties imposed by contract for nonperformance are void outright (§ 9-08-03), and a clause fixing damages in advance is void unless actual damage would be impracticable or extremely difficult to fix (§ 9-08-04). A late fee set at a level that looks punitive rather than like a genuine estimate of what a late payment actually costs you is therefore attackable in North Dakota on grounds that have nothing to do with a cap -- and § 47-16-13.3 unconscionability sits behind that. Keep the figure defensible and keep a reason for it. Separately, North Dakota has no statute setting the order in which you must apply a tenant's payment, so whether a payment goes to rent first or to fees first is a contract question here, not a statutory one.
notes: CONFIRMED ABSENT as to a cap; the operative limits are elsewhere. | Basis: complete Chapter 47-16 read from the official compilation (ndlegis.gov/cencode/t47c16.pdf) on 2026-09-27 -- confirmed directly that no section in the chapter mentions a late fee, a late charge, a cap, or an order of applying payments; plus an official ndlegis.gov full-text search for "late fee" on 2026-09-27 (792 hits, NO Century Code hit). This closes a gap in how the absence had been supported: late-fee's ND note said 'confirmed: full read of ch. 47-16 contains no late-fee provision', which does not exclude a cap living outside the chapter (instruction 7's failure mode). It has now been excluded statewide. | TWO FAILED 2025 BILLS, both confirmed not enacted against the current compilation rather than by reading the bill history: SB 2236 would have amended § 47-16-20 to add an eight percent cap -- § 47-16-20 as it now reads is the unchanged 'Rents - When payable' section. SB 2235 (69th LA) would have addressed 'rents and the priority of payments under a rental agreement' -- no payment-priority rule exists in the chapter. K.4 pending-bill trap: a later session searching 'late fee' will surface SB 2236's 8% figure in engrossed bill text and could take it for law. | SUPPORTING SECONDARY EVIDENCE, cited as corroboration not authority: 2021 HB 1442 testimony from a renters' legal-aid witness states 'Current ND law does not have a limit on the amount of a late rent fee that can be imposed upon a renter', and High Plains Fair Housing Center testimony on SB 2236 describes leases in its database charging $10 up to '$100 + $100 per week thereafter'. | Prompted by gap-discovery source 2: the real lease used charges a flat $35 after the tenth of the month. See edu-prohibited-lease-terms-nd.

title: Stating the Purpose of the Lease Gives You Two Extra Remedies
bodyText: North Dakota attaches a specific consequence to a lease that states what the property is leased for. When real property is leased for a particular purpose the tenant must not use it for any other purpose, and if the tenant does, you may either hold the tenant responsible for the safety of the property during that use in all events, or treat the contract as rescinded (§ 47-16-11). The first of those is unusual and worth understanding: it is not a negligence standard. During a use outside the stated purpose the tenant answers for the property's safety whatever the cause, which shifts a category of loss you would otherwise carry. The second lets you treat the lease as at an end without waiting on the eviction chapter's grounds. Both depend on the lease actually stating a purpose -- which the residential-use clause does -- so this is a right you either capture in the drafting or forfeit silently.
notes: N.D.C.C. § 47-16-11, complete Chapter 47-16 primary text. | ZERO rows in the library cited § 47-16-11 before this one. Found by the gap-discovery source 3 scenario screen ('tenant runs a business from the unit', 'tenant lists the unit on Airbnb'), which reached it by walking the core chapter section by section against the ND-active rows -- the section is not something a keyword probe for short-term rentals or business use would return. | OPT-IN LANDLORD RIGHT (instruction 30): the remedy is conditioned on the lease stating a particular purpose. residential-use-only (tagged ND) supplies that condition, so ND leases built from this library do capture it; the point of the row is that a landlord who deletes or waters down that clause loses § 47-16-11 as well, which is not obvious from the clause text. | RELATIONSHIP TO THE EVICTION CHAPTER: § 47-32-01(8) makes violating a material term of a written lease an eviction ground on three days' notice of intention to evict. § 47-16-11's rescission route is a separate, direct contractual remedy under ch. 47-16 -- the same distinction edu-early-termination-grounds-nd draws for §§ 47-16-16 and 47-16-17, and this row belongs with those two. | NOT DETERMINED: whether 'treat the contract as rescinded' permits retaking possession without an eviction action. It almost certainly does not -- § 32-03-29's treble damages for forcible exclusion apply regardless of who is right about the lease (see edu-self-help-eviction-ban-nd) -- and the body deliberately does not suggest otherwise. No ND case law read.

title: Notice of Claims Against the Property
bodyText: If Tenant receives notice of any proceeding to recover the property or its possession -- including a foreclosure action, a tax proceeding, or a claim by any person other than Landlord -- Tenant will inform Landlord immediately and deliver the notice to Landlord. Tenant is responsible to Landlord for all damages Landlord sustains because Tenant failed to inform Landlord of a written notice or failed to deliver it. Tenant will not recognize or attorn to any person other than Landlord as the owner or landlord of the property without Landlord's consent or a judgment of a court of competent jurisdiction.
notes: N.D.C.C. § 47-16-25, complete Chapter 47-16 primary text: 'Every tenant who receives notice of any proceeding to recover the real property occupied by the tenant, or the possession thereof, must: 1. Inform the tenant's landlord immediately of the notice; and 2. Deliver the notice to the landlord. The tenant shall be responsible to the landlord for all damages which the landlord may sustain by reason of any omission by the tenant to inform the landlord of the notice or to deliver it to the landlord, if such notice is in writing. The attornment to a stranger is void unless made with the consent of the landlord or in consequence of a judgment of a court of competent jurisdiction.' | ZERO rows in the library cited § 47-16-25 before this one. Found by the gap-discovery source 3 scenario screen ('lender forecloses', 'a third party claims the property'). | WHY A LEASE CLAUSE AND NOT ONLY EDUCATION: the duty and the damages consequence exist by statute whatever the lease says, but they are worthless in practice if the tenant does not know them -- and the statute conditions the damages liability on the notice being 'in writing', which the clause does not restate because a landlord is better served by the broader contractual duty. RECOMMENDED rather than REQUIRED: North Dakota does not require the lease to contain this. | THE ATTORNMENT SENTENCE is the operative protection in a foreclosure or a disputed sale -- it stops a purported new owner from establishing a tenancy relationship directly with your tenant. Tied to edu-selling-rented-property-nd (§§ 47-16-28, 47-16-29, 47-16-30). | NOT PROPAGATED to any other state: § 47-16-25 is ND law. SD's Field Code ancestry makes an analog likely there but that is a candidate for SD's own session, never an inheritance. | No display collision: new topic_key, no supersedes relationship, and no existing ND-tagged row covers this subject.

title: When a Tenant Leaves Early: What You Can Collect and What You Must Do
bodyText: North Dakota's rules here are narrower than they look, and they differ depending on how the tenancy ended. If you evict, the tenant stays liable for rent for the remainder of the term, and that section expressly does not relieve you of the duty to mitigate damages (§ 47-16-13.7). If the lease is terminated, you have a claim for possession and for rent and a separate claim for actual damages for breach (§ 47-16-13.4). If a lease ends before the time originally agreed, the tenant must pay the due proportion for the use actually made, unless that use was merely nominal and of no benefit to the tenant (§ 47-16-21). What North Dakota does not have is a general statutory duty to mitigate covering every tenant who simply leaves: the mitigation section is written into the habitability group, applying to a party aggrieved under §§ 47-16-13.1 through 47-16-13.6 (§ 47-16-13.5), and the duty otherwise appears only in § 47-16-13.7 for an evicted tenant and § 47-16-17.1(5) for a domestic violence termination. Do not treat that as licence to sit on an empty unit and bill the departed tenant: your own lease promises reasonable mitigation efforts, common law may supply the rest, and a flat early-termination or lease-break fee is separately exposed as a contractual penalty under § 9-08-03 or as liquidated damages under § 9-08-04. Re-rent, document the effort, and charge actual loss.
notes: N.D.C.C. §§ 47-16-13.4, 47-16-13.5, 47-16-13.7, 47-16-21, with §§ 9-08-03 and 9-08-04. Complete Chapter 47-16 primary text; ch. 9-08 read from the official compilation on 2026-09-27. | §§ 47-16-13.4 and 47-16-21 had ZERO rows in the library before this one; § 47-16-13.5 appeared only inside edu-holdover-damages-nd's notes. Found by the gap-discovery source 3 scenario screen ('tenant wants out early', 'tenant abandons mid-term'). | DISAGREEMENT RECORDED RATHER THAN RECONCILED, per the standing rule. A research pass run for this project on 2026-09-27 characterised § 47-16-13.5's mitigation duty as 'Present -- general'. The primary text does not read that way: the section opens 'Any party aggrieved under sections 47-16-13.1 through 47-16-13.6 may recover appropriate damages. However, the aggrieved party has a duty to mitigate damages.' On its face the mitigation sentence attaches to the aggrieved party that the first sentence defines, which is scoped to the habitability group. This row states the narrower, text-bound reading and flags the difference; it does not adopt the broader one, and it does not rely on the narrower one to tell a landlord it is safe not to mitigate. Resolving it needs ND case law, which was not read. | NOT DETERMINED: whether ND common law imposes a general landlord mitigation duty on abandonment; whether § 47-16-21 applies to a tenant-caused early end or only to a termination by operation of law. | See edu-prohibited-lease-terms-nd on lease-break fees and edu-holdover-damages-nd for the §§ 32-03-27 and 32-03-28 double-damages measures, which are the separate holdover case.

title: Fire or Casualty Damage
bodyText: If the property is damaged or destroyed by fire or other casualty to an extent that enjoyment of the property is substantially impaired, Tenant may either (a) immediately vacate the property and notify Landlord in writing within fourteen days afterward of Tenant's intention to terminate this Lease, in which case this Lease terminates as of the date Tenant vacated, or (b) if continued occupancy is lawful, vacate only the part of the property made unusable by the casualty, in which case Tenant's Rent obligation is reduced in proportion to the loss in fair rental value of the property. If this Lease terminates under this Section, Landlord will return all prepaid Rent and the Security Deposit that Tenant is entitled to recover, accounting for Rent as of the date of the casualty. Tenant remains responsible for damage caused by Tenant's own negligence. Nothing in this Section limits any right Tenant has under applicable law.
notes: NE: Read section-open 2026-09-27 from nebraskalegislature.gov (official legislative compilation) in the built-in browser, via the official keyword search at /laws/search_keyword.php. Gap-discovery backfill, instruction 36 sources 3 and 4. CONTROLLING TEXT: Neb. Rev. Stat. §76-1429 (Fire or casualty damage), read verbatim. (1)(a) tenant may immediately vacate and give WRITTEN notice of intent to terminate within FOURTEEN days thereafter, and the agreement then terminates as of the date of vacating -- not the date of notice. (1)(b) if continued occupancy is lawful, tenant may vacate the unusable part and rent liability is reduced in proportion to the diminution in FAIR RENTAL VALUE. (2) on termination the landlord 'shall return all prepaid rent and security recoverable under section 76-1416'; accounting occurs as of the DATE OF THE CASUALTY; and the tenant remains responsible for damage caused by his own negligence. Source: Laws 1974, LB 293, s29 -- never amended, so no currency question (instruction 34). *** WHY THIS ROW EXISTS: §76-1429 was cited NOWHERE in the Nebraska library before today, and Nebraska was the ONLY one of the project's 14 states with no fire/casualty clause -- KS, ND, SD, MN, CA, NV, TX, FL and AZ all have one. The NE citation inventory ran 76-1427 -> 76-1430, skipping 76-1428 and 76-1429, so the 'full URLTA read' recorded as gap-discovery source 1 had a two-section hole. Found by the source-4 sweep, not by the statute walk. *** INSTRUCTION 18 (do not import another state's architecture): Nebraska's mechanic is NOT Kansas's. K.S.A. 58-2562 runs on a 5-day notice; §76-1429 runs on 14 days AFTER vacating. Drafting this from the KS or AZ row would have shipped the wrong number. The 14-day figure and the vacate-then-notify order were both taken from the primary text. NOT WAIVABLE: §76-1415(1)(a) voids any lease provision waiving a tenant's rights under the Act, so the closing sentence is not mere boilerplate.

title: Fire or Casualty - What You Owe Back, and When the Clock Starts
bodyText: Three details of Nebraska's fire-and-casualty rule catch landlords out. FIRST, the termination date is the date the tenant VACATED, not the date you received their notice: the tenant vacates first and then has fourteen days to notify you in writing, so a notice that arrives two weeks later still ends the tenancy as of the earlier move-out date, and rent is accounted for as of the date of the casualty itself (§76-1429). SECOND, you owe back all prepaid rent plus the security deposit the tenant can recover under §76-1416 - the casualty does not convert the deposit into damages, and the §76-1416 return deadline and penalty still apply. THIRD, a tenant who stays but loses part of the unit owes proportionally less rent, measured by the drop in FAIR RENTAL VALUE, not by floor area. The one thing that stays with the tenant is damage caused by their own negligence. You cannot contract around any of this: §76-1415(1)(a) voids a lease term waiving the tenant's rights under the Act. And if the tenancy ends, §76-1405 puts a duty to mitigate damages on the aggrieved party, so re-letting effort is expected rather than optional.
notes: NE: Read section-open 2026-09-27 from nebraskalegislature.gov (official legislative compilation) in the built-in browser, via the official keyword search at /laws/search_keyword.php. Gap-discovery backfill, instruction 36 sources 3 and 4. CONTROLLING TEXT: §76-1429 read verbatim (see casualty-termination-ne for the full quotation), plus §76-1405 read verbatim: '(1) The remedies provided by the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act shall be so administered that the aggrieved party may recover appropriate damages. The aggrieved party has a duty to mitigate damages.' §76-1416 (deposits) was already read in the original NE pass and is unchanged. WHY SEPARATE FROM THE CLAUSE: the three traps here are landlord-facing operational consequences (which date controls, that the deposit is NOT convertible to damages, that the abatement measure is fair rental value rather than square footage) and do not belong in tenant-facing lease text. §76-1405 IS ALSO A NEW CITATION for Nebraska: the duty to mitigate was cited nowhere in the library, though default-by-tenant-ks-ne already promises mitigation 'to the extent required by applicable law', so the clause was already correct by deference -- this row supplies the statutory basis rather than fixing an error. NOT RESEARCHED: whether Nebraska case law measures 'diminution in fair rental value' by any particular method, and whether a casualty caused by the tenant's negligence forfeits the (1)(a) termination right (the statute makes the tenant liable for the damage but does not say the right is lost). Both flagged, not resolved.

title: Meth Labs: You Must Report, You Must Not Re-Rent, and You Can Terminate in Three Days
bodyText: Nebraska has a four-section scheme for methamphetamine-contaminated rentals that sits outside the landlord-tenant act entirely, and it imposes real duties on you. YOU MUST REPORT: a property owner with knowledge of a clandestine drug lab on their property must report it as soon as practicable to local law enforcement or the Nebraska State Patrol (§71-2433). YOU MUST NOT RE-RENT: you may not permit human habitation or use of contaminated property until rehabilitation is complete and the local public health department has released the property, and knowingly violating that carries a civil penalty of up to $1,000 enforced by the Department of Health and Human Services (§71-2434(3)). YOU PAY FOR THE OVERSIGHT: the local public health department may charge you for the costs of monitoring the rehabilitation (§71-2434(2)). YOU CAN GET THE TENANT OUT FAST: notwithstanding any other provision of law, if leased property contains a clandestine drug lab you may terminate the lease on THREE DAYS' written notice for the purpose of rehabilitating it (§71-2435) - no cure period, and it overrides the usual 14-day and 7-day notice mechanics. 'Contaminated property' reaches any enclosed area intended for human habitation that has been contaminated by methamphetamine, its residue, or other substances from such a lab (§71-2432(2)).
notes: NE: Read section-open 2026-09-27 from nebraskalegislature.gov (official legislative compilation) in the built-in browser, via the official keyword search at /laws/search_keyword.php. Gap-discovery backfill, instruction 36 sources 3 and 4. CONTROLLING TEXT: Neb. Rev. Stat. §§71-2432, 71-2433, 71-2434 and 71-2435, all four read verbatim section-open. §71-2432 defines 'clandestine drug lab', 'contaminated property' and 'rehabilitate'. §71-2435 quoted in full: 'Notwithstanding any other provision of law, if leased property contains a clandestine drug lab, an owner may terminate the lease agreement upon three days written notice for the purpose of rehabilitating the contaminated property in accordance with the rules and regulations adopted and promulgated pursuant to section 71-2434.' §71-2434(3): 'The owner or owners of contaminated property shall not permit the human habitation or use of such property until the rehabilitation of such property has been completed and the property has been released ... An owner who knowingly violates this subsection may be subject to a civil penalty not to exceed one thousand dollars.' *** HOW FOUND, AND WHY IT WAS MISSED: the term 'methamphetamine laboratory' returned 0 hits; 'clandestine' returned exactly these four sections. That is the search-engine characteristic recorded on edu-confirmed-absences-outside-title-ne -- a phrase search would have declared this absent. The scheme was cited NOWHERE in the Nebraska library. *** INSTRUCTION 33 CHECK (shared clause forfeiting a state right), RUN AND CLEAN: default-by-tenant-ks-ne already reads 'except where applicable law permits Landlord to proceed without giving Tenant an opportunity to cure', so the §71-2435 three-day no-cure right is NOT contractually surrendered and no clause edit is owed. No new lease clause is proposed either: §71-2435 operates 'notwithstanding any other provision of law', so the right does not depend on lease language, and a clause restating it would add drafting risk without adding a right. *** CURRENCY (instruction 34): §71-2433 was amended by Laws 2025, LB317, s375, which substituted the renamed 'Department of Water, Energy, and Environment' among the agencies receiving the State Patrol's report. The owner's reporting duty itself is unchanged by that amendment. NOT READ: the DHHS rules and regulations adopted under §71-2434(1), which set the actual rehabilitation standards, deadlines and disposal requirements -- these are Nebraska Administrative Code, outside the statutes-only boundary of this search, and are flagged per instruction 16 as needing agency-rulemaking monitoring rather than bill tracking.

title: Selling the Property, or Changing Managers - How You Actually Get Off the Hook
bodyText: Nebraska releases a selling landlord from future liability, but only if you do two specific things. FIRST, give the tenant WRITTEN NOTICE of the conveyance: a landlord who conveys the premises in a good-faith sale to a bona fide purchaser is relieved of liability under the lease and the Act only as to events occurring AFTER that written notice (§76-1420(1)). Events before it stay yours. SECOND, deal with the deposit separately: the release does NOT cover money and property the tenant is entitled to under §76-1416, so you remain personally liable for the security deposit and prepaid rent unless you ASSIGN them to the purchaser and give the tenant written notice of the assignment - which then does release you. Selling without assigning the deposit leaves you exposed for it after you no longer hold it. The same structure covers a manager: a manager is relieved of liability as to events after written notice to the tenant that their management has ended (§76-1420(2)). Two cautions. The section opens 'Unless otherwise agreed', so a lease or purchase agreement can change this allocation - check what yours says. And a change of owner or manager also restarts your §76-1417 disclosure duty, since the tenant is entitled to the current owner's and manager's name and address.
notes: NE: Read section-open 2026-09-27 from nebraskalegislature.gov (official legislative compilation) in the built-in browser, via the official keyword search at /laws/search_keyword.php. Gap-discovery backfill, instruction 36 sources 3 and 4. CONTROLLING TEXT: Neb. Rev. Stat. §76-1420 (Limitation of liability), read verbatim, both subsections. (1) releases the conveying landlord 'as to events occurring subsequent to written notice to the tenant of the conveyance', conditioned on a 'good faith sale to a bona fide purchaser', but 'the landlord remains liable to the tenant for any property and money to which the tenant is entitled under section 76-1416, except that assignment of any security deposits or prepaid rents to a bona fide purchaser with written notice to the tenant shall serve to relieve the conveying landlord of any further liability under section 76-1416.' (2) is the manager analog. Both open 'Unless otherwise agreed', which is why the row says the allocation is alterable. Source: Laws 1974, LB 293, s20; Laws 2001, LB 7, s15. *** WHY THIS ROW EXISTS: §76-1420 was cited NOWHERE in the Nebraska library, and Nebraska had no row of any kind for selling a tenanted property or changing managers, while WY, KS, ND, MN, OH, NV and AZ all do. Found by the statute-wide 'landlord' sweep described on edu-confirmed-absences-outside-title-ne, which is also how §§76-1422, 76-1428 and 76-1429 surfaced. This is the direct Nebraska analog of A.R.S. §33-1325, the gap Arizona's own scenario screen found (AZ log §18.2). *** DELIBERATELY NOT SAID: whether the lease binds the purchaser at all, which is common-law assignment and conveyance doctrine, not §76-1420, and was not researched. Also not researched: whether a foreclosure sale counts as a 'good faith sale to a bona fide purchaser' for this section -- Nebraska has no tenant-protection-on-foreclosure statute at all (see edu-confirmed-absences-outside-title-ne), so the interaction is untested here. §76-1417's disclosure duty was read in the original NE pass and is cross-referenced, not re-verified today.

title: Your House Rules Are Enforceable Only If They Clear Six Tests
bodyText: Nebraska lets you adopt rules about the tenant's use and occupancy of the premises, but a rule is enforceable against the tenant only if ALL SIX of these hold (§76-1422): its purpose is to promote the appearance, convenience, safety or welfare of the tenants, to preserve your property from abusive use, or to distribute services and facilities fairly; it is reasonably related to that purpose; it applies to all tenants in the premises in a fair manner; it is explicit enough to fairly inform the tenant what they must or must not do; it is not a device for evading your own obligations; and the tenant had notice of it when they entered into the lease. ADDING A RULE MID-TENANCY is allowed on different terms: a rule adopted after the lease is signed binds the tenant if you give reasonable notice of its adoption AND it 'does not work a substantial modification of his bargain'. So a new quiet-hours rule will usually stick; a new rule that effectively re-prices the tenancy or strips away something they bargained for will not. Enforcement runs through the ordinary noncompliance route at §76-1431, which means a rule violation is handled as a lease breach with the notice and cure mechanics that go with it - not as an independent ground for immediate termination.
notes: NE: Read section-open 2026-09-27 from nebraskalegislature.gov (official legislative compilation) in the built-in browser, via the official keyword search at /laws/search_keyword.php. Gap-discovery backfill, instruction 36 sources 3 and 4. CONTROLLING TEXT: Neb. Rev. Stat. §76-1422 (Rules and regulations), read verbatim. The six conditions in the row are subdivisions (1) through (6) in order, compressed but not reordered or generalized. Closing paragraph quotes the statute's final sentence: 'A rule or regulation adopted after the tenant enters into the rental agreement is enforceable against the tenant if reasonable notice of its adoption is given to the tenant and it does not work a substantial modification of his bargain.' The §76-1431 enforcement hook is express in the statute's opening ('It is enforceable as provided in section 76-1431'). Source: Laws 1974, LB 293, s22 -- never amended. *** WHY THIS ROW EXISTS: §76-1422 was cited NOWHERE in the Nebraska library, even though the NE-active set carries at least five clauses that ARE house rules within the meaning of the section -- common-area-use, no-disturbance, guest-policy, guest-policy-day-limit, parking-ne and smoking-policy -- and the library already has the analogous row for Kansas (edu-rules-regulations-enforceability-ks) and for NV and AZ. Nebraska was the gap. *** PRODUCT CONSEQUENCE worth Taylor's attention, recorded not acted on: condition (6) requires notice AT LEASE SIGNING, so any house rules delivered as a separate document after signing are on the weaker mid-tenancy footing. addendum-precedence and entire-agreement govern how attached rules are incorporated; whether Steinoak's flow actually delivers rules at signing is an app question, not a statutory one (instruction 23 -- ask Claude Code to check the real flow rather than infer it). NOT RESEARCHED: Nebraska case law applying 'substantial modification of his bargain', which is the only genuinely soft edge in the section.

title: Towing From Your Lot - No Signs, No Lawful Tow, and No Kickbacks
bodyText: Nebraska conditions a private tow on posted signs, and the rule splits by city size. OUTSIDE Omaha and Lincoln, parking in a PROPERLY POSTED restricted lot without the consent of the owner or tenant authorized to give permission is an infraction, and the vehicle may be towed at the lot owner's or tenant's request (§60-2401.01). IN Omaha (metropolitan class) and Lincoln (primary class), unless the city has adopted a conforming ordinance, vehicles parked without consent are subject to towing 'if the lot is properly posted' (§60-2401). Either way the signs carry the whole thing, and §60-2402 sets what they must say: they must be readily visible and must state the purpose or purposes for parking on the lot, the hours of restricted parking, and WHO TO CONTACT for information about a towed vehicle. A lot with no signs, or signs missing any of those three items, gives you no lawful tow. DO NOT TAKE A KICKBACK: an owner or tenant causing a vehicle to be towed 'shall not solicit or accept therefor a commission, gift, gratuity, or any form of compensation or wealth' from the towing business (§60-2411). Free towing arrangements and per-tow payments from the operator are exactly what this prohibits. The rest is on the tower, not you, but it affects your tenants: the tower must verify that whoever ordered the tow is really the lot's owner or tenant (§60-2409), notify law enforcement of the plate within 24 hours (§60-2403), and send the vehicle's owner and any lienholder a certified-mail notice within 15 business days (§60-2410(2)). Towing and storage become a lien on the vehicle but never on its contents, and the vehicle can be disposed of after 90 days (§60-2410(1)).
notes: NE: Read section-open 2026-09-27 from nebraskalegislature.gov (official legislative compilation) in the built-in browser, via the official keyword search at /laws/search_keyword.php. Gap-discovery backfill, instruction 36 sources 3 and 4. CONTROLLING TEXT: Neb. Rev. Stat. §§60-2401, 60-2401.01, 60-2402, 60-2403, 60-2409, 60-2410 and 60-2411, all read verbatim section-open. §60-2411 quoted in full: 'Any owner or tenant causing the towing away of a vehicle shall not solicit or accept therefor a commission, gift, gratuity, or any form of compensation or wealth from the person or business towing away the vehicle.' §60-2402's three sign contents are verbatim. CLASS-OF-CITY SCOPE IS REAL, NOT DECORATIVE: §60-2401 applies to 'cities of the metropolitan or primary class' and §60-2401.01 applies 'Except in cities of the metropolitan or primary class' -- Nebraska's metropolitan class is Omaha and its primary class is Lincoln. The city identifications are from general knowledge of Nebraska's statutory city classes and were NOT read from the classification statute today; the statutory text supports the metropolitan/primary split itself, which is what the row turns on. §60-2401 also carries an 'ordinance conforming to section 60-2401.01' escape that a city may have used, so an Omaha or Lincoln landlord should check the local ordinance -- flagged per instruction 20, not resolved. *** WHY THIS ROW EXISTS: the whole Chapter 60 scheme was cited NOWHERE in the Nebraska library. This is the same gap Arizona's scenario screen found (AZ log §18.2, edu-towing-az) and NV and TX already have rows for. NO CLAUSE CONFLICT: parking-vehicle-rules and parking-ne already defer to applicable law on towing, so nothing in the lease contradicts this and no clause edit is owed -- the exposure is operational (a landlord who tows off an unposted lot), not textual. No penalty section was located for a §60-2411 violation; the prohibition's consequence is therefore UNRESOLVED and the row does not assert one.

title: Nebraska Does Regulate Radon - In New Construction, Not in Disclosure
bodyText: Nebraska requires no radon disclosure to tenants, but it does regulate radon in new buildings, and that reaches you if you build or bought new. New construction built after September 1, 2019 that is intended to be regularly occupied by people must be built using radon resistant new construction (§76-3504). The required minimum standards are specific: sealed or gasketed sump lids; a passive subslab depressurization system with a vent pipe of at least three inches running up through the building and terminating at least twelve inches above the roof and at least ten feet from any window or opening; separate vent pipes where interior footings divide the subslab material; visible interior vent pipes labelled 'Radon Reduction System' on each floor and in accessible attics; and an electrical circuit terminated in an approved box near the anticipated fan location so an active system can be added later. THERE ARE ONLY TWO EXEMPTIONS THAT APPLY TO A DWELLING (§76-3505): the project used the design of a licensed architect or professional engineer, or the county's average radon concentration is below 2.7 picocuries per liter as determined by the state. The third exemption - a local building official deciding it is unnecessary - is expressly unavailable 'other than for any residential dwelling unit', so it does not help a rental. Converting the passive system to an active one later is expressly permitted (§76-3506). Nebraska is among the highest-radon states in the country, so a passive system that was never activated is a live habitability and marketing question even though no statute makes you test or disclose.
notes: NE: Read section-open 2026-09-27 from nebraskalegislature.gov (official legislative compilation) in the built-in browser, via the official keyword search at /laws/search_keyword.php. Gap-discovery backfill, instruction 36 sources 3 and 4. CONTROLLING TEXT: Neb. Rev. Stat. §§76-3504 and 76-3505 read verbatim section-open; §§76-3501, 76-3502, 76-3503, 76-3506 and 76-3507 identified by section number and title from the official search results and NOT read in full today -- the row relies on 76-3504 and 76-3505 for every operative statement, and on 76-3506's title ('Conversion of passive radon mitigation system to active radon mitigation system authorized') for the single sentence about conversion, which is a title-level claim and is flagged as such. §76-3505's third exemption is quoted accurately: it applies 'other than for any residential dwelling unit', which is why the row says only two exemptions reach a rental. *** WHY THIS ROW EXISTS: the Radon Resistant New Construction Act, §§76-3501 to 76-3507, was cited NOWHERE in the Nebraska library -- despite sitting in CHAPTER 76, the same chapter as the URLTA, which makes it the clearest single demonstration that the 'check adjacent chapters' rule (instruction 7) has to mean adjacent ARTICLES of the same chapter too, not just other chapters. The existing row edu-no-radon-tenant-disclosure-ne is not wrong -- there is still no tenant disclosure duty -- but it left a reader with the impression that Nebraska does not legislate on radon, and it has been amended today to point here. *** THE 2.7 pCi/L COUNTY EXEMPTION IS NOT RESOLVED FOR ANY COUNTY: §76-3505(2) delegates the determination to the department under §76-3507 and the row deliberately does not name any county as exempt. Determining which Nebraska counties fall below 2.7 pCi/L requires the department's determination, which is agency output rather than statute (instruction 16). NOT RESEARCHED: whether a pre-2019 building that is later remodeled comes within §76-3504 ('new construction' is not defined in the sections read), and the penalty or enforcement route for non-compliant construction -- §71-3517 ('Violations; civil and criminal penalties') sits in the separate radon PROFESSIONALS licensing article and was not read, so it must not be assumed to enforce §76-3504.

title: Medical Cannabis Is Now Legal in Nebraska - Your Smoking Ban Still Works, Your Crime Clause Does Not
bodyText: Nebraska voters legalized medical cannabis in 2024, and the practical effect on a lease is narrower than most landlords expect. What changed: it is no longer an offense under state OR local law for a qualified patient to use, possess and acquire an allowable amount of cannabis for a medical condition, or for a caregiver to obtain and deliver it for them, and that conduct is removed from the Uniform Controlled Substances Act (§71-24,105). What did NOT change: nothing in the act requires you to permit cannabis on your property, so a contractual no-smoking clause remains enforceable against a qualified patient as an ordinary lease term. What you should stop relying on: any lease or statutory hook keyed to ILLEGAL or CRIMINAL drug activity. A registered patient's medical use is no longer illegal under state law, so it cannot support Nebraska's fast-track eviction for drug-related criminal activity under §76-1431, and treating it as criminal conduct is a real risk. Enforce it as a breach of your smoking or house-rules term instead, on the ordinary notice-and-cure track. Two further cautions: cannabis remains illegal under federal law, which still matters for federally assisted housing; and a request to use a non-smoked form as a disability accommodation is a fair-housing question under §20-319(2)(b), not a cannabis question.
notes: NE: Read section-open 2026-09-27 from nebraskalegislature.gov (official legislative compilation) in the built-in browser, via the official keyword search at /laws/search_keyword.php. Gap-discovery backfill, instruction 36 sources 3 and 4. CONTROLLING TEXT: Neb. Rev. Stat. §71-24,105 read verbatim section-open. Source line: 'Initiative Law 2024, No. 437, s3' -- an enacted ballot initiative, which satisfies instruction 17 (confirm enactment, not introduction): this is in the official compilation with an initiative-law source line, not a pending measure. The section makes qualified-patient and caregiver conduct 'not an offense under state or local law' and removes it from the Uniform Controlled Substances Act. Related sections identified by number and title only, NOT read: §71-24,103 (Nebraska Medical Cannabis Patient Protection Act, how cited), §71-24,104 (Terms, defined), §§71-24,106 to 71-24,114 (the Nebraska Medical Cannabis Regulation Act and commission). *** THE KEY NEGATIVE IS NOT FULLY PROVEN AND IS STATED CAREFULLY: the row says nothing in the act REQUIRES a landlord to permit cannabis. §71-24,105 imposes no landlord duty on its face and the statute-wide 'landlord' sweep run today returned NO section in the 71-24,1xx range, which is good evidence that no landlord-accommodation provision exists anywhere in either act. But §71-24,104's definitions and the Patient Protection Act's remaining sections were not read, so this is recorded as strong-but-not-exhaustive rather than closed. A landlord-facing provision would have had to use the word 'landlord' to appear in that sweep. *** WHY THIS ROW EXISTS: smoking-policy (a shared clause tagged all 14 states) bans marijuana smoking by name for Nebraska, and the library had no Nebraska row acknowledging that medical cannabis is now lawful here. The clause itself is FINE and NO EDIT IS PROPOSED -- it is a contractual ban, which the act does not disturb. The exposure is the §76-1431 mischaracterization risk, which is education, not drafting. This is the instruction 33 shape in reverse: not a shared clause giving away a state right, but a state law quietly narrowing what an existing clause's enforcement theory can reach. NOT RESEARCHED: whether any Nebraska authority addresses cannabis as a reasonable accommodation in housing, and the commission's regulations.

title: No Duty to Pay Interest on a Security Deposit
bodyText: Nebraska imposes no duty to hold a security deposit in an interest-bearing account, to pay the tenant interest on it, or to keep it in a separate or escrow account. You may hold it with your own funds and keep any interest it earns. What Nebraska does regulate is the amount (one month's rent, plus up to one quarter of a month's rent as a pet deposit) and the return: a written itemized accounting and refund within fourteen days of demand after the tenancy ends, with a penalty for wrongful retention (§76-1416). If you operate in other states, do not carry this one across - deposit-interest duties are one of the most common state divergences in this area, and several states in this library do impose them.

title: How a Nebraska Eviction Runs - and the Second Statute Nobody Reads
bodyText: Nebraska has TWO possession procedures, and which one you are in matters. The landlord-tenant act's own route is an action for possession: you file a complaint for restitution of the premises (§§76-1440, 76-1441), the case is tried on a short statutory timetable, and on a judgment for you the court issues a writ of restitution (§76-1446), with appeal governed by §76-1447. Separately, Nebraska's older forcible entry and detainer statutes, §§25-21,219 to 25-21,235, supply a parallel route with their own jurisdiction, notice-to-leave, trial, restitution and appeal-bond mechanics, and §25-21,220 says expressly that those provisions are not exclusive. Three things to keep straight. First, you cannot take possession yourself: self-help lockouts, removals and service shutoffs give the tenant remedies under §76-1430, and §76-1436 limits recovery of possession to the statutory process. Second, the tenant can turn the nonpayment case into a money fight - in an action for possession based on nonpayment, or an action for rent where the tenant is still in possession, the tenant may counterclaim for anything recoverable under the lease or the Act, and the court may order rent paid into court and net the two sides off (§76-1428). If no rent remains due after that netting, judgment on possession goes to the TENANT. Third, that cuts your way too: if the tenant's defense or counterclaim is without merit and not raised in good faith, you may recover reasonable attorney's fees (§76-1428(1)).
notes: NE: Read section-open 2026-09-27 from nebraskalegislature.gov (official legislative compilation) in the built-in browser, via the official keyword search at /laws/search_keyword.php. Gap-discovery backfill, instruction 36 sources 3 and 4. CONTROLLING TEXT: Neb. Rev. Stat. §76-1428 read verbatim section-open, both subsections -- the counterclaim, pay-into-court and netting mechanics and the bad-faith attorney-fee award are all quoted from it. The Chapter 25 forcible entry and detainer sections are identified by section number and title from the official search (§§25-21,219 jurisdiction, 25-21,220 against whom / not exclusive, 25-21,221 notice to leave, 25-21,226 trial and judgment, 25-21,230 writ of execution form, 25-21,234 and 25-21,235 appeal and supersedeas) and were NOT read in full today. The 'not exclusive' statement rests on §25-21,220's title, which is a title-level claim and is flagged as such -- the row says the route exists and is parallel, and deliberately states no Chapter 25 notice period or bond figure, because those were not read. §§76-1440, 76-1441, 76-1446, 76-1430 and 76-1436 are carried from the original NE pass. *** WHY THIS ROW EXISTS: Nebraska had no eviction-procedure row at all, while SD, TX, FL and AZ each have one, and §76-1428 was cited NOWHERE in the library -- it is one of the two sections (with §76-1429) that the NE citation inventory skipped between 76-1427 and 76-1430. *** THE §76-1428 FEE AWARD IS A LANDLORD-FAVOURABLE OMISSION, not just a gap: edu-statutory-attorney-fee-actions-ne told Nebraska landlords which statutory fee awards exist and did not list this one. That row is amended today to add it. This row is a map, not a procedure manual, and says so by omission.

title: Things Nebraska Has No Statute For - Checked Across the Whole Code
bodyText: Seven things landlords ask about that Nebraska has no statute on anywhere in its code, not merely nothing in the landlord-tenant act. (1) NO TENANT PROTECTION ON FORECLOSURE: Nebraska has no statute requiring notice to tenants of a pending foreclosure and none giving a tenant the right to stay after a foreclosure sale. The federal Protecting Tenants at Foreclosure Act is what governs, and it is federal law that does not depend on Nebraska adopting anything. (2) NO CASH-RENT RECEIPT DUTY: nothing requires you to give a written receipt for rent paid in cash. Give one anyway - it is your proof of payment as much as theirs. (3) NO HOLDING-DEPOSIT RULES: nothing regulates a pre-lease holding or reservation deposit, what it may be used for, or whether it is refundable if the applicant backs out. Your written agreement is the only thing governing it, so put the terms in writing. (4) NO STATE RENTAL REGISTRATION OR LICENCE: there is no statewide rental registry or landlord licence. Omaha and Lincoln run their own programmes and are not resolved here. (5) NO SQUATTER-SPECIFIC REMEDY: Nebraska has no separate unauthorized-occupant or squatter-removal statute; an occupant with no right to be there is removed through the ordinary possession and forcible-entry routes. (6) NO MOLD RULES: no mold disclosure duty, no remediation standard, no mold-specific habitability provision. (7) NO TYPOGRAPHY REQUIREMENTS: no Nebraska statute makes any residential lease term depend on being bold, underlined, capitalised, in a minimum type size, or in a separate document. Nothing in your lease is void for how it is formatted.

Quoting does not force a phrase ('"convenience fee"' returned MORE results than the bare terms), and multi-word input is matched loosely across the words, so 'holding deposit' returned 58 banking-deposit sections and 'application fee' 648. A nonsense control term ('zzzqqqxyzzy') returned 0, so a 0-hit result IS meaningful. Method therefore used the most DISTINCTIVE SINGLE WORD per topic and reviewed every hit across all result pages (pagination is the 'start' POST parameter; 25 per page). Absences below are statutes-only: the Nebraska Administrative Code, municipal codes and case law were not searched. CONFIRMED ABSENT x7, STATUTE-WIDE, each with the terms run. (1) FORECLOSURE: 'foreclosure tenant' (11 results, all reviewed: §§25-202, 25-1104, 25-328, 76-238, 76-301, 77-203, 40-101, 71-15,113, 25-1533, 36-105 -- none a tenant protection). The statute-wide 'landlord' sweep returned no foreclosure section. Several other states in this library DO have one (NV, CA, MN, NJ, FL, AZ), so this is a real divergence, not an untested guess. The PTFA reference is general knowledge, NOT read from primary source -- flagged per instruction 16 as federal and outside any state bill-tracking watch. (4) RENTAL REGISTRATION: 'rental registration' (17 results, all tax, vehicle and gaming). Omaha and Lincoln programmes flagged, not resolved, per instruction 20. (5) SQUATTER: 'unauthorized occupant' (1 result, §25-21,277, diversion of utility services -- not a removal remedy). (6) MOLD: 'mold' (6 results: §§79-10,110, 79-10,110.02, 77-2701.47, 44-5004, 2-3991, 2-2624 -- school health-and-safety levies, manufacturing equipment, health insurance and dairy packaging), 'mildew' (1, §2-2624), 'fungus' (6, all pesticide, nail-technology and plant-pest definitions). This is the cleanest absence in the set. (7) TYPOGRAPHY (instruction 28): 'underlined' (3 results: §§21-214, 25-2602.02, 45-808 -- co-operative definitions, an arbitration-contract statement and a consumer contract; none landlord-tenant), 'boldface' (25 results, all reviewed -- the Chapter 76 hits are §76-2110 condominium and time-share disclosure, §§76-2719, 76-2720, 76-2722 equity-purchase contracts, §76-2713 foreclosure consulting and §76-3112 private transfer fees, none of which reaches a residential lease), 'conspicuous' and 'separate writing' (143 and 123 results; no §76-14xx hit on the pages reviewed). The Nebraska Administrative Code, municipal codes and case law were NOT searched, so each item above is 'no Nebraska STATUTE', which is what the row claims and no more.

title: Steam Radiator Cover Notice
bodyText: [BUILDER: attach as a rider to the lease wherever the unit has steam radiators; Landlord must also give this notice in writing at least once a year and post it in the common area where tenant notices are posted.] Steam Radiator Covers. Tenant may ask Landlord in writing to cover each steam radiator in Tenant's unit with an insulating material or cover that protects tenants, occupants and others from burns caused by contact with the radiator. Landlord will install the covers within 90 days after receiving Tenant's written request.
notes: NJ: Gap-discovery backfill 2026-09-27 (instruction 36). Source 2 (real-lease comparison) lead: NJ Realtors Form 125-10/2022 carries a steam-radiator rider. Verified against the chapter law on the Legislature's site: P.L.2021, c.259 (approved 2021-11-08; effective the first day of the third month after enactment), codified N.J.S.A. 52:27D-198.20. 1.a: within 90 days of a tenant's written request, 'an owner of a residential rental property shall cover each steam radiator in the tenant's unit' with insulating material or a cover protecting against burns. 1.b: owner must notify tenants of the right to request covers 'as a rider to any written residential lease agreement and in writing at least annually', and post in common areas where tenant notices are displayed. 1.c: fine up to $500 by the enforcing agency; 1.d: injured tenant, occupant or other person has a private action. The act does not define 'residential rental property' (so no unit-count threshold stated) - builder should include this rider for any unit with steam radiators. No prescribed wording; body tracks the statute. Relation to case law: J.H. v. R&M Tagliareni, LLC (N.J. 2019) held no landlord duty where the tenant controlled the radiator heat - the statute now imposes the duty on request. LAYOUT: lease RIDER (instruction 28); annual written notice and common-area posting are outside the lease. CONDITIONAL on steam radiators.

title: Private Well Water Test Results
bodyText: The property's drinking water comes from a private well. Tenant acknowledges receiving a written copy of the most recent water test results for the property under the New Jersey Private Well Testing Act. Landlord will have the water tested at least once every five years as the Act requires, and will give Tenant a written copy of each new test result within 30 days after Landlord receives it.
notes: NJ: Gap-discovery backfill 2026-09-27 (instruction 36). Source 2 lead: NJ Realtors Form 125-10/2022 §42 (Private Well Testing). Controlling text read on the FindLaw host copy (current as of 2024-01-01; not compared with the official site): N.J.S.A. 58:12A-32 (Private Well Testing Act, N.J.S.A. 58:12A-26 to -37): a lessor of property whose potable water supply is a private well must test within 18 months after 2002-09-14 and at least once every five years thereafter; give a written copy of results to each rental unit within 30 days after receipt; give a new lessee a written copy of the most recent results; seasonal rentals may instead post the results inside the unit. Test parameters, certified-lab requirement and penalties are elsewhere in the Act (not read). CONDITIONAL on a private-well water supply. Lease text is an acknowledgment plus the ongoing duty; the duty exists regardless of the lease.

title: Fire and Other Casualty
bodyText: If the property is damaged by fire without the fault of Tenant, Landlord will repair it as quickly as possible, and Rent will stop until the property has been fully repaired. If the building is totally destroyed by fire or otherwise without the fault of Tenant, Rent will be paid up to the date of destruction, and this Lease will then end.
notes: NJ: Gap-discovery backfill 2026-09-27 (instruction 36). Source 2 lead: NJ Realtors Form 125-10/2022 §21 (Fire and Other Casualty). NJ had no casualty row. Controlling text read section-open 2026-09-26 (official N.J.S.A. text pasted by Taylor): N.J.S.A. 46:8-6 (fire injury without lessee's fault: landlord repairs 'as speedily as possible'; in default of repair 'the rent shall cease' until complete repair) and 46:8-7 (total destruction 'by fire or otherwise' without lessee's fault: rent paid to the time of destruction, then the lease ends). Both apply only where the lease does not 'otherwise stipulate', so this clause restates the statutory defaults rather than varying them - a deliberate choice (tenant-neutral; no waiver risk under N.J.S.A. 46:8-48). Form 125 departs from the defaults (90-day repair window / cancellation); not adopted. Partial-destruction-by-other-casualty (non-fire) is not addressed by either section; the clause is silent on it. Checklist row 63 already cited these sections without a row.

title: Owners Must Carry Liability Insurance
bodyText: New Jersey requires the owner of a rental unit to carry liability insurance of at least $500,000 for combined property damage and bodily injury, or at least $300,000 for an owner-occupied multifamily home of four or fewer units. Owners must register the certificate of insurance with the municipality each year. A municipality can fine a noncompliant owner $500 to $5,000.
notes: NJ: Gap-discovery backfill 2026-09-27 (instruction 36). Source 2 lead: NJ Realtors Form 125-10/2022 §22 cites the insurance minimums. Verified against the chapter law on the Legislature's site: P.L.2022, c.92 (signed 2022-08-05), codified N.J.S.A. 40A:10A-1 (coverage: $500,000; $300,000 for owner-occupied multifamily of four or fewer units) and 40A:10A-2 (annual registration of the certificate with the municipality; fine $500-$5,000 by summary proceeding). Effective: 90 days (new policies) / 180 days (renewals and the multifamily provision) after enactment; DCA Local Finance Notice 2022-23 gives 2022-11-03 and 2023-02-01. The chapter law states no definition of 'rental unit' (per the fetched text). Not lease content; no clause. Outside the landlord-tenant title (gap-discovery source 4 shape).

title: Towing From Rental Property
bodyText: A New Jersey landlord cannot simply have a tenant's or visitor's car towed because the lease allows it. A tow without the vehicle owner's consent is lawful only if the landlord has a private-property towing contract with the tow company, has authorized removal of that particular vehicle, and the car goes to secure storage within a reasonable distance. Most properties must also post a sign at least 36 by 36 inches at every vehicle entrance stating when parking is allowed, that violators will be towed at the owner's expense, and the tow company's name, contact details, charges and storage address.
notes: NJ: Gap-discovery backfill 2026-09-27 (instruction 36). Source 3 (scenario screen) gap: 'car towed from the lot' - parking-vehicle-rules defers to law (NJ note added 2026-09-26); an education row makes the preconditions visible, as AZ did (edu-towing-az). Controlling text read 2026-09-26 on the Justia host copy (history lines checked): Predatory Towing Prevention Act, N.J.S.A. 56:13-7 et seq. (L.2007, c.193); 56:13-13 (amended 2017, c.321): contract, 36x36-inch sign content at all vehicular entrances, per-vehicle owner authorization, secure storage within a reasonable distance; the host summary reports the signage requirement does not apply to single-family units or owner-occupied structures of six or fewer units (not read verbatim - body says 'most properties'); 56:13-16 (amended 2023, c.132): no patrol/surveillance towing without the owner's specific request; release of a hooked-but-unmoved vehicle; notice to owner, lessor and lienholder within 30 days.

title: Occupancy by Children
bodyText: Children who are members of Tenant's household may live at the property. Each child who will live at the property is to be listed with the other occupants under this Lease's occupancy terms. Landlord places no restriction on occupancy by children other than those occupancy terms, which apply to every occupant regardless of age. [If the property is housing for older persons that qualifies for the fair-housing exemption for such housing, replace this Section with a statement of the property's age requirements for occupancy.]
notes: NV: NRS 118A.200(3)(c), Section-open read of revisor text on leg.state.nv.us in Taylor's browser 2026-09-27 (compilation Rev. 4/15/2026, 2025 session incorporated; section history line checked): every written rental agreement must contain provisions relating to "occupancy by children or pets"; 118A.200(9) makes a nonconforming agreement unlawful to use and a contravening provision void. pet-policy-nv covers pets; no NV row covered children until this pass. Surfaced by gap-discovery source 2 (NV log backfill section, Part 1): the GLVAR lease's occupant clause is silent on children too, and mapping it against the (3) list exposed the gap. 118A.200(5)(a) presumes no restriction on children absent a written agreement. Familial status is a protected class (NRS 118.100, edu-fair-housing-nv), so the clause states no child-specific limit; neutral occupancy limits stay in permitted-occupants. BUILDER: offer the age-restricted-housing bracket only on the landlord's say-so; the federal and state exemption texts for housing for older persons were not read. (3)(c) text is unchanged by AB 121 and SB 201 (2025) per the session-law check recorded on edu-lease-content-requirements-nv; effective_from blank (long-standing).

title: Required Fees
bodyText: In addition to the Monthly Rent and any deposit stated in this Lease, Tenant is required to pay the following fees, for the purposes stated: [list each required fee - its amount, when it is due and the purpose for which it is required, e.g. "a nonrefundable cleaning charge of $___, due at signing, to pay for cleaning the premises after Tenant vacates" - or state "None"]. Any required fee that is payable every rental period is included in the Monthly Rent and is not charged in addition to it, except a utility fee that this Lease identifies with the Monthly Rent as the law allows. No charge applies to a late or partial payment of Rent, or to a dishonored check or other returned payment, except a late fee or returned-payment charge stated in this Lease.
notes: NV: NRS 118A.200(3)(e) and (3)(g), Section-open read of revisor text on leg.state.nv.us in Taylor's browser 2026-09-27 (compilation Rev. 4/15/2026, 2025 session incorporated; section history line checked): the lease must contain provisions relating to "fees which are required and the purposes for which they are required" and "charges which may be required for late or partial payment of rent or for return of any dishonored check". Before this row no NV clause listed required fees with their purposes, and late-fee-nv and returned-payments-nv are optional rows, so a lease without them said nothing on (3)(g). The last sentence closes (3)(g) whether or not those rows are used, and covers partial payments, which no NV row mentioned (118A.200(5)(c)'s no-charge presumption applies only where there is no written agreement). Periodic fees: 118A.200(6)-(8) (rent-single-figure-nv). BUILDER: a payment whose purpose is to remedy a rent default, repair damage or clean is a security deposit whatever it is called (118A.240). It counts toward the three-month cap (security-deposit-cap-nv) and must be refundable, except a reasonable nonrefundable cleaning charge (118A.242(8)). Don't let a user list a "nonrefundable pet fee" or "damage fee" here. This row gives security-deposit-return-nv's "nonrefundable cleaning charge ... stated in this Lease" a place in the lease. Surfaced by gap-discovery source 2: the GLVAR lease's summary-of-monies section lists each fee by name, the library had no counterpart. (3)(e) and (3)(g) are unchanged by the 2025 bills per the session-law check on edu-lease-content-requirements-nv; effective_from blank (long-standing).

title: Tenant-Performed Repairs and Maintenance
bodyText: [Optional. Include only if Landlord and Tenant agree that Tenant will perform specified tasks.] Tenant agrees to perform the following specified repairs, maintenance tasks or minor remodeling: [list each task specifically, e.g. replace heating and air-conditioning filters every [number] months with filters Landlord provides; replace light bulbs; keep the pool clean and its water balanced]. Landlord and Tenant make this agreement in good faith. Tenant is not entering into it because Landlord or Landlord's agent refused to perform any repair, maintenance task or remodeling that Landlord is required by law to perform, and it does not reduce Landlord's obligations to any other tenant. Landlord remains responsible for keeping the property habitable as applicable law requires, and nothing in this Section requires Tenant to pay any fee or charge for work that is Landlord's duty, except work needed because of a condition caused by the deliberate or negligent act or omission of Tenant, a member of Tenant's household, or another person on the premises with Tenant's consent.
notes: NV: NRS 118A.290(2)-(5), Section-open read of revisor text on leg.state.nv.us in Taylor's browser 2026-09-27 (compilation Rev. 4/15/2026, 2025 session incorporated; section history line checked) (A. 1999, 2007, 2023). (2): landlord and tenant "may agree that the tenant is to perform specified repairs, maintenance tasks and minor remodeling only if" the agreement is in good faith and does not diminish the landlord's obligations to other tenants. (3): not in good faith if the landlord owes the work under (1) and the tenant agrees because the landlord refused it. (4): no fee or charge for work that is the landlord's (1) duty (the 2023 home-warranty deductible ban, edu-habitability-duty-nv). (5): charges allowed for tenant-caused conditions. OPT-IN LANDLORD RIGHT (instruction 30): without a written list the tasks stay with the landlord. The recital cannot make the agreement good faith; it records the facts the statute tests. Drafted conservatively: tasks are listed specifically, habitability stays with Landlord, and there is no charge for landlord-duty work. Whether (2) lets a (1) repair itself be shifted is not settled by the text and is not relied on. Surfaced by gap-discovery source 2: the GLVAR lease's maintenance section assigns minor repairs, filters, yard and pool care to the tenant. landscaping-irrigation and snow-removal already allocate those tasks; the builder should not list them twice. Not shareable with tenant-repair-agreement-tx (TX's bold/underline and cost-shifting rules).

title: Designated Repairer for Tenant Repairs
bodyText: [Optional. Include only if Landlord wants to designate who performs this work.] If applicable law permits Tenant to have work done at Landlord's expense because Landlord failed to make a repair or to supply an essential service after notice, that work must be performed by [name the person or firm, or describe a class of persons or firms qualified to do the work, e.g. "a contractor holding a Nevada license for that type of work"], and Tenant will comply with this specification. This Section does not otherwise limit any remedy applicable law gives Tenant.

title: Political Signs in HOA and Condo Communities
bodyText: If the rental is in a common-interest community (a homeowners' or condominium association), the association may not prohibit a unit's owner or an occupant - which includes your tenant - from displaying political signs in the part of the property the owner or occupant has the right to use exclusively. Protected signs are those supporting or opposing a candidate, political party or ballot question in a federal, state, local or association election. Each may be no larger than 24 by 36 inches, only one sign per candidate, party or ballot question is protected, and signs must follow any law on posting political signs. While a tenant occupies the unit, you as the owner may not display a political sign there unless the tenant consents in writing. The rule binds the association and its governing documents; it does not address what your lease may say about signs.

title: Removing a Squatter or Unauthorized Occupant
bodyText: A person who enters your property without the authority of you, your representative or your tenant and does not leave after a written notice to surrender is guilty of forcible detainer, as is anyone who holds possession by force or threats. For a squatter there is a fast court process. Serve a written notice to surrender the way eviction notices are served. It must name the court and tell the occupant: that they may contest by filing an affidavit before the court closes on the fourth judicial day after service; that the court may order the sheriff or constable to remove them within 24 hours; and that property left behind will be stored safely and may be disposed of after 14 calendar days, with inventory, moving and storage costs payable before release. When the notice expires, file an affidavit of complaint with a copy of the notice and proof of service. If the occupant did not contest, or the contest raises no legal defense, the court must order removal within 24 hours; if it raises a defense, a hearing is held within 7 judicial days. An occupant who entered peaceably under an invalid lease or someone else's fraud may be given up to 20 days to leave. Keep property left behind in safe storage for 21 days after the removal or surrender before disposing of it: the notice says 14 days, but the removal section separately requires 21 days' storage. Vehicles go through the abandoned-vehicle law. If every unauthorized adult occupant has been arrested for housebreaking or unlawful occupancy, you may instead retake possession and change the locks, posting a notice with the court and contest details for at least 21 days and filing a copy with the court within 1 day. You may recover three times your actual damage to real and personal property from a person guilty of forcible entry or forcible detainer. Your tenant, as an occupant you authorized, may use the same process. For a tenant or former tenant, use the eviction procedures for tenants instead.
notes: NV: NRS 40.230, 40.240, 40.412 and 40.414, Section-open read of revisor text on leg.state.nv.us in Taylor's browser 2026-09-27 (compilation Rev. 4/15/2026, 2025 session incorporated; section history line checked) (40.230 and 40.240 A. 2015; 40.412 and 40.414 added 2015, no later amendment). 40.414 was supplied by Taylor in text batch 2, but no row cited it. The body tells landlords to wait 21 days. GUESTS: 40.240(1)(b) reaches only a person who entered WITHOUT authority. A guest who came in with the tenant's permission fits (1)(a) only if holding "by force or threats of violence", so the body does not promise this process for an ordinary overstaying guest. 40.412(4): the lock-change route is unavailable if any unauthorized occupant is still in the dwelling. title: Lease Translation When You Advertise in Another Language
bodyText: If, in your business, you advertise a rental in a language other than English and negotiate the lease in that language - orally or in writing, yourself or through an employee or agent - you must give a translation of the lease in that language to the tenant, and to anyone else who may sign it, before it is signed. This applies to a lease or rental agreement of at least one month for a dwelling used as a residence. The translation must include every term and condition; names, addresses, numbers, dollar amounts, dates and words with no accepted translation may stay in English. A later document that substantially changes the parties' rights needs a translation too; routine house rules and furniture inventories do not. If you don't comply, the tenant may cancel (rescind) the lease, and a knowing violation is a deceptive trade practice.
notes: NV: NRS 598.9731-598.9739 and 598.09227, Section-open read of revisor text on leg.state.nv.us in Taylor's browser 2026-09-27 (compilation Rev. 4/15/2026, 2025 session incorporated; section history line checked). (3)(b): "a lease, sublease, rental contract or agreement or other contract or agreement containing a term of tenancy" of at least 1 month for a dwelling, apartment, mobile home or other dwelling unit used as a residence. title: Repair Orders and Receivership for Multifamily Rentals
bodyText: If you rent out two or more units on one parcel, your county (outside cities) or city must act when it finds that the property violates a habitability standard, a housing or building code, or a habitability, building-safety or fire-safety law badly enough to substantially endanger the health and safety of residents or the public. It must order you to repair, rehabilitate or abate the condition by a deadline. The notice and order is posted on the property and sent by certified mail to you and each affected resident, and it states that you may not retaliate against any tenant. If you don't comply, the county or city can sue to have the property declared substandard and obtain a repair order and civil penalties, and the local government or a nonprofit representing tenants can ask the court to appoint a receiver after 30 days' posted and mailed notice. Once a receiver is appointed you may not collect rent, interfere with the receiver, or encumber or transfer the property; the receiver collects the rents, makes the repairs and may borrow against the property. The court will order you to pay the local government's costs and attorney's fees. If tenants cannot safely stay, it will also order moving costs and up to 120 days of rent differential as relocation benefits, plus a first right to return; a tenant who caused the conditions gets no relocation benefits.

title: Health District Rules for Rental Units
bodyText: In a county served by a district board of health, the board may adopt and enforce regulations on health hazards in rental dwelling units - any biological, physical or chemical exposure, condition or public nuisance that may harm health - and recover its enforcement costs. If it has adopted regulations on the condition of rental units, you must give a copy to a tenant who asks for one. A tenant who gave you written notice of a habitability failure that you did not fix, or reasonably try to fix, within the statutory time may send a copy of that notice to the district board of health. If an inspection finds that you or the tenant failed to keep the unit habitable, the board may take enforcement action or refer the matter to its administrative hearing process.
